61545.q: Which coastal area of Tuscany was for a long time a marshland full of malaria and was then drained?
61545.e: Because of malaria, few people lived in the Maremma. Drainage in the 19th and 20th centuries turned it into farmland.
61545.m: The Maremma changed from marsh to farmland.

61546.q: Which small Tuscan town is known for its medieval tower houses?
61546.e: In the Middle Ages, rich families built residential towers as high as possible as a sign of their power. Of around 70 towers, about 15 still survive in San Gimignano today.
61546.m: San Gimignano is the town of tower houses.

61547.q: Which bridge has connected the north-west of the Peloponnese to the mainland since 2004?
61547.e: The cable-stayed bridge over the Gulf of Corinth is about 2.9 km long. It was opened shortly before the 2004 Olympic Games.
61547.m: The Rio-Antirrio Bridge spans the Gulf of Corinth.

61548.q: Which mountain range rises between Sparta and Kalamata?
61548.e: At over 2400 m, the Taygetus is the highest mountain range in the Peloponnese. It separates Laconia from Messenia and stretches far to the south.
61548.m: The Taygetus is the highest mountain range of the Peloponnese.

61549.q: Which canal has separated the Peloponnese from the rest of the Greek mainland since 1893?
61549.e: The Corinth Canal, about 6 kilometres long, cuts through the narrow isthmus between the Aegean and the Ionian Sea. Strictly speaking, the Peloponnese has been an island ever since.
61549.m: The Corinth Canal separates the Peloponnese from the mainland.

61550.q: Which ancient city in the Peloponnese was famous for its tough upbringing and its warriors?
61550.e: In Sparta, boys from the age of seven were raised as warriors in strict groups. To this day, “spartan” means simple and harsh.
61550.m: Sparta was known for its strict warrior training.

61551.q: Which Bronze Age citadel in the Peloponnese is known for its Lion Gate?
61551.e: Mycenae was the centre of the culture named after it. The Lion Gate from the 13th century BC is its landmark.
61551.m: The Lion Gate is the landmark of Mycenae.

61552.q: Which late Byzantine ruined city near Sparta is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
61552.e: In the 14th and 15th centuries Mystras was a cultural centre of Byzantium. Churches with frescoes and palaces climb up a hillside.
61552.m: Mystras is a Byzantine ruined city near Sparta.

61553.q: Which barren peninsula in the south of the Peloponnese is known for its tower houses and old family feuds?
61553.e: The people of the Mani built fortified stone towers and stayed largely independent for a long time. Blood feuds were common there until the 19th century.
61553.m: The Mani is the land of tower houses.

61554.q: Which city is the largest in the Peloponnese and an important ferry port for Italy?
61554.e: Patras lies in the north-west on the gulf of the same name. Ferries sail from here to Ancona, Bari and Venice.
61554.m: Patras is the largest city of the Peloponnese.

61555.q: Which naval battle off the Peloponnese in 1827 helped decide the Greek struggle for independence?
61555.e: In the Bay of Navarino near Pylos, a British, French and Russian fleet destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet. This paved the way for Greek independence.
61555.m: The Battle of Navarino helped Greece to independence.

61556.q: Which event in July 1974 led to the division of Cyprus?
a: A coup by Greek nationalists and the Turkish military intervention
The Republic of Cyprus joining the EU
61556.e: The military junta in Athens backed a coup aimed at union with Greece. Turkey then intervened militarily and has occupied the north ever since.
61556.m: Since 1974 Cyprus has in effect been divided.

61557.q: Which country is the only one to recognise the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, declared in 1983?
61557.e: The UN Security Council declared the 1983 declaration invalid. Internationally, the north is regarded as part of the Republic of Cyprus.
61557.m: Only Turkey recognises Northern Cyprus as a state.

61558.q: How did the communities vote on the Annan Plan for reunification in 2004?
a: The Greek Cypriots rejected it, the Turkish Cypriots approved it
The Turkish Cypriots rejected it, the Greek Cypriots approved it
61558.e: About 76 per cent of Greek Cypriots rejected the UN plan, while about 65 per cent of Turkish Cypriots approved it. As both had to agree, it failed.
61558.m: The Annan Plan failed in 2004 because the Greek Cypriots voted no.

61559.q: What does the term “Enosis” mean in the history of Cyprus?
61559.e: In the 20th century many Greek Cypriots demanded enosis, meaning union with Greece. Turkish Cypriots countered with the demand for partition (taksim).
61559.m: Enosis means the union of Cyprus with Greece.

61560.q: Which areas of Cyprus still belong to the United Kingdom today?
a: The military bases of Akrotiri and Dhekelia
61560.e: At independence in 1960, Britain kept two military bases as sovereign areas. They lie in the south of the island.
61560.m: Akrotiri and Dhekelia are British military bases on Cyprus.

61561.q: Since Cyprus joined the EU in 2004, what applies to the north of the island?
a: It is a separate EU member
It is part of the Schengen Area
It has used the euro ever since
61561.e: Legally, the whole island joined the EU. Because the government does not control the north, EU law is suspended there.
61561.m: EU law does not apply in northern Cyprus for now.

61562.q: Which ghost town near Famagusta has been a closed military zone since 1974?
61562.e: The hotel district of Varosha was abandoned in a rush in 1974 and sealed off. Since 2020, parts of it have been open to visitors again, which has been criticised internationally.
61562.m: Varosha is the ghost town of Famagusta.

61563.q: What has divided the capital Nicosia into a northern and a southern part since 1974?
a: A buffer zone monitored by the UN
61563.e: The buffer zone, also called the Green Line, is monitored by UN troops. Since 2008 it has been possible to cross it on foot in Ledra Street, a shopping street.
61563.m: Nicosia is divided by the UN buffer zone.

61564.q: Which three countries became guarantor powers for the order of the Republic of Cyprus in 1960?
61564.e: The Treaty of Guarantee was meant to secure the constitution and independence of Cyprus. Turkey justified its intervention in 1974 with this treaty.
61564.m: Greece, Turkey and Britain are the guarantor powers of Cyprus.

61565.q: In which city was Albania’s independence declared in 1912?
61565.e: Ismail Qemali proclaimed independence on 28 November 1912 in the port city of Vlorë. Tirana only became the capital in 1920.
61565.m: Albania became independent in Vlorë in 1912.

61566.q: What triggered serious unrest in Albania in 1997?
a: The death of the head of state
61566.e: Many Albanians had put their savings into fraudulent pyramid schemes. Their collapse led to uprisings and the breakdown of state order.
61566.m: In 1997 pyramid schemes plunged Albania into crisis.

61567.q: Which river in Albania was protected in 2023 as one of Europe’s first wild river national parks?
61567.e: The Vjosa flows for a long stretch without any dams. The national park is meant to keep it as a free-flowing river.
61567.m: The Vjosa is a protected wild river in Albania.

61568.q: Since which year has Albania been a member of NATO?
61568.e: Albania joined NATO on 1 April 2009 together with Croatia. Before that, it had cut itself off from all alliances for decades.
61568.m: Albania has been in NATO since 2009.

61569.q: What is Albania’s status in relation to the EU (as of 2025)?
a: It is a candidate country negotiating membership
It has been an EU member since 2004
Like Norway, it is only in the EEA
It rejected membership in a referendum
61569.e: The European Council granted Albania candidate status in 2014. Accession negotiations were formally opened in 2022.
61569.m: Albania is an EU candidate country.

61570.q: Which language family does Albanian belong to?
a: To the Indo-European languages, as its own branch
To the Slavic languages, like Serbian
To the Romance languages, like Italian
To the Turkic languages, like Turkish
61570.e: Albanian is an Indo-European language but forms its own branch with no close relatives. There are two main dialects, Gheg in the north and Tosk in the south.
61570.m: Albanian is a separate branch of the Indo-European languages.

61571.q: What mostly shapes the landscape of Albania?
a: Mountains, with a narrow coastal plain
Bogs and lakes as in Finland
61571.e: A large part of Albania is mountainous. The highest mountain is Korab on the border with North Macedonia, at about 2760 m above sea level. The flat land is mainly along the Adriatic coast.
61571.m: Albania is a mountainous country with a narrow coastal plain.

61572.q: Which Roman long-distance road began on the Albanian coast at Dyrrachium, today’s Durrës?
61572.e: The Via Egnatia led across the Balkans to Byzantium. It extended the Via Appia, which ended at Brindisi on the other side of the Adriatic.
61572.m: The Via Egnatia began at Durrës.

61573.q: To which Italian port did the freighter “Vlora” bring about 20,000 Albanian refugees in August 1991?
61573.e: After the end of the dictatorship, many Albanians fled across the Adriatic. Pictures of the hopelessly overcrowded ship went around the world; most were sent back.
61573.m: In 1991 tens of thousands of Albanians reached Bari by ship.

61574.q: When did Croatia join the European Union?
61574.e: Croatia became the 28th member of the EU on 1 July 2013. After Slovenia, it was the second successor state of Yugoslavia in the Union.
61574.m: Croatia has been in the EU since 2013.

61575.q: Which Roman emperor had a palace built in Split that now forms the old town?
61575.e: Diocletian retired to his palace on the Adriatic around 305. Later, the inhabitants built their houses into its walls.
61575.m: Split’s old town lies inside Diocletian’s Palace.

61576.q: When did Croatia declare its independence from Yugoslavia?
61576.e: On 25 June 1991 Croatia declared itself independent. A war followed that lasted until 1995.

61577.q: Which largest peninsula in the Adriatic does Croatia share with Slovenia and Italy?
61577.e: Most of Istria belongs to Croatia, a small part to Slovenia and a tiny tip to Italy. Well-known places are Pula and Rovinj.
61577.m: Istria is the largest peninsula in the Adriatic.

61578.q: Which national park near Šibenik is known for the travertine falls of Skradinski buk?
61578.e: The River Krka flows through a karst gorge and forms several waterfalls. At Skradinski buk the water tumbles down over many steps.
61578.m: Krka National Park lies near Šibenik.

61579.q: Which town on the Danube became a symbol of the Croatian War after a siege lasting months in 1991?
61579.e: Vukovar was almost completely destroyed by the Yugoslav People’s Army and Serbian units. After the town fell, war crimes were committed.
61579.m: Vukovar is a symbol of the Croatian War.

61580.q: Which item of clothing owes its name to Croatian soldiers in the 17th century?
61580.e: Croatian horsemen serving France wore knotted neckcloths. The French named these “cravate” after them.
61580.m: The cravat is named after the Croats.

61581.q: Which old Slavic script was used in Croatia for church texts into modern times?
61581.e: The Glagolitic script goes back to Cyril and Methodius, the apostles to the Slavs. It survived particularly long in Croatia, for example on the Baška tablet.
61581.m: Croatia kept the Glagolitic script particularly long.

61582.q: Which river delta in southern Croatia is known for growing mandarins?
61582.e: The mouth of the Neretva was drained in the 19th and 20th centuries. Today citrus fruit grows there, especially mandarins.
61582.m: Mandarins grow in the Neretva Delta.

61583.q: Which group of islands in the Aegean was under Italian rule from 1912 to 1947?
61583.e: Italy occupied the Dodecanese in 1912 during its war against the Ottoman Empire. Only the peace treaty of 1947 gave the islands to Greece.
61583.m: The Dodecanese only became Greek after the Second World War.

61584.q: How was the caldera of Santorini formed?
a: By a huge volcanic eruption in the Bronze Age
61584.e: The Minoan eruption in the 2nd millennium BC made the magma chamber collapse. The sea filled the crater, and today’s island forms a ring around the caldera.
61584.m: Santorini is the rim of a collapsed volcano.

61585.q: Which largest island of the Dodecanese was the seat of the Knights of St John?
61585.e: The Knights of St John ruled Rhodes from 1309 to 1522. Their fortified old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
61585.m: Rhodes was the fortress of the Knights of St John.

61586.q: Which Aegean island became a focal point of refugee movements to Europe from 2015?
61586.e: Lesbos lies only a few kilometres off the Turkish coast. Hundreds of thousands of refugees reached the island in boats, and the Moria camp burned down in 2020.
61586.m: Lesbos lies close to the Turkish coast and became the arrival island for many refugees.

61587.q: Which treaty set the borders of the new Turkey in 1923, including for the Aegean islands?
61587.e: The Treaty of Lausanne replaced the Treaty of Sèvres, which was never carried out. The islands of Imbros (Gökçeada) and Tenedos off the Dardanelles went to Turkey; most other Aegean islands stayed Greek.
61587.m: The Treaty of Lausanne set Turkey’s borders in 1923, including in the Aegean.

61588.q: Which resin is produced only in the south of the island of Chios?
61588.e: The mastic shrub only gives a usable resin in southern Chios. The mastic villages were therefore wealthy for centuries.
61588.m: Mastic is the resin of Chios.

61589.q: On which Dodecanese island was the famous physician Hippocrates born?
61589.e: Hippocrates lived in the 5th century BC and is regarded as the father of medicine. Kos also has a sanctuary of Asclepius, the god of healing.
61589.m: Hippocrates came from the island of Kos.

61590.q: Which Aegean island is regarded as a “Blue Zone”, where a strikingly large number of people live to a very old age?
61590.e: On Ikaria, an above-average number of people live to over 90. Researchers suspect causes such as diet, exercise and close communities.
61590.m: On Ikaria many people live to a very old age.

61591.q: On which island in the northern Aegean was the goddess of victory found in 1863 that now stands in the Louvre?
61591.e: The Winged Victory of Samothrace once stood in a sanctuary on the island. Today it stands at the top of a great staircase in the Louvre.
61591.m: The Winged Victory of Samothrace comes from the island of Samothrace.

61592.q: Which EU member state lies geographically entirely in Asia?
61592.e: The island of Cyprus lies in the eastern Mediterranean off the coast of Anatolia and geographically belongs to Asia. Politically and culturally it is closely linked with Europe.
61592.m: Cyprus is geographically Asian and politically European.

61593.q: Which country in the South Caucasus is partly counted as part of Europe, depending on where the border is drawn?
61593.e: Depending on the definition, the border runs through the Caucasus or north of it. Georgia also sees itself politically as a European country and is an EU candidate.
61593.m: Georgia lies on the border between Europe and Asia.

61594.q: According to the common definition today, what forms the border between Europe and Asia in the north?
a: The Ural Mountains and the Ural River
The River Ob and the Altai Mountains
61594.e: The border usually runs along the eastern edge of the Ural Mountains and along the Ural River to the Caspian Sea. The Swedish officer Philip Johan von Strahlenberg suggested the Urals as the border in the 18th century.
61594.m: In the north the Ural Mountains and Ural River separate Europe from Asia.

61595.q: Roughly what share of Russia’s area lies in Europe?
61595.e: European Russia covers just under 4 million km² out of about 17 million km². Most of the country lies in Siberia and the Far East.
61595.m: Only about a quarter of Russia lies in Europe.

61596.q: Where does the majority of Russia’s population live?
a: In the European part west of the Urals
61596.e: About three quarters of the people in Russia live in the European part. Moscow and Saint Petersburg are also there.

61597.q: What is the European part of Turkey called?
61597.e: East Thrace lies west of the Bosporus and Dardanelles and borders Greece and Bulgaria. Edirne is an important city in this region.
61597.m: East Thrace is the European part of Turkey.

61598.q: Which strait lies on the border line if the border is drawn through the Kuma-Manych Depression and the Sea of Azov?
61598.e: In this definition, the border runs from the Caspian Sea through the lowland to the Sea of Azov. From there, the Strait of Kerch connects to the Black Sea.
61598.m: The Strait of Kerch connects the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.

61599.q: Which sea lies entirely within Turkish territory between two straits of the Europe-Asia border?
61599.e: The Sea of Marmara is a small inland sea. In the north-east and the south-west it is connected to the neighbouring seas by narrow straits.
61599.m: The Sea of Marmara lies entirely in Turkey.

61600.q: Which country in the South Caucasus has its capital right on the Caspian Sea and is partly counted as European?
61600.e: Baku lies on the Absheron Peninsula on the Caspian Sea. Depending on where the border is drawn, a small part of Azerbaijan north of the main Caucasus ridge lies in Europe.
61600.m: Azerbaijan, with Baku, lies on the Caspian Sea.

61601.q: What does the Italian word “Mezzogiorno” literally mean?
61601.e: At midday the sun is in the south. That is why Mezzogiorno also means the south of Italy.
61601.m: Mezzogiorno means midday and refers to southern Italy.

61602.q: Apart from the southern mainland, which regions are usually also part of the Mezzogiorno?
61602.e: The Mezzogiorno includes Abruzzo, Molise, Campania, Apulia, Basilicata and Calabria, as well as the large islands of Sicily and Sardinia.
61602.m: Sicily and Sardinia also belong to the Mezzogiorno.

61603.q: What is meant by the “Questione meridionale”?
a: The economic and social backwardness of the south since unification
The dispute over the status of Rome
The question of South Tyrolean autonomy
The conflict over the Adriatic border
61603.e: After unification in 1861, a big gap between north and south became clear. The debate about its causes and solutions is called the Southern Question.
61603.m: The Southern Question describes the gap between northern and southern Italy.

61604.q: Which state institution supported the development of southern Italy from 1950 into the 1980s?
61604.e: The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno financed roads, irrigation and industry. It was dissolved in 1984 because its effects fell short of expectations.
61604.m: The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno was meant to develop the south.

61605.q: What did critics call large, isolated industrial plants in the south that attracted hardly any suppliers?
61605.e: Examples are the steelworks in Taranto and chemical plants in Sicily. They created jobs but hardly triggered broad development.
61605.m: Isolated large industry in the south was mockingly called cathedrals in the desert.

61606.q: Which farming structure held back the development of the Mezzogiorno for a long time?
61606.e: A few large landowners owned a lot of land, which was farmed extensively by day labourers. The land reform of 1950 redistributed part of it.
61606.m: Latifundia shaped farming in the south.

61607.q: Which criminal organisation has its origins in Calabria?
61607.e: The ’Ndrangheta comes from Calabria and is now seen as one of the most powerful mafia organisations, including in the international cocaine trade.

61608.q: Which kingdom covered most of the Mezzogiorno until 1860/61?
61608.e: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, with its capital Naples, was conquered by Garibaldi’s Expedition of the Thousand and became part of the Kingdom of Italy.
61608.m: Before unification the south belonged to the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

61609.q: What effect did the economic situation in the Mezzogiorno have on the population in the 20th century?
a: Heavy emigration to northern Italy and abroad
City dwellers returning to the countryside
61609.e: Millions of people moved to Turin, Milan, the USA or Switzerland. In the 1950s and 1960s many southern Italians worked in Swiss factories and on building sites.
61609.m: Many people from the Mezzogiorno emigrated, including to Switzerland.

61610.q: Which organisation with roots in Naples and Campania is a typical example of organised crime in the south?
61610.e: The Camorra is not a single organisation but a network of clans in and around Naples. It is active in the waste business and drug trafficking, among other things.
61610.m: The Camorra is the clan network of Campania.

61611.q: In Alpine geology, what is meant by a “nappe”?
a: A slab of rock pushed far over other rocks
A horizontal layer of lake clay
A thin layer of soil over the bedrock
A solidified lava layer from a volcano
61611.e: Nappes are large packages of rock that were detached from their place of origin during mountain building and pushed many kilometres over other rocks.
61611.m: A nappe is a package of rock moved a long way.

61612.q: Which two continental plates or continental margins collided when the Alps were formed?
a: Europe and the North American Plate
The Indian and the Eurasian Plate
61612.e: The Alps were formed when the Adriatic (Apulian) Plate, a spur of Africa, collided with the European continental margin and the ocean in between disappeared.
61612.m: The Alps formed from the collision of Adria and Europe.

61613.q: What is the order of the major nappe systems in the Swiss Alps from bottom to top?
61613.e: At the bottom lie the nappes from the European shelf, above them those from the ocean area, and at the top the Austroalpine nappes that come from the Adriatic margin.
61613.m: The Austroalpine nappes lie at the top of the nappe stack.

61614.q: What is an isolated remnant of a nappe, cut off by erosion and lying on younger ground, called?
61614.e: A klippe is a detached remnant of a nappe that lies on other rocks like a foreign body.
61614.m: A klippe is an isolated remnant of a nappe.

a: A place where erosion has cut through the nappe and deeper units can be seen
A cave formed by limestone dissolving
A gap in a glacial moraine
A natural rock arch in a ridge
61615.e: In a window the upper nappe has been worn away, so you look through it at the rocks below, for example in the Tauern Window in Austria.
61615.m: In a tectonic window you look through a nappe at deeper rocks.

61616.q: Which geologist from western Switzerland brought together the nappe structure of the Alps into a complete theory around 1902?
61616.e: The Lausanne geologist Maurice Lugeon presented a complete nappe theory of the Alps in 1902. Albert Heim accepted it in the same year.
61616.m: Maurice Lugeon founded the nappe theory of the Alps in 1902.

61617.q: Which line separates the Southern Alps from the rest of the Alps in Switzerland?
61617.e: The Insubric Line is part of the Periadriatic Seam. South of it lie the Southern Alps, which were hardly thrust northwards.
61617.m: The Insubric Line separates the Southern Alps from the main body of the Alps to the north.

61618.q: Which nappe unit forms the summit of the Matterhorn?
a: The Molasse of the Swiss Plateau
The granite of the Aar Massif
61618.e: The summit pyramid consists of gneisses of the Dent Blanche nappe, which comes from the Adriatic continental margin. That is why people speak of the “African” summit of the Matterhorn.
61618.m: The Matterhorn summit comes from the Adriatic continental margin.

61619.q: Which sequence of rocks typically formed in the sea in front of the growing Alps and was later overridden itself?
61619.e: Flysch consists of alternating layers of sandstone, marl and clay deposited in deep water in front of the advancing nappes.
61619.m: Flysch is a marine rock from the early phase of Alpine formation.

61620.q: Where were the rocks of the Helvetic zone originally deposited?
a: On the shelf at the southern edge of Europe
On the floor of a deep ocean
On the edge of the Adriatic Plate
In freshwater lakes of the Swiss Plateau
61620.e: The Helvetic sediments come from the shallow European continental shelf. Towards the south the layers become thicker and richer in limestone.
61620.m: The Helvetic zone comes from the European shelf.

61621.q: Where does the Helvetic zone get its name from?
a: From Helvetia, the Latin name for Switzerland
From the Helvetic Confession of the Reformed Church
61621.e: The system was first described in Switzerland and named after Helvetia. Many of its type localities are here.
61621.m: The Helvetic zone is named after Helvetia.

61622.q: Which type of rock mainly makes up the Helvetic nappes?
61622.e: The Helvetic nappes consist mainly of sedimentary rocks from the Jurassic, the Cretaceous and the early Tertiary, especially limestones and marls.
61622.m: Helvetic nappes consist mainly of limestone and marl.

61623.q: What happened to the Helvetic sediments during mountain building?
a: They were sheared off the crystalline basement and pushed north
They sank completely into the Earth’s mantle
They stayed flat and undisturbed in place
61623.e: The sediments came loose from their basement along soft layers and were thrust over as the northernmost part of the nappe stack.
61623.m: The Helvetic sediments were sheared off their basement.

61624.q: Which mountain in eastern Switzerland is a textbook example of folded Helvetic limestone layers?
61624.e: On the Säntis, the folds of the Helvetic Säntis nappe are superbly exposed.
61624.m: The Säntis impressively shows folded Helvetic limestones.

61625.q: Which pale, karst-forming Lower Cretaceous limestone forms many striking rock faces in the Helvetic zone, for example on the Schrattenfluh?
61625.e: Schrattenkalk is a pale, massive limestone from the Lower Cretaceous. It tends to form karst and creates limestone pavements (Schratten).
61625.m: Schrattenkalk is a typical limestone of the Helvetic nappes.

61626.q: What are the Helvetic units called that were deposited on the southernmost edge of the shelf and mark the transition to the ocean?
61626.e: The Ultrahelvetic comes from the very southern edge of the European shelf, right at the transition to the Penninic ocean.
61626.m: The Ultrahelvetic is the southernmost part of the Helvetic zone.

61627.q: Which mountain chain by Lake Walen is made of Helvetic limestone layers and shows striking layer edges?
61627.e: The Churfirsten consist of Helvetic Cretaceous limestones tilted to the north, whose layer edges drop steeply to Lake Walen.
61627.m: The Churfirsten are built of Helvetic limestones.

61628.q: Where does the name Penninic come from?
a: From the Pennine Alps in Valais
61628.e: The name comes from the Pennine Alps (Valais Alps), in Latin Mons Poeninus. Deriving it from Hannibal is considered wrong.
61628.m: The Penninic is named after the Pennine Alps.

61629.q: From which area of deposition does a large part of the Penninic rocks come?
a: From the Tethys, an ocean between Europe and Adria
From the Molasse sea on the Swiss Plateau
From the ancient valley of the Rhine
From an inland lake in the Jura
61629.e: The Penninic nappes come from the ocean area of the Tethys, including the Piedmont-Liguria Ocean, and from the continental Briançonnais in between.
61629.m: Penninic rocks mostly come from the Tethys.

a: Remains of oceanic crust and mantle
Fossilised coral reefs of a shallow sea
Pebbles from an old river delta
Sandstones turned to glass by heat
61630.e: Ophiolites are rock sequences of serpentinite, gabbro and basalt. They prove that an ocean once lay between Europe and Adria.
61630.m: Ophiolites are remains of a former ocean floor.

61631.q: Which grey, finely layered rock from the Penninic zone is named after a Swiss canton?
61631.e: Bündner schists are limy, clayey deep-sea sediments of the Tethys that are widespread in the Grisons.
61631.m: Bündner schists are typical rocks of the Penninic zone.

61632.q: The Penninic zone consists of several nappes. What is a nappe in Alpine geology?
a: A package of rock pushed far over other rocks
A thin layer of glacier ice
A flat lava layer from a volcano
61632.e: When the Alps formed, huge packages of rock were sheared off and pushed over each other, some more than a hundred kilometres. Such packages are called nappes.
61632.m: The Alps are built of nappes pushed over each other.

61633.q: In which canton do deep Penninic gneiss nappes lie at the surface over large areas?
61633.e: In Ticino the Penninic zone was strongly uplifted and worn away. That is why deep gneiss nappes such as the Maggia or the Leventina nappe appear there.
61633.m: In Ticino deep Penninic gneisses lie at the surface.

61634.q: Which nappe unit do the Mythen near Schwyz form?
61634.e: The Mythen belong to the Penninic klippe nappe, which, like the Préalpes, lies on younger Helvetic rocks and flysch.
61634.m: The Mythen are a Penninic klippe on younger ground.

61635.q: In which Swiss valley is there a large tectonic window where Penninic rocks appear from under Austroalpine nappes?
61635.e: In the Lower Engadine Window, the River Inn has cut through the Austroalpine nappes, so the Penninic rocks below can be seen. It reaches as far as Prutz in Tyrol.
61635.m: In the Lower Engadine you see Penninic rocks through a window.

61636.q: What is special about the Glarus Thrust?
a: Older rocks lie on much younger ones
Younger rocks lie on older ones
61636.e: Along a sharp line, Verrucano about 260 to 300 million years old was pushed onto flysch that is only 35 to 50 million years old.
61636.m: At the Glarus Thrust old lies on young.

61637.q: What is the reddish Permian rock above the Glarus Thrust called?
61637.e: Verrucano is a reddish, coarse rock made of fragments from the Permian period. It forms the older, upper part of the thrust.
61637.m: Red Verrucano lies above the Glarus Thrust.

61638.q: Which rock lies below the Glarus thrust plane?
a: Moraine from the last Ice Age
61638.e: Under the thrust lies slaty flysch that was deposited about 35 to 50 million years ago.
61638.m: Young flysch lies under the Glarus Thrust.

61639.q: Roughly how far north were the rocks at the Glarus Thrust pushed?
61639.e: The upper mass of rock was moved about 40 kilometres north over the younger layers.
61639.m: The Glarus Thrust has a displacement of about 40 kilometres.

61640.q: Under which name did the area of the Glarus Thrust become a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008?
61640.e: In July 2008 UNESCO added the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona as a World Natural Heritage Site.
61640.m: The Tectonic Arena Sardona has been World Natural Heritage since 2008.

61641.q: What is the hole through the rock of the Tschingelhörner called, through which the sun shines on the church of Elm twice a year?
61641.e: The Martinsloch is a natural hole in the ridge of the Tschingelhörner. Twice a year sunbeams fall through it onto Elm.
61641.m: The sun shines on Elm through the Martinsloch.

61642.q: What is the outcrop near Sool in the lower Sernf Valley called, where you can see the thrust plane up close?
61642.e: At the Lochsite (Lochseite) near Sool, the sharp boundary surface with a pale layer of limestone is easy to reach on the valley floor.
61642.m: At the Lochsite you can touch the thrust.

61643.q: How did Albert Heim first explain the rock layers in Glarus before he accepted the nappe theory in 1902?
61643.e: For a long time Heim supported the “Glarus double fold”, meaning two folds facing each other. Only in 1902 did he accept the thrust, in a letter to Lugeon.
61643.m: Albert Heim first believed in a Glarus double fold.

61644.q: Which explanation for the rock layers in Glarus finally won through around 1900?
a: A single great thrust of rock nappes
A double fold made of two folds
61644.e: For a long time Albert Heim’s double fold was accepted. Around 1900 the nappe theory won through: older rocks had been pushed far over younger ones as a nappe.
61644.m: The rock layers in Glarus are a great thrust.

61645.q: On which soft rock layers did the pile of sediments slide when the Folded Jura was formed?
a: On Triassic layers of salt and anhydrite
61645.e: The Jura layers were sheared off over Triassic layers of salt and anhydrite. These acted like a lubricant.
61645.m: The Folded Jura slid on Triassic salts.

61646.q: What does “distant push” mean in the formation of the Folded Jura?
a: The push of the Alps was passed across the Swiss Plateau into the Jura
The Jura was lifted from below by volcanoes
Glaciers pushed the Jura folds together
The Rhine Graben pulled the Jura north
61646.e: The pressure from the formation of the Alps was passed beneath the Molasse basin to the sediments of the Jura, which folded into ridges there.
61646.m: The Folded Jura was formed by a distant push from the Alps.

61647.q: What is a narrow gorge cut by a river right across a Jura ridge called?
61647.e: A cluse cuts across a ridge, as at Balsthal or Moutier. Cluses are important transport routes.
61647.m: A cluse is a gorge cutting across a Jura ridge.

61648.q: What is a long valley carved out by erosion along the crest of a Jura fold called?
61648.e: In a combe, erosion has broken through the hard limestone cover of an arch and cleared out the softer layers in the core.
61648.m: A combe lies hollowed out along the crest of an arch.

61649.q: In Jura tectonics, what is an upward-arched fold called?
61649.e: An anticline (arch, saddle) is arched upwards.
61649.m: A Jura arch is an anticline.

61650.q: Which part of the Jura do the high plateaus of the Franches-Montagnes belong to?
a: To the Plateau Jura, as part of the Folded Jura
61650.e: The Franches-Montagnes are a folded high plateau. As Plateau Jura they belong to the Folded Jura and must not be confused with the Tabular Jura.
61650.m: The Franches-Montagnes belong to the Plateau Jura of the Folded Jura.

61651.q: In Jura tectonics, what is a downward-bent fold between two arches called?
61651.e: A syncline is a trough in which the layers are bent downwards. Long valleys such as the Val de Travers often lie in such troughs.
61651.m: A Jura fold bent downwards is called a syncline.

61652.q: Which process shaped karst landscapes with sinkholes, caves and underground drainage in the Folded Jura?
a: Limestone being dissolved by water containing carbonic acid
61652.e: Rainwater with dissolved carbon dioxide dissolves limestone. This creates sinkholes, caves and areas without surface streams, as in the Vallée de Joux.
61652.m: Water containing carbonic acid turns the Jura limestone into karst.

61653.q: How does the Tabular Jura differ from the Folded Jura?
a: Its layers lie mostly flat and unfolded
It is much higher than the Folded Jura
61653.e: In the Tabular Jura the layers lie almost horizontally like tables. They were not folded into ridges but at most broken into blocks.
61653.m: In the Tabular Jura the rock layers lie almost flat.

61654.q: In which cantons does the Tabular Jura mainly lie?
61654.e: The eastern Tabular Jura reaches from Basel-Landschaft through Aargau, and further north the Randen in Schaffhausen belongs to it. In the west lies the Ajoie in the canton of Jura.
61654.m: The Tabular Jura lies in northern Switzerland.

61655.q: Which tectonic event broke the Tabular Jura into many blocks?
a: The sinking of the Upper Rhine Graben
The eruption of the Hegau volcanoes
The thrust in the Glarus region
The retreat of the Rhône Glacier
61655.e: As the Upper Rhine Graben sank from the early Tertiary onwards, the layers broke along faults into separate blocks.
61655.m: The Upper Rhine Graben broke the Tabular Jura into blocks.

61656.q: Which rocks mainly make up the Tabular Jura?
61656.e: The Tabular Jura consists mainly of Triassic and Jurassic limestones, such as Muschelkalk, Hauptrogenstein and Malm.
61656.m: The Tabular Jura is made mainly of Triassic and Jurassic limestones.

61657.q: Which landform is typical of the Tabular Jura in Basel-Landschaft and Aargau?
a: Wide plateaus with steeply cut valleys
61657.e: Typical features are table-like plateaus into which streams have cut steep-sided valleys.
61657.m: The Tabular Jura shows plateaus with deeply cut valleys.

61658.q: Which upland in Schaffhausen belongs to the unfolded Jura?
61658.e: The Randen lies in the canton of Schaffhausen and is part of the unfolded Tabular Jura, which continues into the Swabian Jura.
61658.m: The Randen belongs to the Tabular Jura.

61659.q: In which Aargau municipality of the Tabular Jura were many Triassic Plateosaurus skeletons found in a clay pit?
61659.e: Many Plateosaurus skeletons were found in the clay pit at Frick in the Fricktal. The Dinosaur Museum in Frick shows the finds.
61659.m: Frick is an important site for Plateosaurus finds.

61660.q: What is the Molasse of the Swiss Plateau made of?
a: Debris eroded from the rising Alps
Coral reefs of a tropical sea
61660.e: Rivers carried pebbles, sand and clay from the growing Alps into the foreland. These became conglomerates, sandstones and marls.
61660.m: The Molasse is the eroded debris of the young Alps.

61661.q: Why did a basin form north of the Alps in which the Molasse could be deposited?
a: The European plate bent downwards under the weight of the Alps
A meteorite made a crater in the Swiss Plateau
Glaciers scraped out the Swiss Plateau deeply
61661.e: The weight of the mountains pressed the Earth’s crust in front of them downwards. This created a foreland basin that filled with debris.
61661.m: The Molasse basin was formed by the weight of the Alps.

61662.q: Which four groups of Molasse are distinguished, from oldest to youngest?
a: Lower Marine, Lower Freshwater, Upper Marine, Upper Freshwater Molasse
Lower Freshwater, Lower Marine, Upper Freshwater, Upper Marine Molasse
Upper Marine, Lower Marine, Upper Freshwater, Lower Freshwater Molasse
Lower Marine, Upper Marine, Lower Freshwater, Upper Freshwater Molasse
61662.e: Sea and land alternated twice: first the Lower Marine Molasse, then the Lower Freshwater Molasse, then the Upper Marine and finally the Upper Freshwater Molasse.
61662.m: In the Molasse, sea and fresh water alternated twice.

61663.q: Roughly when was the Molasse deposited?
61663.e: The Molasse formed in the Oligocene and Miocene, that is from about 34 to 5 million years ago.
61663.m: The Molasse was deposited in the Oligocene and Miocene.

61664.q: Which Molasse group does Bernese sandstone belong to, from which many buildings in Bern’s old town are made?
61664.e: Bernese sandstone is a marine sandstone of the Upper Marine Molasse. It was mainly quarried at Ostermundigen.
61664.m: Bernese sandstone comes from the Upper Marine Molasse.

61665.q: What is the strip of Molasse along the edge of the Alps called, whose layers are folded, stacked in slices and tilted steeply?
61665.e: At the edge of the Alps, the Molasse was pushed together during the late stage of mountain building. This zone is called the Subalpine Molasse.
61665.m: The Subalpine Molasse is folded and steeply tilted.

61666.q: How thick can the Molasse get in places in the foreland basin?
61666.e: Near the edge of the Alps, the Molasse reaches a thickness of over 4000 metres in places; towards the Jura it becomes thinner.
61666.m: At the edge of the Alps the Molasse is several kilometres thick.

61667.q: Why are coarse Molasse pebbles found mainly near the edge of the Alps, but fine clays further into the basin?
a: The rivers lost power as they left the mountains and dropped the coarse material first
The glaciers sorted the material by size
The wind blew the pebbles back to the edge of the Alps
Coarse pebbles only formed later through weathering
61667.e: As the rivers entered the flat foreland, they slowed down. Coarse material stayed behind in debris fans, while fine material was carried far away.
61667.m: Coarse Molasse debris lies near the Alps, fine material further out.

61668.q: Which animals prove with their fossil teeth that the Swiss Plateau was at times covered by the sea?
61668.e: Shark teeth are often found in the Marine Molasse. They show that the Molasse basin was connected to the sea.
61668.m: Shark teeth in the Molasse prove there was once a sea.

a: A conglomerate of rounded, cemented pebbles
61669.e: Nagelfluh is a conglomerate: rounded river pebbles that are joined into solid rock by a binding material, usually limy.

61670.q: Where does the name “Nagelfluh” come from?
a: When weathered, the pebbles stick out of the wall like nail heads
The rock used to be made into nails
A mountain called Nagel gave it its name
You could not hammer nails into it
61670.e: Weathered pebbles stick out of the binding material like the heads of nails (“Nagel” is German for nail). “Fluh” means a steep rock face in Swiss German.
61670.m: Nagelfluh got its name because the stones stick out like nail heads.

61671.q: How can you tell the difference between a conglomerate such as Nagelfluh and a breccia?
a: Conglomerates have rounded pieces, breccias angular ones
Conglomerates are volcanic, breccias are not
Breccias contain only sand, conglomerates only clay
Conglomerates are soft, breccias melt easily
61671.e: Rounded pebbles show a long journey in a river. Angular fragments in a breccia were hardly moved.
61671.m: Nagelfluh has round stones, breccia angular ones.

61672.q: Which mountain in Central Switzerland is mostly made of tilted layers of Nagelfluh?
61672.e: The Rigi is mostly built of Nagelfluh of the Subalpine Molasse, the remains of an old debris fan. Only in the south do limestone cliffs such as the Vitznauerstock rise up.
61672.m: The Rigi is a Nagelfluh mountain.

61673.q: Which mountain in the canton of St Gallen is considered the highest Nagelfluh mountain in Europe?
61673.e: The Speer north of Lake Walen is about 1950 m high and is considered the highest Nagelfluh mountain in Europe.
61673.m: The Speer is the highest Nagelfluh mountain in Europe.

61674.q: In which depositional setting did the Nagelfluh of the Molasse form?
a: In river debris fans at the edge of the Alps
On the floor of a deep ocean
61674.e: Rivers from the Alps built up large debris fans at the edge of the mountains. Their pebbles later hardened into Nagelfluh.
61674.m: Nagelfluh formed from old debris fans of Alpine rivers.

61675.q: Which upland between the Emmental and the Entlebuch is made of Nagelfluh and known for its panned gold?
61675.e: The Napf uplands are a former Molasse debris fan. Fine flakes of gold from the Nagelfluh are found in the streams of the area.
61675.m: In the Napf area you can pan gold from the Nagelfluh.

61676.q: Which rockslide of 1806 broke away along tilted Nagelfluh layers of the Rossberg?
61676.e: In the Goldau rockslide, Nagelfluh layers slid off on layers of marl and buried the village. About 450 people died.
61676.m: The Goldau rockslide happened along Nagelfluh layers.

61677.q: Which rocks make up most of the Aar Massif?
61677.e: The Aar Massif belongs to the crystalline basement. It consists mainly of gneisses and granites, along with schists and amphibolite.
61677.m: The Aar Massif consists mainly of granite and gneiss.

61678.q: How long ago did the Central Aar Granite intrude into the Earth’s crust?
61678.e: The Central Aar Granite solidified about 300 million years ago, long before the Alps formed.
61678.m: The Aar Granite is about 300 million years old.

61679.q: How did the old basement rock of the Aar Massif reach the surface?
a: It was lifted up when the Alps formed
It flowed out of a volcano as lava
It was deposited on the seabed
61679.e: The Aar Massif is a central massif of old European basement rock. It was lifted up when the Alps formed, and erosion exposed it.
61679.m: The Aar Massif is a central massif of old basement rock.

61680.q: Which pass lies in the area of the largest body of granite in Switzerland, the Central Aar Granite?
61680.e: The Central Aar Granite is exposed over about 500 km² in the area of the Grimsel, Göscheneralp and Reuss Valley.
61680.m: The Aar Granite is exposed at the Grimsel.

61681.q: In which mountain massif to the south-west does the Aar Massif continue underground?
61681.e: South-west of Leuk the Aar Massif dips under younger rock nappes. It continues in the Mont Blanc and Aiguilles Rouges massifs, which are also made of old granite and gneiss.
61681.m: The Aar Massif continues in the Mont Blanc Massif.

61682.q: What is geologically striking about the rock of the Jungfrau?
a: Older crystalline rock lies above younger limestone
It is made entirely of sandstone
It is made of meteorite rock
61682.e: Normally younger layers lie above older ones. At the Jungfrau, gneiss of the Aar Massif was pushed slightly north over younger limestones when the Alps formed.
61682.m: At the Jungfrau old crystalline rock lies above younger limestone.

61683.q: In which rock does the Gotthard Base Tunnel begin at Erstfeld in the north?
a: In the granite and gneiss of the Aar Massif
In the limestone of the Jura
In the Molasse of the Swiss Plateau
In the dolomite of the Southern Alps
61683.e: The tunnel begins at Erstfeld in the Aar Massif, then crosses the Tavetsch intermediate massif and the Gotthard Massif and ends in the gneisses of the Leventina.
61683.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel begins in the Aar Massif.

61684.q: What are the Eiger and the Titlis on the northern edge of the Aar Massif mainly made of?
61684.e: The Eiger and the Titlis consist mainly of limestone that was once deposited in the sea. On the northern edge, this sedimentary cover lies on the granite and gneiss of the Aar Massif.
61684.m: On the northern edge of the Aar Massif, limestone sediments lie on the crystalline rock.

61685.q: How can geologists work out where an erratic boulder came from?
a: By comparing its rock with rocks in the Alps
By counting growth rings in the rock
61685.e: Certain types of rock only occur in a few places. If a block matches a particular granite in Valais, you know where it came from and so the route of the glacier.
61685.m: The type of rock reveals where an erratic boulder comes from.

61686.q: Why are glacial boulders also called “erratic blocks”?
a: Because they seem to have wandered, from Latin errare
Because they are made of ore
61686.e: Latin errare means to wander. The blocks seem to have travelled because they do not match the rock around them.
61686.m: Erratic blocks get their name because they seem to have wandered.

61687.q: From what size do earth scientists speak of an erratic boulder rather than glacial debris?
a: From about a hundred cubic metres
61687.e: The usual dividing line between glacial debris and an erratic boulder is a volume of about one cubic metre.
61687.m: An erratic boulder is larger than about one cubic metre.

61688.q: Which erratic boulder in Geneva harbour carries the reference point for all height measurements in Switzerland?
61688.e: The Repère Pierre du Niton is on the Pierre du Niton. Its height of 373.6 m above sea level is the basis of Swiss height measurement.
61688.m: The Pierre du Niton is the starting point of Swiss height measurement.

61689.q: Which glacier brought the granite boulders from the Mont Blanc area to the southern foot of the Jura?
61689.e: The Ice Age Rhône Glacier reached across the Swiss Plateau to the Jura and dropped blocks from the Valais Alps there.
61689.m: The Rhône Glacier brought Valais granite to the Jura.

61690.q: Which engineer from Valais was among the first to argue that glaciers had once covered large parts of the Alps and the foreland?
61690.e: From moraines and erratic boulders, Ignaz Venetz concluded there had once been a great glaciation. At first only Jean de Charpentier supported him.
61690.m: Ignaz Venetz was a pioneer of the Ice Age theory.

61691.q: Which naturalist spread the Ice Age theory internationally with his work “Études sur les glaciers” of 1840?
61691.e: Louis Agassiz, born in Môtier in the canton of Fribourg, studied glaciers and made the Ice Age theory famous with this work.
61691.m: Louis Agassiz made the Ice Age theory famous.

61692.q: Which erratic boulder near Steinhof in the canton of Solothurn, at about 1700 cubic metres, is one of the largest in Switzerland?
61692.e: The Grossi Flue near Steinhof measures about 1697 m³. The Rhône Glacier brought it from the Valais Alps.
61692.m: The Grossi Flue in Steinhof is a huge erratic boulder.

61693.q: Why are silicate erratic boulders on the Swiss Plateau also valuable for nature?
a: Rare, acid-loving lichens and mosses grow on them
They store groundwater for drinking water
They contain valuable ores for mining
They help migrating birds to navigate
61693.e: On the limestone-rich Swiss Plateau, granite blocks provide a habitat for over 80 kinds of lichen and about 30 mosses that hardly find anywhere else to grow.
61693.m: Erratic boulders are islands of life for rare lichens and mosses.

61694.q: Which mineral is rock crystal made of?
61694.e: Rock crystal is colourless, transparent quartz with the chemical formula SiO2.
61694.m: Rock crystal is pure, clear quartz.

61695.q: What hardness does quartz have on the Mohs scale?
61695.e: Quartz has a Mohs hardness of 7. It scratches glass and steel, but is scratched by topaz and corundum.
61695.m: Quartz has a hardness of 7 on the Mohs scale.

61696.q: In Switzerland, what are the people called who search the Alps for crystals?
61696.e: Strahler search rock clefts for crystals. The name comes from the old word “Strahl” for rock crystal. Säumer led pack animals over passes, Sennen make cheese on alpine pastures and Köhler made charcoal.
61696.m: In Switzerland, crystal hunters are called Strahler.

61697.q: Where do Alpine rock crystals typically form?
a: In clefts where hot watery solutions deposited quartz
In lava flows that cooled quickly
61697.e: Hot, mineral-rich solutions circulated in clefts in granite and gneiss. As they cooled, the crystals grew from them over a long time.
61697.m: Alpine rock crystals grow in clefts from hot solutions.

61698.q: What gives smoky quartz its brown to black colour?
a: Natural radioactive radiation in the rock
61698.e: Natural radiation from the surrounding granite changes the crystal lattice where aluminium atoms are built in. This gives the quartz its smoky colour.
61698.m: Smoky quartz is darkened by natural radiation.

61699.q: What did crystal hunters discover on the Planggenstock above the Göscheneralp in 2005?
a: A cleft with huge rock crystals
61699.e: Franz von Arx and Paul von Känel opened the cleft in September 2005 and recovered the crystals in summer 2006. The largest crystals are over a metre long.
61699.m: The Planggenstock cleft was discovered in 2005.

61700.q: Where can you see the largest crystal groups from the Planggenstock today?
a: In the Natural History Museum of Bern
In the Swiss National Museum in Zurich
61700.e: The Natural History Museum of Bern shows almost 2 tonnes of rock crystal from the Planggenstock. The largest group weighs about 300 kg, and its central crystal is 107 cm long.
61700.m: The Planggenstock crystals are in the Natural History Museum of Bern.

61701.q: In which rock was the cleft on the Planggenstock?
a: In the granite of the Aar Massif
In the limestone of the Säntis nappe
61701.e: The cleft lies at about 2600 m above sea level in the granite of the Aar Massif in the canton of Uri.
61701.m: The Planggenstock crystals grew in Aar Granite.

61702.q: Which of these gemstones is a form of quartz?
61702.e: Amethyst is purple quartz. Citrine, rose quartz, smoky quartz and the almost black morion are also quartz. Diamond is carbon, ruby is corundum and emerald is beryl.
61702.m: Amethyst, citrine and smoky quartz are coloured quartzes.

61703.q: On what date did the Basel earthquake happen?
61703.e: The earthquake happened on 18 October 1356, St Luke’s Day.
61703.m: The Basel earthquake happened on 18 October 1356.

61704.q: Why was the number of deaths in Basel relatively low?
a: Many people fled the city after a foreshock in the afternoon
The city was almost empty because of the plague
The earthquake happened in the middle of winter
All the houses were made of stone
61704.e: A first shock in the afternoon warned the people. The stronger shocks followed in the evening, when many were already outside the walls.
61704.m: A foreshock saved many lives in Basel.

61705.q: What also caused great damage after the earthquake in Basel?
a: A city fire that lasted about eight days
61705.e: Knocked-over hearth fires and lights started a fire that ravaged the city for about eight days.
61705.m: After the earthquake Basel burned for days.

61706.q: Which well-known building in Basel was badly damaged in the 1356 earthquake?
61706.e: In the first shock the choir of the Minster collapsed, and later the roof fell into the nave too. The Spalentor and Town Hall were only built after the earthquake, the Messeturm in the 21st century.
61706.m: Basel Minster was badly damaged in 1356.

61707.q: Why are there only a few traces of the 1356 earthquake to be seen in Basel today?
a: The city was quickly rebuilt afterwards
The earthquake only destroyed wooden houses
The Rhine washed the ruins away
Basel was founded in a new place
61707.e: After the earthquake and the city fire, Basel was rebuilt within a few decades. Traces can still be seen on a few buildings, for example on the tower of the Lohnhof.
61707.m: Traces of the earthquake can still be seen at the Lohnhof in Basel.

61708.q: What magnitude do most estimates give for the Basel earthquake?
61708.e: Most estimates are between 6.0 and 6.3, and some newer studies go up to nearly 7. It is considered the strongest historically recorded earthquake north of the Alps in Central Europe.
61708.m: The Basel earthquake had a magnitude of about 6 to 7.

61709.q: How many castles around Basel were damaged by the earthquake?
61709.e: About 40 castles in the surrounding area were damaged. Damage was reported up to 50 kilometres away.
61709.m: The Basel earthquake damaged about 40 castles.

61710.q: Which institution monitors earthquakes in Switzerland today?
a: The Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich
The Federal Office of Meteorology in Geneva
61710.e: The Swiss Seismological Service (SED) at ETH Zurich runs the national measuring network and assesses the earthquake hazard.
61710.m: The SED at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes in Switzerland.

61711.q: At about 9 km long, which firn stream is the longest tributary of the Great Aletsch Glacier?
61711.e: The Grosser Aletschfirn is about 9 km long and on average almost 1.5 km wide. The Jungfraufirn measures just under 7 km, the Grüneggfirn only about 3 km.
61711.m: The Grosser Aletschfirn is the longest tributary of the Aletsch Glacier.

61712.q: Which crossing at 3173 m links the Aletsch area with the Lötschental?
61712.e: The Lötschenlücke lies at the upper end of the Grosser Aletschfirn. High-altitude mountaineers cross it to reach the Lötschental.
61712.m: The Lötschenlücke leads from the Aletschfirn into the Lötschental.

61713.q: Which firn stream is one of the tributaries of the Great Aletsch Glacier?
61713.e: The Ewigschneefeld, about 8 km long, flows south from the Mönchsjoch. The Claridenfirn, on the other hand, is in the Glarus Alps.
61713.m: The Ewigschneefeld feeds the Aletsch Glacier from the Mönchsjoch.

61714.q: Which river flows out of the Great Aletsch Glacier?
61714.e: The Massa flows from the glacier mouth through the Massa Gorge and joins the Rhône at Bitsch. Its water is used in the Bitsch power station.
61714.m: The Massa is the outflow of the Aletsch Glacier.

61715.q: How can researchers reconstruct earlier lengths of the Aletsch Glacier over thousands of years?
a: With wood and soil finds that the ice releases
With temperature measurements in today’s ice
With satellite images from the Middle Ages
With annual rings in the glacier ice
61715.e: Trees that were once overrun by advancing ice can be dated with tree rings and radiocarbon. This shows the glacier lengths of about the last 3200 years.
61715.m: Old wood reveals how long a glacier used to be.

61716.q: The catchment area of the Massa measures 195 km², and in 1973 about two thirds of it was covered by glaciers. How large was the glaciated area?
61716.e: Calculation: 195 km² × 2/3 = 130 km². At that time this also included the Upper and Middle Aletsch Glaciers.
61716.m: Two thirds of 195 square kilometres is 130 square kilometres.

61717.q: Around 1850 the Aletsch Glacier measured about 105.6 km², and in 2017 only 78.5 km². By roughly what percentage has its area shrunk?
61717.e: Calculation: (105.6 − 78.5) ÷ 105.6 = 27.1 ÷ 105.6 ≈ 0.26. So the area has shrunk by about a quarter.
61717.m: Since 1850 the Aletsch Glacier has lost about a quarter of its area.

61718.q: By how much did the ice surface in the lower parts of the Aletsch Glacier sink each year between 2001 and 2014?
61718.e: During this period the surface in the lower part sank by more than 5 m every year. The ice does not flow down quickly enough to make up for this loss.
61718.m: In the lower part several metres of Aletsch ice melt every year.

61719.q: Roughly how much ice did the Aletsch Glacier lose at its lowest measuring point at 1980 m in the 2024 measuring year?
61719.e: At the lowest measuring point about 11 m of ice melted in 2024. A large glacier mouth and a lake also formed at the tongue.
61719.m: The tongue of the Aletsch Glacier loses many metres of ice every year.

61720.q: Which observatory at 3571 m on the edge of the Aletsch area was opened in 1937?
61720.e: The Sphinx Observatory on the Jungfraujoch was opened in 1937 and lies above the Jungfraufirn. The Riederfurka station by the lower glacier was only built in 1976.
61720.m: The Sphinx Observatory has stood on the Jungfraujoch since 1937.

61721.q: Which pass road winds in hairpin bends right past the Rhône Glacier?
61721.e: The Furka road climbs from Gletsch up to the Hotel Belvédère, right next to the Rhône Glacier. The ice grotto is also there.
61721.m: The Furka road runs past the Rhône Glacier.

61722.q: Over its first 2.5 km, the Rhône Glacier drops by about 600 m. What is the average gradient on this section?
61722.e: Calculation: 600 m ÷ 2500 m = 0.24, which is 24%. Over its whole length the average gradient is only about 16%.
61722.m: The gradient is the difference in height divided by the horizontal distance.

61723.q: At roughly what height does the tongue of the Rhône Glacier end today?
61723.e: The tongue now lies above 2200 m on a rock step above the valley floor. In the 19th century it reached several hundred metres lower.
61723.m: The tongue of the Rhône Glacier now lies above 2200 metres.

61724.q: On average, how much did the ice thickness of the Rhône Glacier decrease each year since 1874?
61724.e: On the long-term average, the glacier got about a quarter of a metre thinner every year. In hot years, however, the tongue now loses several metres.
61724.m: Since 1874 the Rhône Glacier has got on average a quarter of a metre thinner each year.

61725.q: What was tested over several days at the Rhône Glacier in August 2008?
61725.e: A wind barrier was meant to keep warm air away from the ice. At eleven measuring stations, cooling of at most 3 °C was recorded over more than six days.
61725.m: In 2008 a wind barrier against warm air was tested at the Rhône Glacier.

61726.q: What can you visit at the Rhône Glacier every summer since the 19th century?
a: An ice grotto cut by hand
An underground power station in the ice
A ski lift on the glacier tongue
A railway station under the glacier
61726.e: Since 1870 a new grotto has been cut into the ice every year, because the glacier moves. Today it is protected from melting in summer with blankets.
61726.m: The ice grotto in the Rhône Glacier is cut anew every year.

61727.q: Around 1850 the Rhône Glacier covered about 20.2 km², and in 2018 only 14.64 km². How much area has it lost?
61727.e: Calculation: 20.2 km² − 14.64 km² = 5.56 km², so about 5.6 km². That is more than a quarter of the area in 1850.
61727.m: Since 1850 the Rhône Glacier has lost more than a quarter of its area.

61728.q: Since 1874 the Rhône Glacier has retreated by an average of about 8.5 m per year. What is the calculated retreat from 1874 to 2024?
61728.e: Calculation: 2024 − 1874 = 150 years; 150 × 8.5 m = 1275 m, so about 1.3 km.
61728.m: A retreat of 8.5 metres a year adds up to about 1.3 kilometres in 150 years.

61729.q: According to GLAMOS, what percentage of their ice volume did Swiss glaciers lose in 2023?
61729.e: For 2023, GLAMOS reported a loss of 4.4%. It was the second extreme melting year in a row.
61729.m: In 2023 Swiss glaciers again lost about four per cent of their ice.

61730.q: In 2024 Swiss glaciers lost 1.1 km³ of ice, which was 2.3% of their volume. Roughly how large was the volume before the loss?
61730.e: Calculation: 1.1 km³ ÷ 0.023 ≈ 47.8 km³, so about 48 km³. After the loss about 46.5 km³ remained.
61730.m: The starting volume can be calculated from the loss and the percentage.

61731.q: The ice volume of Swiss glaciers fell from 74.9 km³ (2000) to 46.5 km³ (2024). By roughly what percentage has it shrunk?
61731.e: Calculation: (74.9 − 46.5) ÷ 74.9 = 28.4 ÷ 74.9 ≈ 0.38. So almost two fifths of the ice has disappeared since 2000.
61731.m: Since 2000 Swiss glaciers have lost almost two fifths of their volume.

61732.q: According to GLAMOS, what percentage of their ice volume did Swiss glaciers lose in the 2025/26 measuring year?
61732.e: GLAMOS reported a loss of over 5% for 2026, just behind the record year 2022. Over five years almost 20% of the ice was lost.
61732.m: In 2026 Swiss glaciers lost over five per cent of their ice.

61733.q: Why do glaciers melt particularly strongly when the freezing level stays above 4000 m for a long time?
a: Then it also thaws in the high accumulation areas
Then a lot of fresh snow falls there
Then the meltwater freezes again at once
Then the sun shines less strongly
61733.e: If the freezing level is very high, the snow melts away even at 3500 m. Then glaciers also lose ice where they would normally gain mass.
61733.m: A high freezing level makes even high glaciers melt.

61734.q: According to a study, by what share did the volume of Swiss glaciers shrink between 1931 and 2016?
61734.e: A study by ETH Zurich and the WSL compared historical aerial photos with today’s data. It found that glacier volume roughly halved in these 85 years.
61734.m: Between 1931 and 2016 Swiss glacier volume roughly halved.

61735.q: According to GLAMOS, which glacier in Valais disappeared in 2026?
61735.e: GLAMOS listed the glacier on the Bella Tola in Valais and the Griessfiren and Plattalvafirn in the Glarus region as gone. Small glaciers at medium altitudes are hit first.
61735.m: Small glaciers like the one on the Bella Tola disappear first.

61736.q: According to GLAMOS, how many Swiss glaciers disappeared between 2016 and 2023?
61736.e: According to GLAMOS, 159 glaciers disappeared completely during this period, which is 11% of the number in 2016. They were mainly very small glaciers.
61736.m: Between 2016 and 2023 over a hundred small Swiss glaciers disappeared.

61737.q: In 2026 Swiss glaciers lost about 2200 billion litres of water from July to September. How many cubic kilometres is that?
61737.e: 1 km³ is 10⁹ m³ and so 10¹² litres. 2200 billion litres is 2.2 × 10¹² litres, so 2.2 km³.
61737.m: One cubic kilometre holds a million million litres.

61738.q: Why does a glacier losing its snow cover in summer make the shrinking even worse?
a: Bare ice is darker than snow
61738.e: Fresh snow reflects up to about 90% of the radiation, bare glacier ice much less. If the ice becomes free of snow early in summer, it melts much faster.
61738.m: Snow-free glacier ice melts faster because it absorbs more radiation.

61739.q: In which order, from oldest to youngest, are the classic Alpine glacial periods?
61739.e: The order follows the alphabet of the river names G, M, R, W. The Würm glaciation is the youngest of them.
61739.m: From oldest to youngest, the classic Alpine ice ages follow the alphabet.

61740.q: Which two researchers founded the classic division of the Alpine glacial periods with their work “Die Alpen im Eiszeitalter” (1901 to 1909)?
61740.e: Penck and Brückner distinguished four glacial periods and named them after rivers in the Alpine foreland. Their scheme was later extended with further glacial periods.
61740.m: Penck and Brückner coined the names of the Alpine ice ages.

61741.q: In which place in the canton of Zurich were skeleton remains of mammoths from the last glacial period found, which can now be seen in a museum?
61741.e: Mammoth bones were found in a bog near Niederweningen in 1890 and 2003. The Mammoth Museum shows the finds from the Würm glaciation.
61741.m: Mammoths from the last ice age were found in Niederweningen.

61743.q: Which glacial period led to the greatest advance of glaciers into the northern Alpine foreland?
61743.e: During the Riss glaciation the glaciers reached further into the foreland than in the Würm glaciation, in Switzerland as far as the Jura. Würm moraines therefore lie inside the older deposits.
61743.m: The Riss glaciation brought the largest glacier advance into the Alpine foreland.

61744.q: Which warm period came directly before the Würm glaciation?
61744.e: The Eemian interglacial began about 126,000 years ago and lasted about 11,000 years. It was followed by the Würm glaciation.
61744.m: Before the last ice age came the Eemian warm period.

61745.q: What are peaks that stuck out of the network of ice streams during the glacial period called?
61745.e: Nunatak is a word from Greenlandic. Such ice-free peaks gave plants a refuge during the Ice Age.
61745.m: A nunatak is an ice-free peak sticking out of the glacier.

61746.q: What is the last short cold spell at the end of the Würm glaciation, about 12,000 years ago, called?
61746.e: After the warming of the Allerød, it became much colder again for a good 1000 years, and glaciers advanced again. The phase is named after the mountain avens (Dryas).
61746.m: The Younger Dryas was the last cold spell of the Ice Age.

61747.q: What are colder phases with glacier advances within a glacial period called?
61747.e: The Würm glaciation was marked by climate fluctuations. Cold phases of advance are called stadials, warmer phases in between interstadials.
61747.m: A stadial is a cold phase of advance within an ice age.

61748.q: Roughly how much lower was sea level at the time of the greatest ice cover in the last ice age?
61748.e: Huge ice sheets on the continents locked up so much water that sea level fell by about 120 m. As a result, the North Sea and the Bering Strait, for example, ran dry.
61748.m: In the last ice age sea level was about 120 metres lower.

61749.q: What are the oldest glacial gravels on the Swiss Plateau called, which today lie as caps on hills such as the Irchel?
61749.e: The Deckenschotter were deposited in the valley floors of the time during early glacial periods. Since then the rivers have cut deep down, so today they lie on hilltops.
61749.m: The Deckenschotter are the oldest gravels of the Swiss Plateau.

61750.q: Why does the bedrock of some valleys on the Swiss Plateau lie far below today’s valley floor?
61750.e: The glaciers scraped channels into the rock, in places hundreds of metres deep. Later, gravel and lake deposits filled these basins up again.
61750.m: Ice Age glaciers overdeepened many valleys.

61751.q: What is the fine sediment called that was blown by the wind from the areas in front of glaciers and is found near Basel, for example?
61751.e: During the cold, dry phases the wind blew dust out of the gravel plains with little vegetation. It was deposited as loess, from which fertile soils developed.
61751.m: Loess is Ice Age wind-blown dust.

61752.q: How were kettle holes formed, which are often found on the Swiss Plateau as small lakes or bogs?
61752.e: When the glacier retreated, separated blocks of ice were left in the gravel. When they melted, the surface sank and hollows formed, often with lakes.
61752.m: Kettle holes form when buried blocks of ice melt.

61753.q: Why did the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen only form after the last ice age?
a: The Rhine was forced into a new bed
A glacier cut out the step
61753.e: Ice Age gravels buried the old bed of the Rhine. The river found a new course and now plunges over hard Jura limestone into the softer old channel.
61753.m: The Rhine Falls formed because the Rhine looked for a new bed after the ice age.

61754.q: Into which bedrock did the glaciers mainly scrape the basins of the Swiss Plateau?
61754.e: The bedrock of the Swiss Plateau consists of Molasse sandstones, marls and Nagelfluh. These relatively soft rocks were easy to scrape out.
61754.m: The glaciers shaped the Swiss Plateau in soft Molasse rocks.

61755.q: What are finely layered deposits in glacial lakes called, in which one light and one dark band together show one year?
61755.e: In summer coarser, light material is deposited, in winter fine, dark clay. By counting the pairs of layers, periods of time can be worked out.
61755.m: Varves are annual layers in lake deposits.

61756.q: Why are Ice Age gravels on the Swiss Plateau especially important today?
a: They store a lot of groundwater
61756.e: The very permeable layers of gravel and sand form large aquifers. A large part of Swiss drinking water comes from such groundwater.
61756.m: Ice Age gravels are important groundwater stores.

61757.q: Which upland between Bern and Lucerne stayed free of ice during the maximum of the last ice age?
61757.e: The glaciers flowed around the high Napf area but did not reach it. That is why typical moraines of the last ice age are missing there.
61757.m: In the last ice age the Napf area rose ice-free above its surroundings.

61758.q: What is the moraine ridge on which parts of Zurich’s old town and the Lindenhof lie?
a: An end moraine from a halt in the glacier’s retreat
A dam built up by people
61758.e: As it melted back, the Linth-Rhine Glacier stopped several times and pushed debris into ridges. Such an end moraine from the Zurich stage also dams Lake Zurich.
61758.m: End moraines mark places where a glacier stood still for a longer time.

61759.q: What does the Swiss measuring network GLAMOS observe?
61759.e: GLAMOS stands for Glacier Monitoring Switzerland. It measures the length, mass and volume of Swiss glaciers and is run by several universities.

61760.q: Which federal office is one of the funders of GLAMOS?
61760.e: GLAMOS is supported by MeteoSwiss as part of GCOS Switzerland, by the FOEN, by the Swiss Academy of Sciences and by swisstopo.
61760.m: The FOEN helps fund glacier monitoring.

61761.q: Since when have changes in glacier length been observed systematically in Switzerland?
61761.e: The measurement series of glacier lengths begin in 1880, and glacier reports have been published since 1881. This makes Switzerland one of the pioneering countries in glacier monitoring.
61761.m: Switzerland has observed its glacier lengths since 1880.

61762.q: On how many glaciers does GLAMOS measure the mass balance directly in the field each year (as of 2024)?
61762.e: In 2024 the annual mass balance was measured on 21 glaciers, with winter measurements on 14. The values are scaled up to all glaciers with models.
61762.m: GLAMOS measures the mass balance directly on about twenty glaciers.

61763.q: On just under how many glaciers was the change in length measured in 2023?
61763.e: In 2023, 95 glaciers were measured, and 93 of them had retreated. The measurements are taken at the glacier tongue.
61763.m: Almost all measured glaciers retreated in 2023.

61764.q: Why are glacier measurements that have been running for over a hundred years especially valuable for research?
a: They show long-term changes in the climate
They show where gold lies in the ice
They measure the strength of earthquakes
61764.e: Individual years vary a lot. Only long series, such as on the Claridenfirn since 1914/15, clearly show how the climate changes over decades.
61764.m: Long measurement series make climate change visible.

61765.q: Over which period is the hydrological year for glacier mass balance calculated?
61765.e: The hydrological year begins in autumn with the build-up of snow and ends after summer with the melt. In this way it covers a complete cycle.
61765.m: Glacier balances run from October to September.

61766.q: What is used to measure melting directly on the glacier?
61766.e: Ablation stakes are drilled into the ice; the distance to the ice surface shows how much has melted. In addition, the amount of snow is measured in snow pits.
61766.m: Stakes in the ice can be used to measure melting directly.

61767.q: What does a negative mass balance of a glacier mean?
a: It loses more mass than it gains
It gains more snow than melts
61767.e: The mass balance is the difference between gain from snow and loss from melting. If it is negative, the ice volume shrinks.
61767.m: With a negative mass balance, more ice melts than new snow is added.

61768.q: How does the geodetic method for working out changes in volume work?
a: By analysing pollen in the ice
61768.e: Elevation models of the surface are made from aerial photos, laser scans or satellite data. Comparing two points in time shows the change in thickness and volume.
61768.m: Comparing elevation models shows how much ice a glacier has lost.

61769.q: What is the sudden outburst of a glacial lake with a flood wave called by experts?
61769.e: In a glacial outburst flood, a lake dammed by ice or moraine empties suddenly. In English it is also called a GLOF, in Icelandic a jökulhlaup.
61769.m: A glacial outburst flood is the sudden outburst of a glacial lake.

61770.q: Which valley in Valais was devastated in 1818 by the outburst of a lake dammed by ice from the Giétro Glacier?
61770.e: Ice falling from the Giétro Glacier dammed the Dranse into a lake. When the ice dam broke in June 1818, a flood wave swept through the Val de Bagnes as far as Martigny.
61770.m: The outburst flood of 1818 devastated the Val de Bagnes as far as Martigny.

61771.q: Which engineer had a tunnel dug through the ice dam at the Giétro Glacier in 1818 to lower the lake?
61771.e: Ignaz Venetz lowered the lake level considerably with the tunnel and so reduced the amount of floodwater. He later also became known as a pioneer of the Ice Age theory.
61771.m: In 1818 Ignaz Venetz fought the danger at the Giétro Glacier.

61772.q: Why can an ice-dammed lake suddenly empty once it reaches a certain depth?
a: The ice dam starts to float
The lake becomes too heavy for the rock
61772.e: Ice is lighter than water. If the lake gets deep enough, the water pressure lifts the ice dam and the water finds a way out under the glacier.
61772.m: An ice dam can float if the lake behind it gets too deep.

61773.q: Which valley is threatened by the Lac des Faverges at the Plaine Morte Glacier, which bursts out every year?
61773.e: Since 2011 the lake has emptied under the glacier almost every year. The water flows via the Trüebbach into the Simme at Lenk.
61773.m: When it bursts out, the Lac des Faverges threatens the area around Lenk in the Simmental.

61774.q: What measure was taken at the Plaine Morte Glacier in 2019 to reduce the danger of a large lake outburst?
a: A channel about 800 m long in the ice
61774.e: After the large outburst in 2018, a channel was cut through the ice so that the water could drain away continuously. Because it filled with snow in winter, a second channel was made in 2022.
61774.m: A channel in the ice lets the glacial lake drain in a controlled way.

61775.q: What was built at the Lower Grindelwald Glacier in 2009 to empty the glacial lake in a controlled way?
61775.e: A rockfall on the Eiger in 2006 had encouraged a lake to form. The tunnel from the glacier gorge protects the Lütschine valley from a flood wave.
61775.m: A tunnel protects Grindelwald from the glacial lake bursting out.

61776.q: Why are moraine-dammed glacial lakes considered especially dangerous?
a: The loose dam can erode quickly
The dam is made of concrete
61776.e: Moraines consist of loose debris. If water flows over the dam or seeps through it, it can quickly break open and cause a flood.
61776.m: Moraine dams are loose and can break suddenly.

61777.q: Which event can trigger a flood wave from a glacial lake without the dam breaking straight away?
a: Ice or rock falling into the lake
61777.e: If masses of ice or rock fall into the lake, they suddenly push water out of the way. The resulting surge wave can flow over the dam and destroy it.
61777.m: A fall into a glacial lake can cause a dangerous surge wave.

61778.q: Which alp in the Grisons was hit by the sudden draining of the Calderas glacial lake in June 2024?
61778.e: In June 2024 the Calderas glacial lake in the municipality of Surses drained without warning. The water triggered debris flows and threatened buildings near Tigias on the Alp Flix.
61778.m: In June 2024 a glacial outburst flood hit the Alp Flix.

a: A creeping mixture of debris and ice
A glacier made of pure ice
A glacier with blocks of ice in a lake
61779.e: Rock glaciers consist of frozen debris held together by ice in the spaces between the stones. They creep slowly downhill.
61779.m: A rock glacier is a creeping body of debris and ice.

61780.q: How high is the ice content under the layer of blocks of active rock glaciers often?
61780.e: Under the coarse top layer there is a body often containing 40 to 70% ice, sometimes more. This ice is part of the permafrost.
61780.m: Rock glaciers contain a lot of ice under their cover of debris.

61781.q: How fast do active rock glaciers typically move?
61781.e: Active rock glaciers usually creep only decimetres to metres per year. With warmer permafrost, many have become faster in recent decades.
61781.m: Rock glaciers usually creep less than a metre a year.

61782.q: What are active rock glaciers an important sign of?
61782.e: Active rock glaciers need permanently frozen ground. Their lower limit roughly matches the lower limit of patchy permafrost.

61783.q: In which region is the intensively studied Murtèl-Corvatsch rock glacier?
61783.e: A borehole was drilled at Murtèl-Corvatsch in 1987 and is one of the oldest permafrost measuring sites in the Alps. The Engadine is one of the best-studied rock glacier regions.
61783.m: The Murtèl-Corvatsch rock glacier lies in the Upper Engadine.

61784.q: Apart from frozen slope debris, what else can a rock glacier develop from?
61784.e: Rock glaciers can also develop from debris-covered cirque glaciers or debris-rich moraines. What matters is that ice and debris creep slowly in the permafrost.
61784.m: Debris-covered cirque glaciers can also become rock glaciers.

61785.q: Why are rock glaciers not counted by experts as true glaciers?
a: On the outside they consist only of debris
They do not move at all
61785.e: No ice can be seen on the surface, only coarse blocks. They form from frozen slope debris in permafrost and are classed under geomorphology.
61785.m: Rock glaciers are permafrost landforms, not real glaciers.

61786.q: How can you recognise an active rock glacier in the landscape?
a: By a green covering of grass
By bare ice on the surface
61786.e: Active rock glaciers have a steep front and a lumpy surface with ridges and furrows, similar to a lava flow. Inactive forms have gentler fronts and often plants growing on them.
