61786.m: An active rock glacier has a steep front and a lumpy surface.

61787.q: How thick are rock glaciers typically?
61787.e: Rock glaciers are usually 30 to 50 m thick, a few hundred metres long and 100 to 200 m wide. Some reach several kilometres in length.
61787.m: Rock glaciers are usually a few dozen metres thick.

61788.q: What is a fossil rock glacier?
a: An ice-free body of debris that no longer moves
A rock glacier under a glacier
61788.e: Fossil rock glaciers lie outside today’s permafrost and no longer contain ice. They are ice-free debris deposits of former rock glaciers.
61788.m: A fossil rock glacier no longer contains any ice.

61789.q: Roughly when was the Little Ice Age?
61789.e: The Little Ice Age was a cooler phase from the late Middle Ages into the 19th century. Around 1850 many Alpine glaciers reached their last maximum.
61789.m: The Little Ice Age lasted roughly from the 14th to the 19th century.

61790.q: How can you often recognise the glacier extent of around 1850 in the landscape today?
a: By moraine ridges with hardly any plants
By erratic boulders on the Swiss Plateau
By kettle lakes in the Jura
61790.e: The moraines of 1850 are young and therefore have only sparse plant cover. They clearly frame the areas in front of the glaciers.
61790.m: Young moraines with hardly any plants show the glacier extent around 1850.

61791.q: Which phase of low solar activity fell within the Little Ice Age?
61791.e: In the Maunder Minimum from 1645 to 1715, hardly any sunspots were observed. The slightly reduced radiation probably contributed to regional cooling.
61791.m: The Maunder Minimum was a time with very few sunspots.

61792.q: Which volcanic eruption in Iceland came before the particularly harsh winter of 1783/84?
61792.e: The Laki fissure released gases and sulphur for months in 1783. Europe then had an exceptionally cold winter.
61792.m: The Laki eruption of 1783 brought Europe a harsh winter.

61793.q: Which glacier reached particularly far down into the valley at its maximum around 1855, to about 1000 m above sea level?
61793.e: Around 1855 its tongue reached far out of the gorge towards Grindelwald-Grund. Today it lies high up in the gorge.
61793.m: Around 1855 the Lower Grindelwald Glacier reached almost into the village.

61794.q: In how many major phases did Alpine glaciers advance during the Little Ice Age?
61794.e: The glaciers advanced in the late 16th century, around the middle of the 17th century and until the middle of the 19th century. In doing so they destroyed farms and settlements.
61794.m: Alpine glaciers advanced strongly three times in the Little Ice Age.

61795.q: Roughly how far has the tongue of the Great Aletsch Glacier retreated since 1870?
61795.e: After the maximum of the Little Ice Age, the tongue has retreated more than 3 km up the valley since 1870. In places the ice has become over 100 m thinner since 1850.
61795.m: The Aletsch Glacier has become more than three kilometres shorter since 1870.

61796.q: Which hypothesis explains why Alpine glaciers began to retreat from about 1860, even though it had hardly got any warmer?
a: Soot from industry darkened the snow
More rainfall made the ice melt
Earthquakes broke off the glacier tongues
A higher albedo warmed the air
61796.e: A 2013 study puts the early retreat down to soot from burning coal. The dark soot lowered the albedo of the snow and increased melting.
61796.m: Industrial soot probably sped up glacier retreat after 1850.

61797.q: Why is the glacier extent around 1850 often used as a reference point for comparisons?
a: It is the last maximum before the warming
It was the first to be measured by satellite
The glaciers were at their smallest then
It marks the end of the Würm glaciation
61797.e: Around 1850 many Alpine glaciers reached their last maximum, and after that industrialisation and warming began. The clearly visible moraines allow an exact comparison.
61797.m: The maximum around 1850 is the usual starting point for glacier comparisons.

61798.q: What effect did the glacier advances of the Little Ice Age have on mountain villages?
a: The passes were open all year
61798.e: Advancing glaciers destroyed alpine huts, fields and some houses. Some communities held processions of prayer so that the ice would stop.
61798.m: In the Little Ice Age advancing glaciers threatened farms and pastures.

61799.q: What rank did the Gorner Glacier system have for connected glacier area in the Alps (as of 2017)?
61799.e: At about 41 km² (2017), the Gorner Glacier system is the second largest connected glacier area in the Alps after the Aletsch Glacier.
61799.m: The Gorner Glacier is the second largest glacier system in the Alps.

61800.q: Roughly how long was the Gorner Glacier in 2013?
61800.e: At about 12.4 km, it was the third longest glacier in the Alps in 2013. It lies in the Monte Rosa massif south-east of Zermatt.
61800.m: The Gorner Glacier is about twelve kilometres long.

61801.q: Which glacier is the main branch of the Gorner Glacier system and begins at the Signalkuppe?
61801.e: The Grenz Glacier starts at the 4554 m Signalkuppe and flows north-west along the Lyskamm. It forms the main stream of the system.
61801.m: The Grenz Glacier is the main branch of the Gorner Glacier.

61802.q: What happens to the Gornersee, which forms every spring where the Grenz and Gorner Glaciers meet?
a: It empties in a few days in summer
It freezes into a solid block of ice
It is pumped out through a pipeline
61802.e: Between June and September, the ice-dammed lake usually drains within a few days. The flow in the Gornerbach then rises to up to 150 m³/s.
61802.m: The Gornersee drains within a few days every summer.

61803.q: Which hut stands at 2883 m on a rocky ridge above the former meeting point of the Gorner and Grenz Glaciers?
61803.e: The Monte Rosa Hut is the starting point for climbing Monte Rosa. From the Gornergrat you reach it across the glacier.
61803.m: The Monte Rosa Hut sits high above the Gorner Glacier.

61804.q: In which year did the Gorner Glacier reach its last maximum?
61804.e: By 1859 the glacier had advanced about 600 m in about 60 years, destroying alpine huts and farmland. It has been retreating ever since.
61804.m: The Gorner Glacier reached its last maximum in 1859.

61805.q: Into which river does the meltwater of the Gorner Glacier flow in Zermatt?
61805.e: The Gornerbach feeds the Gornera via the Furggbach, and in Zermatt the Gornera joins other streams to form the Matter Vispa. This flows through the Matter Valley to the Rhône.
61805.m: Water from the Gorner Glacier flows via the Matter Vispa to the Rhône.

61806.q: What happened in the Gorner Glacier system in 2019?
a: The Gorner and Grenz Glaciers separated
61806.e: Because of the loss of ice, the connection between the upper Gorner Glacier and the Grenz Glacier broke in 2019. As a result, the connected area dropped sharply.
61806.m: In 2019 the Gorner Glacier separated from the Grenz Glacier.

61807.q: The Gorner Glacier system covered about 66 km² in 1850 and about 41 km² in 2015. By roughly what percentage has it shrunk?
61807.e: Calculation: (66 − 41) ÷ 66 = 25 ÷ 66 ≈ 0.38. So more than a third of the area has disappeared.
61807.m: The Gorner Glacier system has lost over a third of its area since 1850.

61808.q: In which mountain massif does the Gorner Glacier lie?
61808.e: The Gorner Glacier lies south-east of Zermatt in the Monte Rosa massif. Its accumulation area reaches up to the summit region above 4000 m.
61808.m: The Gorner Glacier flows down from the Monte Rosa massif.

61809.q: Why do researchers drill ice cores from the glacier high up on Monte Rosa?
a: The ice stores climate data from past centuries
The ice is sold as drinking water
They are looking for oil under the ice
They use them to measure earthquakes
61809.e: At the Colle Gnifetti at 4452 m, the ice is very cold and hardly melts. Dust, gases and traces of past temperatures are trapped in its layers.
61809.m: Ice cores are an archive of the climate.

61810.q: What has happened to the former tongue of the Gorner Glacier, the Boden Glacier?
a: It has melted away because of the retreat
It was buried by a rockslide
It was removed for a reservoir
It advanced as far as Zermatt
61810.e: The tongue was called the Boden Glacier after the alpine settlement “Im Boden”. Since its maximum in 1859, the glacier has retreated so far that this section has disappeared.
61810.m: The Boden Glacier has disappeared because of glacier retreat.

61811.q: From which mountain did the mass of rock break away in 1806 that buried the village of Goldau?
61811.e: The break began at the Gnipenspitze on the southern flank of the Rossberg. From there the layers slid about 1000 m down into the valley between the Rossberg and the Rigi.
61811.m: The Goldau rockslide came from the Rossberg.

61812.q: Roughly how many people died in the Goldau rockslide of 1806?
61812.e: 457 people died in the rockslide, as well as 323 head of cattle. After the Basel earthquake, it is considered the largest documented natural disaster in Switzerland.
61812.m: The Goldau rockslide killed about 450 people.

61813.q: Which rock layer acted as a sliding surface in the Goldau rockslide?
61813.e: Water seeped through cracks in the Nagelfluh and softened the marl beneath. The Nagelfluh slid down the valley on this slippery layer.
61813.m: At Goldau softened marl became a slide for the Nagelfluh.

61814.q: Roughly what was the volume of the Goldau rockslide?
61814.e: Almost 40 million cubic metres of Nagelfluh crashed into the valley and covered about 6.5 km². That is more than ten times the Bondo rockslide of 2017.
61814.m: At Goldau almost 40 million cubic metres of rock crashed into the valley.

61815.q: What effect did the Goldau rockslide have on Lake Lauerz?
a: A flood wave about 20 m high
It drained through a new outlet
61815.e: Part of the mass fell into the lake and, according to eyewitnesses, set off a wave about 20 m high. The lake also lost about a seventh of its area.
61815.m: The Goldau rockslide caused a high flood wave in Lake Lauerz.

61816.q: Roughly how long did the actual fall of the rock masses at Goldau last?
61816.e: The mass raced from the Rossberg into the valley in less than three minutes. Escape was therefore impossible for most residents.
61816.m: The Goldau rockslide lasted only a few minutes.

61817.q: What is the Goldau rockslide considered the starting point of in Swiss history?
a: The first nationwide collection of donations
61817.e: After the disaster, money for victims of a natural disaster was collected throughout Switzerland for the first time. The rockslide was also the first to be studied scientifically.
61817.m: Goldau started the tradition of nationwide donation appeals in Switzerland.

61818.q: Why did the slope of the Rossberg already lack support at its foot before 1806?
a: An Ice Age glacier had worn it away
A quarry had hollowed it out
Road building had cut into it
61818.e: During the Ice Age, an arm of the Reuss Glacier eroded the foot of the slope. The layers, tilted down towards the valley, were left exposed without support.
61818.m: Ice Age glaciers weakened the foot of the Rossberg.

61819.q: Which leisure attraction today lies in the middle of the area covered by the Goldau rockslide?
61819.e: The Goldau Nature and Animal Park lies among huge boulders from 1806. The boulders still shape the landscape today.
61819.m: In Goldau Animal Park you walk among rockslide boulders.

61820.q: What happened on Piz Cengalo years before the rockslide of 2017?
a: A large rockfall into the Val Bondasca
Nothing, the face was considered stable
61820.e: On 27 December 2011, 1.5 to 2 million cubic metres of rock fell into the Val Bondasca. After that the flank was monitored constantly.
61820.m: A large mass of rock already fell from Piz Cengalo in 2011.

61821.q: What was a large catch basin built above Bondo in 2014 and 2015 for?
a: To hold back debris flows from the Val Bondasca
As a swimming lake for tourists
61821.e: The basin held about 50,000 m³, or about 200,000 m³ including the extra margin. Even so, the debris flows of 2017 filled it several times.
61821.m: The Bondo basin is meant to hold back debris flows.

61822.q: How was Bondo warned of approaching debris flows from the Val Bondasca after 2012?
a: Trip wires set off traffic lights and text messages
Seismometers in the village set off sirens
Watchmen on a hut report by radio
A gauge in the village stream rings the church bells
61822.e: Trip wires are stretched across the stream bed above the village. If a debris flow breaks them, traffic lights turn red and those in charge receive a text message.
61822.m: In Bondo broken wires set off the debris flow alarm.

61823.q: Roughly how much warning time did the alarm system in the Val Bondasca provide?
61823.e: The sensors are about a kilometre above the village. Before a debris flow arrives, there are about four minutes left to close roads and bridges.
61823.m: A few minutes’ warning is enough to close roads in time.

61824.q: Why could a debris flow form in Bondo straight after the rockslide in 2017, even though it was not raining?
a: The rock smashed a small glacier
A reservoir in the valley burst
A thunderstorm the evening before had soaked the ground
61824.e: The mass of rock hit a small glacier below the face. The crushed ice and meltwater turned the mass into a liquid debris flow.
61824.m: Crushed glacier ice can turn a mass of rock into a debris flow.

61825.q: Which process is considered an important cause of the instability of the north face of Piz Cengalo?
61825.e: Rising temperatures make the ice in the rock clefts thaw, which used to hold the rock together. The steep granite face therefore loses strength.
61825.m: Thawing permafrost loosens steep rock faces.

61826.q: Roughly how many buildings in and around Bondo were damaged in 2017?
61826.e: The debris flows damaged 99 buildings, a third of them beyond repair. Destroyed barns and alpine huts came on top of that.
61826.m: The debris flows of 2017 damaged almost a hundred buildings in Bondo.

61827.q: Where were the eight missing people when the Bondo rockslide happened in 2017?
a: On a hike in the Val Bondasca
On a building site in the village
On a train in the Bregaglia
61827.e: All eight had spent the night in the Sciora Hut and were on their way through the Val Bondasca below Piz Cengalo. The village itself had been evacuated in time.
61827.m: The Sciora Hut lies in the Val Bondasca below Piz Cengalo.

61828.q: Roughly how high was the damage from the Bondo rockslide of 2017?
61828.e: At the end of 2017 the costs were estimated at about 41 million francs. About two million were raised through donations.
61828.m: The Bondo rockslide cost several dozen million francs.

61829.q: Which glacier broke off above Blatten on 28 May 2025?
61829.e: The Birch Glacier lies on the south-east slope above Blatten in the Lötschental. It was overloaded with rock debris and collapsed almost completely.
61829.m: In 2025 the Birch Glacier buried the village of Blatten.

61830.q: From which peak did rock fall onto the Birch Glacier for days before it broke off?
61830.e: The rock face of the Kleines Nesthorn became unstable from mid-May 2025 and broke away in several falls. The debris piled up on the glacier.
61830.m: Rock from the Kleines Nesthorn overloaded the Birch Glacier.

61831.q: Why did the Birch Glacier collapse in May 2025?
a: Millions of tonnes of rock debris overloaded it
A lake under the ice burst out
61831.e: At the end of May about 9 million tonnes of rock lay on the glacier. The extra weight sped the ice up to about 10 m per day in the end, until it broke off.
61831.m: Too much rock debris can make a glacier collapse.

61832.q: What was unusual about the Birch Glacier in the years before 2025?
61832.e: From about 2019 the lower part advanced about 50 m, while almost all Alpine glaciers were shrinking. The cause was the growing load of debris from above.
61832.m: An advancing glacier can be a warning sign.

61833.q: Which river was dammed into a lake by the masses of debris at Blatten?
61833.e: The deposit blocked the Lonza over more than 2 km. The resulting lake flooded the parts of the village that had not been buried.
61833.m: The debris cone at Blatten dammed the Lonza.

61834.q: When did the authorities order the evacuation of Blatten?
61834.e: About 300 people had to leave Blatten and Ried within two hours, nine days before the collapse. The early evacuation prevented a large number of victims.
61834.m: The early evacuation saved many lives in Blatten.

61835.q: What magnitude did the Swiss Seismological Service record during the main collapse at Blatten?
61835.e: The impact of the masses of ice and rock produced a signal of magnitude 3.1. For a glacier collapse, that is a very strong signal.
61835.m: Large mass movements produce measurable earthquake signals.

61836.q: Roughly what share of the village of Blatten was buried?
61836.e: About 130 houses and the church lie under the debris cone, about nine tenths of the village. In places the cone is up to 100 m thick.
61836.m: Almost the whole village of Blatten lies under the debris.

61837.q: Why had the Birch Glacier already been monitored since the 1990s?
a: Because of an ice break-off in December 1993
Because of a glacial outburst flood in summer 1987
Because of an earthquake in January 1996
Because of a debris flow in autumn 1999
61837.e: On 18 December 1993 a large block of ice broke off. Since then the glacier had been monitored, which made an early warning possible in 2025.
61837.m: Earlier events are often the reason for later monitoring.

61838.q: How many francs did the Swiss Insurance Association estimate the damage in Blatten at?
61838.e: The Insurance Association estimated about 320 million francs of insured damage. In addition, forest, farmland and a nature reserve were lost.
61838.m: The glacier collapse at Blatten caused damage worth hundreds of millions of francs.

61839.q: Which institute in Davos issues the avalanche bulletin in Switzerland?
a: The WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF
The Federal Office of Topography swisstopo
The Federal Office for the Environment FOEN
61839.e: The SLF in Davos produces the avalanche bulletin every day in winter. It was put to a particularly hard test in the avalanche winter of 1999.
61839.m: The SLF in Davos warns of avalanches.

61840.q: Which village in Valais suffered the most avalanche deaths in Switzerland in February 1999?
61840.e: On 21 February 1999 avalanches buried houses and roads in Evolène in the Val d’Hérens. Twelve people died.
61840.m: Evolène was hit hardest by avalanches in 1999.

61841.q: Which village in Tyrol was hit by an avalanche with 31 deaths in February 1999?
61841.e: In Galtür in the Paznaun Valley, 31 people died on 23 February 1999. The disaster showed the scale of that winter across the whole Alpine region.
61841.m: Galtür is the best-known disaster of the 1999 avalanche winter outside Switzerland.

61842.q: Roughly how many damaging avalanches were counted in Switzerland in the winter of 1998/99?
61842.e: The SLF recorded about 1200 avalanches that caused damage. Most came down in the third period of snowfall in February.
61842.m: In the avalanche winter of 1999 over a thousand damaging avalanches came down.

61843.q: Which weather situation brought the huge amounts of snow to the Swiss Alps in February 1999?
a: A southerly upslope situation with foehn
A stable area of high pressure
61843.e: Three north-westerly situations repeatedly brought moist air against the northern side of the Alps at the end of January and in February. The fresh snow added up to several metres.
61843.m: Repeated north-westerly upslope situations caused the avalanche winter of 1999.

61844.q: Which avalanche danger level applied in parts of the Swiss Alps in February 1999?
61844.e: The European avalanche danger scale has five levels. In February 1999 the highest level, 5, was issued several times.
61844.m: In the avalanche winter of 1999 the highest danger level 5 applied in places.

61845.q: How high was the direct and indirect damage to property in the avalanche winter of 1999 in Switzerland?
61845.e: Buildings, forest, roads and lost tourism income added up to over 600 million francs. Many valleys were cut off for days.
61845.m: The avalanche winter of 1999 caused damage worth hundreds of millions of francs.

61846.q: Which protective structures in the starting zone are meant to stop an avalanche from breaking away at all?
61846.e: Snow-supporting structures hold the snowpack in place on steep slopes. Galleries, dams and deflecting walls only protect once the avalanche is already moving.
61846.m: Snow-supporting structures stop avalanches from breaking away.

61847.q: Which maps show municipalities where building is not allowed, or only with conditions, because of avalanches?
61847.e: Hazard maps divide the land into red, blue and yellow zones. In red zones, building is generally forbidden.
61847.m: Hazard maps show where building is dangerous because of avalanches.

61848.q: In which place in the Grisons is the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF based?
61848.e: The SLF has its headquarters in Davos. From there it also produces the avalanche bulletin for the whole of Switzerland.
61848.m: The SLF in Davos produces the avalanche bulletin.

61849.q: Where above Davos was a snow laboratory with a test field for avalanche research opened in 1936?
61849.e: Systematic snow research began on the Weissfluhjoch at about 2660 m. An SLF test field is still there today.
61849.m: The Weissfluhjoch is the birthplace of Swiss avalanche research.

61850.q: How often does the SLF publish the avalanche bulletin in winter?
61850.e: In winter the bulletin comes out at 5 pm and is updated at 8 am. This means snowfall overnight is quickly taken into account.
61850.m: In winter the avalanche bulletin comes out twice a day.

61851.q: How many levels does the European avalanche danger scale have, which the SLF also uses?
61851.e: The scale goes from level 1 “low” to level 5 “very high”. Special care is already needed at level 3 “considerable”.
61851.m: Avalanche danger is given in five levels.

61852.q: Why are slopes of about 30 to 45 degrees particularly dangerous for slab avalanches?
a: Snow stays there but can easily slide off
The snow melts there at once
61852.e: On gentle slopes snow hardly slides off, while on very steep ones it keeps sliding away. In between, a lot of snow builds up that can slide off as a slab.
61852.m: Most slab avalanches break away on slopes from about 30 degrees.

61853.q: In which year was the Federal Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research founded in Davos?
61853.e: In 1931 an avalanche commission was first set up in Bern, followed by the federal institute in 1942. This gave avalanche research a permanent institution.
61853.m: The Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research was founded in the middle of the Second World War.

61854.q: At which avalanche danger level do most fatal avalanche accidents happen in Switzerland?
61854.e: At level 3, slab avalanches can often be triggered by just one person, yet many people still go out. That is why most deaths happen at this level.
61854.m: Most avalanche deaths happen at considerable danger.

61855.q: Which buried layer is regarded as a typical weak layer for slab avalanches in the snowpack?
61855.e: Surface hoar forms on clear nights from fine ice crystals. If it is snowed over, it remains a weak sliding layer for a long time.
61855.m: Buried surface hoar is a dangerous weak layer.

61856.q: Where has the SLF had its headquarters since 1996?
61856.e: At the end of 1996 the SLF moved into its new headquarters on Flüelastrasse in Davos Dorf. Birmensdorf is the headquarters of the WSL, not the SLF.
61856.m: The SLF has its headquarters in Davos Dorf.

61857.q: Which weather situation caused the extreme rainfall on the northern side of the Alps in August 2005?
61857.e: A low moved across the Adriatic towards the north-east and drove moist Mediterranean air from the north against the Alps. It rained heavily there for days.
61857.m: Vb lows often bring particularly heavy, long-lasting rain to the northern side of the Alps.

61858.q: Roughly how much did the damage from the August 2005 floods in Switzerland amount to?
61858.e: The damage was first put at 2.5 billion and later at about 3 billion francs. A large part affected buildings and infrastructure.
61858.m: The 2005 floods caused damage worth billions.

61859.q: Which resort in Obwalden could only be reached by helicopter in August 2005?
61859.e: The Engelberger Aa destroyed the road and railway line. Train services stopped until a new bridge opened in December.
61859.m: In 2005 Engelberg was cut off by the floods.

61860.q: Roughly how high did Lake Lucerne rise above its normal level in August 2005?
61860.e: The lake rose about two metres above its normal level. In Lucerne, parts of the old town were under water.
61860.m: In 2005 Lake Lucerne clearly burst its banks.

61861.q: Which village in the Prättigau was widely flooded in August 2005, in places up to 3 m deep?
61861.e: The Landquart burst its banks in Klosters. In some places the water was up to three metres deep.
61861.m: The Grisons was also badly hit by the floods in 2005.

61862.q: What did the federal government expand in particular as a result of the 2005 floods?
a: Warnings and alerts for natural hazards
Building new dams on the Swiss Plateau
A ban on building along all rivers
61862.e: With the OWARNA project (optimising warnings and alerts for natural hazards), the federal government improved its warnings. Among other things, this led to the joint natural hazards platform of the federal government.
61862.m: After 2005 the federal government expanded warnings of natural hazards.

61863.q: Which river in Schwyz carried about 21 times its normal amount of water at the Brunnen gauge in August 2005?
61863.e: The Muota swelled enormously in the Muotathal and at Brunnen. It flows into Lake Lucerne at Brunnen.
61863.m: In 2005 the Muota carried many times its normal amount of water.

61864.q: Why does it rain particularly heavily on the northern side of the Alps in a Vb situation?
a: Moist Mediterranean air is pushed against the Alps from the north
Dry polar air sinks over the Alps
Warm Saharan air brings thunderstorms from the south
Atlantic air is completely blocked by the Jura
61864.e: The low carries moist air from the Mediterranean in an arc around the Alps. Pushed against the mountains from the north, it rises and rains out.
61864.m: In Vb situations moist air is pushed against the Alps from the north.

61865.q: Which town between two lakes was flooded in August 2005 when Lake Thun rose almost a metre above its damage level?
61865.e: Lake Thun was almost a metre above the damage level. Low-lying districts of Interlaken were under water.
61865.m: High lake levels endanger places on the shore.

61866.q: What is the front part of a debris flow, full of boulders, called?
61866.e: The largest boulders gather at the head, which is why it is particularly destructive. A more liquid part follows behind it.
61866.m: The head is the most dangerous part of a debris flow.

61867.q: What is the fan-shaped deposit at the mouth of a mountain stream valley, on which villages often stand, called?
61867.e: Mountain streams deposit rubble in a fan shape as they enter the flat main valley. Settlements often stand on these fans and are therefore particularly at risk.
61867.m: Many mountain villages stand on alluvial fans of mountain streams.

61868.q: What makes a debris flow different from a flood carrying bedload?
a: Water and solids flow as one mixture
It consists only of water and mud
It moves more slowly than a glacier
61868.e: In a debris flow, water, mud and stones move together as a dense mixture. With bedload, on the other hand, the stones just roll along the bottom of the flowing water.
61868.m: In a debris flow, water and rock flow as one mush.

61869.q: What are the flexible steel cable nets called that hold back debris flows in mountain streams?
61869.e: Ring net barriers are stretched across a stream channel. They hold back rubble and let water through.
61869.m: Ring nets can catch rubble from debris flows.

61870.q: Why is more and more loose material available for debris flows high up in the Alps?
a: Permafrost is thawing and glaciers are releasing debris
More trees are growing up to the summits
Almost all precipitation falls as snow
The streams carry less water in summer
61870.e: Where permafrost thaws and glaciers shrink, a lot of loose debris is exposed. Heavy rain can easily set it moving.
61870.m: Shrinking ice exposes debris that can turn into debris flows.

61871.q: How fast can debris flows typically flow in steep channels?
61871.e: Debris flows reach several metres per second in steep channels. That is too fast to get out of the way in the stream bed.
61871.m: Debris flows are much faster than landslides.

61872.q: Which weather most often triggers debris flows in the Alps?
a: Violent thunderstorms or long periods of steady rain
61872.e: A lot of water in a short time soaks the debris in steep channels. Then it can break loose as a debris flow and flow into the valley.
61872.m: Heavy rainfall is the most common trigger of debris flows.

61873.q: Why do many debris basins have a barrier with openings at the outlet instead of a solid wall?
a: Coarse boulders get caught while water flows away
So fish can swim upstream to spawn
It increases the pressure on the wall
The basin empties itself during floods
61873.e: The openings or beams hold back large boulders and wood. Water and fine material flow on, so the basin does not fill up with water unnecessarily.
61873.m: Permeable barriers separate rubble from water.

61874.q: What is often left lying along the sides of the path of a debris flow?
61874.e: Coarse boulders are left at the edge of the debris flow and form ridges along the sides. They reveal earlier debris flows in the landscape.
61874.m: Side ridges of boulders show where debris flows ran in the past.

61875.q: Which colour marks the zone with medium danger and building conditions on Swiss hazard maps?
61875.e: In the blue zone building is allowed with conditions, such as reinforced walls or raised entrances. The danger there is medium.
61875.m: In the blue zone of the hazard map, building is only allowed with conditions.

61876.q: What does the yellow zone on a Swiss hazard map mean?
61876.e: Yellow areas show a low danger. People inside buildings are hardly at risk, but damage to buildings is possible.
61876.m: Yellow on the hazard map indicates a low danger.

61877.q: What do yellow and white hatched areas on Swiss hazard maps show?
a: A residual danger from very rare events
Areas that have not been studied
Danger zones already protected by structures
61877.e: The hatching stands for events with a very low probability but possibly high intensity. This can be important for sensitive buildings such as hospitals.
61877.m: Yellow and white hatching means a residual danger.

61878.q: Which two factors are combined to sort areas into the danger levels of a hazard map?
a: Slope angle and height above sea level
61878.e: The danger level comes from a matrix of the strength of the event and its probability. Frequent strong events give red, rare weak ones give yellow.
61878.m: The danger level depends on intensity and probability.

61879.q: Which return periods are usually considered for Swiss hazard maps?
61879.e: For frequent, medium and rare events, scenarios with return periods of 30, 100 and 300 years are studied. Even rarer events count as residual danger.
61879.m: Hazard maps are based on scenarios for 30, 100 and 300 years.

61880.q: For which natural hazards do the Swiss cantons produce hazard maps?
61880.e: Hazard maps show where floods, avalanches, landslides and falling stones and boulders are a threat. They are based on the Forest Act and the Hydraulic Engineering Act.
61880.m: Hazard maps show floods, avalanches, landslides and rockfall dangers.

61881.q: Who is responsible for producing hazard maps in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office for the Environment alone
61881.e: The cantons draw up the maps, and the federal government supports them with expertise and money. The municipalities put them into practice in their planning.
61881.m: Hazard maps are produced by the cantons.

61882.q: How do hazard maps become legally binding for landowners?
a: By being included in land use planning
By being entered in the criminal record
By being published in the avalanche bulletin
61882.e: The municipalities transfer the hazard areas into the zoning plan and building regulations. Only then do they apply to planning applications.
61882.m: Hazard maps affect building through the zoning plan.

61883.q: What usually applies to the red zone on a Swiss hazard map?
a: You may only build with reinforced walls
There is no known danger there
61883.e: Red means considerable danger, for example from strong avalanche pressure. People are at risk there even inside buildings, so building is banned.
61883.m: In the red zone building is generally banned.

61884.q: Roughly what share of Swiss forest is protective forest?
61884.e: About half of Swiss forest protects people, settlements and transport routes from natural hazards. The cantons mark out these forests using uniform criteria.
61884.m: About half of Swiss forest is protective forest.

61885.q: Which natural hazards does a protective forest in the mountains mainly protect against?
a: Avalanches, rockfall, landslides and debris flows
61885.e: Trees support the snowpack, slow down stones, hold the soil together with their roots and hold back water. Their care follows the federal NaiS guidelines.
61885.m: Protective forest protects against avalanches, rockfall, landslides and debris flows.

61886.q: Which village in Uri placed the forest above it under protection as early as 1397 with a ban charter?
61886.e: The ban charter forbade cutting trees in the forest above Andermatt, because it protected against avalanches. It is an early example of the idea of protective forests.
61886.m: Andermatt protected its forest as early as the Middle Ages.

61887.q: Which federal law placed mountain forests under federal supervision in 1876 after severe floods?
61887.e: After floods in the 1860s, people recognised the effects of large-scale clear-cutting. The Forest Police Act banned reducing the forest area in the high mountains.
61887.m: Since 1876 the federal government has protected mountain forests by law.

61888.q: Why is a mixed mountain forest of different ages a better protective forest than one where all trees are the same age?
a: It renews itself constantly and stays stable
It no longer needs any care
It casts no shadows in winter
61888.e: Trees of different species and ages do not all fail at the same time. Young trees fill gaps before the protective effect is lost.
61888.m: A varied forest protects for longer than a uniform one.

61889.q: How does a dense mountain forest prevent avalanches from breaking away inside it?
a: Trunks support the snowpack and crowns catch snow
The roots heat up the ground
The forest steers the wind onto the peaks
The needles make snow melt at once
61889.e: The trunks anchor the snowpack and stop it from sliding. The crowns hold back snow, so fewer even layers form.
61889.m: A dense forest stops avalanches from breaking away.

61890.q: Why are long gaps along the line of fall in a forest that protects against rockfall dangerous?
a: Stones gain speed without being slowed
The ground dries out faster there
61890.e: Without trunks, falling stones are not slowed down and get faster and faster. Further down, the trees can then no longer stop them.
61890.m: Gaps in protective forest let stones through unchecked.

61891.q: Through which instrument has the federal government contributed to the care of protective forests since 2008?
a: A protective forest tax by the municipalities
Donations through the Swiss Solidarity charity
61891.e: With the reform of fiscal equalisation (NFA), the federal government and cantons sign four-year programme agreements. The federal government pays for work carried out.
61891.m: The federal government and cantons fund protective forests together.

61892.q: Which beetle particularly threatens protective forests rich in spruce after storms and dry summers?
61892.e: The European spruce bark beetle breeds in huge numbers in weakened spruces. Infested trees die and tear gaps in the protective forest.
61892.m: The spruce bark beetle can kill whole stands of spruce.

61893.q: Which municipality in the Grisons has Brienz/Brinzauls belonged to since 2015?
61893.e: Brienz/Brinzauls was a separate municipality until 2014. Since the merger, the village has belonged to Albula/Alvra in the Albula Valley.

61894.q: Roughly how fast was the village of Brienz/Brinzauls sliding down the valley in 2019?
61894.e: The whole village sits on a sliding mass and moved about one metre per year in 2019. This caused cracks in the houses.
61894.m: In Brienz/Brinzauls the ground is moving together with the whole village.

61895.q: What came down above Brienz/Brinzauls in the night of 15 to 16 June 2023?
a: A large flow of rock debris
A debris flow from a glacial lake
61895.e: About 1.2 million cubic metres of rock came down as a debris flow. It stopped just short of the village, which had been evacuated beforehand.
61895.m: In June 2023 a debris flow came down above Brienz/Brinzauls.

61896.q: Where did the debris flow of June 2023 in Brienz/Brinzauls come to a stop?
a: A few metres from the edge of the village
In the middle of the village square
On the opposite slope near Surava
61896.e: The debris flow stopped just short of the first houses. The village had been evacuated beforehand.
61896.m: In Brienz/Brinzauls the debris stopped just short of the village.

61897.q: Which measure is meant to slow down the landslide at Brienz/Brinzauls in the long term?
a: A concrete wall at the foot of the slope
61897.e: A tunnel in the stable rock under the landslide is meant to drain water away. Less water pressure in the ground slows the movement.
61897.m: Less water in the ground slows a landslide.

61898.q: How is the movement of the slope near Brienz/Brinzauls monitored?
a: Constantly with radar, GPS and other instruments
With only one photo a year
With weather balloons above the village
With instruments on the bed of Lake Maggiore
61898.e: Radar devices, GPS stations and other sensors measure the movement around the clock. This means warnings and evacuations can happen in time.
61898.m: The landslide at Brienz/Brinzauls is monitored around the clock.

61899.q: When did the people of Brienz/Brinzauls have to be evacuated for the second time?
61899.e: Because of increasing movement and the threat of debris falls, residents had to leave the village by 17 November 2024. The evacuation was still continuing in 2025.

61900.q: What rate of movement was measured in the village of Brienz/Brinzauls in autumn 2024?
61900.e: In autumn 2024 the landslide sped up to just under 250 cm per year. Drainage boreholes slowed it down considerably by 2025.
61900.m: The landslide at Brienz/Brinzauls sped up a lot in 2024.

61901.q: Which measure did the municipality plan for buildings in Brienz/Brinzauls in 2025?
a: A protective gallery over the village
61901.e: Buildings are to be moved to safe places on a voluntary basis. Owners could sign up for this in 2025.
61901.m: A partial relocation is being prepared in Brienz/Brinzauls.

61902.q: Which earthquake on 25 July 1855 is considered one of the strongest in Switzerland in recent centuries?
61902.e: The earthquake in the Visp Valley, with an estimated magnitude of around 6.4, damaged many buildings and churches. Rockfalls broke loose in the Matter Valley.
61902.m: The Visp Valley had a very strong earthquake in 1855.

61903.q: In which area was the epicentre of the Valais earthquake of 25 January 1946?
61903.e: The epicentre lay in the Bernese Alps north of Sion. Damage occurred mainly in the Rhône Valley between Sion and Leuk.
61903.m: The 1946 earthquake had its centre in the Rawil area.

61904.q: What did the strong aftershock of 30 May 1946 in Valais trigger?
a: A flood wave on Lake Geneva
61904.e: The aftershock on Ascension Day 1946 made a mass of rock on the Rawilhorn collapse. In this way earthquakes can trigger other natural hazards.

61905.q: How great is the earthquake risk in the Rhône Valley in Valais compared with the rest of Switzerland?
a: It is one of the areas most at risk
It is at the same risk as the Swiss Plateau
It is one of the areas least at risk
There is no earthquake risk there
61905.e: Valais lies in Switzerland’s highest earthquake zone. Strong shaking with severe damage to buildings is possible there.
61905.m: The Rhône Valley lies in Switzerland’s highest earthquake zone.

61906.q: Why are earthquake waves particularly amplified in the Rhône Valley in Valais?
a: Soft, loose sediments fill the valley
The valley lies above a volcano
The glaciers press on the rock
61906.e: Thick, soft deposits make the ground movement swing more strongly. Damage there can be greater than on rock.

61907.q: What does earthquake microzonation, such as that produced for Sion or Brig-Visp, show?
a: The influence of the local ground
61907.e: Microzonations show how strongly the ground changes the earthquake waves at a particular place. Buildings can then be designed accordingly.
61907.m: Microzonations take the ground into account.

61908.q: What has the Valais building law required of all building projects since 2018?
61908.e: Since 1 January 2018 all building projects in Valais have had to be designed according to the SIA 260 earthquake standards. The canton checks this in the planning permission process.
61908.m: Since 2018 every building project in Valais must be earthquake-resistant.

61909.q: According to the canton of Valais, how high could the damage from a magnitude 6 earthquake near Sion be?
61909.e: Because of the dense building in the Rhône Valley, the canton expects damage worth billions. Earthquakes are therefore considered a major risk.
61909.m: A strong earthquake near Sion could cause billions in damage.

61910.q: What does the intensity of an earthquake describe, as opposed to its magnitude?
a: The effect at a particular place
The energy released at the source
The depth of the earthquake source
61910.e: Intensity is graded according to observed damage and what people felt, and it decreases with distance. Magnitude, on the other hand, is a single value for the whole earthquake.
61910.m: Intensity describes the effect of an earthquake at one place.

61911.q: Which pressure pattern typically leads to a bise situation?
a: High pressure in the north, low pressure over the Mediterranean
Low pressure in the north, high pressure over the Mediterranean
High pressure over the Azores, low pressure over Iceland
Low pressure over the Bay of Biscay, high pressure over Italy
61911.e: If there is high pressure north of Switzerland and low pressure over the Mediterranean, air flows from north-east Europe into Central Europe. We experience this flow as the bise.
61911.m: A high in the north and a low in the south create the bise.

61912.q: Why does the bise reach particularly high speeds on Lake Geneva?
a: The Jura and the Alps come closer together and act like a nozzle
The warm lake sucks the air in strongly
The foehn from Valais strengthens it
There are no hills at all around Lake Geneva
61912.e: The Jura and the Alps move closer together towards the south-west. The air is channelled and speeds up, much like water in a nozzle.
61912.m: The nozzle effect between the Jura and the Alps makes the bise in Geneva especially strong.

61913.q: In the Lake Geneva region, what is the strong bise with thick grey cloud called?
61913.e: With the bise noire, a solid layer of cloud covers the region, while the bise claire comes with sunshine. The Joran and Vaudaire are other local winds of western Switzerland.
61913.m: The bise noire is a cold bise under thick cloud.

61914.q: What kind of air does the bise bring to Switzerland?
a: Cold continental air from north-east Europe
Moist sea air from the Atlantic
Hot desert air from the Sahara
Warm, moist air from the Mediterranean
61914.e: The bise brings dry, cold continental air from north-east Europe. That is why it is particularly unpleasantly cold in winter.
61914.m: The bise brings dry, cold continental air.

61915.q: What weather does a bise situation usually bring in summer?
61915.e: In summer the bise usually comes with high pressure and dry air. It is sunny, and temperatures stay pleasant.
61915.m: In summer the bise often brings sunny, fresh weather.

61916.q: What peak gusts are often measured on Lake Geneva during a classic bise situation?
61916.e: On Lake Geneva the bise often reaches average winds of about 60 km/h and gusts over 100 km/h.
61916.m: On Lake Geneva the bise can reach storm strength.

61917.q: What covered cars and lakeside structures in Versoix on Lake Geneva in thick ice in February 2012?
a: Bise whipping icy spray onto the shore
61917.e: During a violent bise and severe frost, lake water splashed onto the shore and froze at once. This created ice sculptures a metre thick.
61917.m: Strong bise and frost can turn lake shores into ice landscapes.

61918.q: Why is the southern side of the Alps usually spared from the bise in a bise situation?
a: The main Alpine ridge holds back the cold air from the north-east
Air pressure in Ticino is always higher
Lake Maggiore warms the bise at once
The bise only blows over the Alps at night
61918.e: The cold air of the bise near the ground is relatively shallow and is held back by the Alps. That is why southern Switzerland is usually not affected by it.
61918.m: The Alps protect southern Switzerland from the bise.

61919.q: What is meant by a sea of fog?
a: A layer of low cloud seen from above
Sea fog on the Atlantic coast
Haze over lakes on summer days
61919.e: If you stand above the layer of low cloud, you see the fog lying below you like a sea. Above it, it is often sunny.
61919.m: A sea of fog is a layer of low cloud seen from above.

61920.q: In which seasons does the sea of fog appear most often on the Swiss Plateau?
61920.e: During the long nights of autumn and winter, the moist air cools down a lot. At the same time, the sun is too weak to break up the layer of fog.
61920.m: Seas of fog belong mainly to autumn and winter.

61921.q: Why is it often sunny and relatively mild above the sea of fog in winter?
a: Drier, warmer air lies above the inversion layer
The sun is closer and stronger there
The fog gives off a lot of heat upwards
There is always foehn above the fog
61921.e: Above the inversion the air is warmer and drier, and clouds hardly form. That is why the sun shines while it is dull and grey below.
61921.m: Above the sea of fog it is often warmer than in the fog.

61922.q: In which areas of Switzerland is fog particularly common?
a: Along the Aare, the Reuss and in Thurgau
In the Upper Engadine and the Valposchiavo
In southern Ticino and the Misox
On the Jungfraujoch and in the Goms
61922.e: The lowlands along the big rivers of the Swiss Plateau are especially prone to fog. Moist air and pools of cold air encourage fog there.
61922.m: River lowlands on the Swiss Plateau are typical fog areas.

61923.q: How has the frequency of fog on the Swiss Plateau changed since the 1970s?
a: It has stayed exactly the same
61923.e: Measurements show fewer foggy days since the 1970s. Reasons include cleaner air and warmer winters.
61923.m: There are fewer foggy days on the Swiss Plateau today than in the past.

61924.q: What is fog called that does not lie on the ground but floats as a layer of cloud at some height?
61924.e: High fog is a low layer cloud (stratus) under an inversion. Below the layer visibility is good, but the sky is grey.
61924.m: High fog is a low layer of cloud above the ground.

61925.q: What is the climate in southern Ticino and on the northern Italian lakes called?
61925.e: The Insubric climate is mild and very sunny, but also has a lot of rain. It shapes the region around Lake Maggiore and Lake Lugano.
61925.m: Southern Ticino has a mild, Insubric climate.

61926.q: With an annual average of about 13 °C (standard period 1991 to 2020), which place is the warmest in Switzerland?
61926.e: Lugano lies low and is protected from cold northern air by the Alps. That is why it has the highest annual average of the Swiss weather stations.
61926.m: Lugano is the warmest measuring site in Switzerland.

61927.q: Which tree particularly shapes the forests at lower altitudes in Ticino?
61927.e: The sweet chestnut was brought in by the Romans and thrives in the mild, moist Insubric climate. For a long time it was an important food.
61927.m: Chestnut forests are typical of the southern side of the Alps.

61928.q: What is the downslope wind called that brings dry, clear and windy weather to Ticino when air is pushed against the Alps from the north?
61928.e: When air is pushed against the Alps from the north, it rains out on the northern side. On the southern side it sinks as a dry north foehn and brings clear views.
61928.m: North foehn brings dry and clear weather to Ticino.

61929.q: Why does extreme heavy rain happen on the southern side of the Alps, especially in autumn?
a: Moist Mediterranean air is pushed against the Alps and lifted
Cold polar air falls straight into the valleys
The lakes suddenly evaporate in autumn
The sun heats the slopes very strongly
61929.e: In autumn the Mediterranean is still warm and supplies a lot of moisture. Southerly winds push this air against the Alps, where it rises and rains out.
61929.m: Mediterranean air pushed against the Alps causes heavy rain in Ticino.

61930.q: How did the annual average temperature in Lugano change from the standard period 1961 to 1990 to the standard period 1991 to 2020?
61930.e: The annual average rose from 11.6 °C to about 13 °C. The rise shows the warming on the southern side of the Alps too.
61930.m: The annual average has also risen clearly in Lugano.

61931.q: Which severe weather hazard is particularly marked in Ticino, as well as in the Napf area and the Jura?
61931.e: Ticino is one of the hail hotspots of Switzerland. Warm, moist air from the south encourages powerful thunderstorms.
61931.m: Hailstorms are particularly common in Ticino.

61932.q: Why is it much colder in the Upper Engadine than in Lugano, even though both regions lie fairly far south?
a: The Upper Engadine is a high valley at about 1800 m
The Upper Engadine is closer to the North Pole
The bise blows constantly in the Upper Engadine
The Upper Engadine gets no hours of sunshine
61932.e: In Switzerland, temperature depends mainly on altitude. The Upper Engadine lies about 1500 m higher than Lugano.
61932.m: Height above sea level affects temperature more than direction does.

61933.q: What is typical of a temperature inversion in the atmosphere?
a: Temperature decreases especially fast with height
61933.e: Normally it gets colder the higher you go. In an inversion it is the other way round: warmer air lies above a cold layer.
61933.m: In an inversion it is warmer higher up than lower down.

61934.q: Why do inversions on the Swiss Plateau often last longer in December than in March?
a: The low sun hardly warms the cold air near the ground
There are no high-pressure areas in March
In December the air is colder at the top than at the bottom
61934.e: Around the winter solstice, days are short and the sun is low. Its energy is often not enough to warm the cold air under the inversion and break up the inversion layer.
61934.m: In midwinter inversions are slow to break up because the sun is weak.

61935.q: Why is air quality often poor during an inversion in winter?
a: The inversion layer stops air from mixing upwards
The warm air above produces pollutants
There is always strong wind during an inversion
The sun destroys oxygen during an inversion
61935.e: The warmer air above the cold air acts like a lid. Exhaust fumes from traffic and heating cannot rise and build up.
61935.m: An inversion acts like a lid over the exhaust fumes.

61936.q: Which pollutant often reaches high levels on the Swiss Plateau during winter inversions?
61936.e: In winter many particles come from wood fires and traffic. During an inversion they collect in the cold air. Ozone, on the other hand, is a typical summer problem.
61936.m: During winter inversions, fine particle pollution often rises.

61937.q: How does a ground inversion form?
a: The ground loses heat at night and cools the air near the ground
The sun heats the ground strongly at midday
Foehn pushes warm air down to the ground
Rain warms the lower layers of air
61937.e: On clear, still nights the ground loses a lot of heat by radiation. The air near the ground becomes colder than the air above it.
61937.m: Clear, still nights create ground inversions.

61938.q: How does a subsidence inversion form in a high-pressure area?
a: Sinking air warms up through compression
Strong wind mixes all the layers
61938.e: In a high-pressure area, air sinks over a large area. As it does so it is compressed and warms up, so a warm layer forms above colder air near the ground.
61938.m: Sinking air in a high warms up and forms an inversion layer.

61939.q: What is cold air called that collects in a hollow or basin?
61939.e: Cold air is heavier than warm air and flows to low-lying places. It stays in hollows and forms a cold air pool.
61939.m: Cold air collects in hollows to form a cold air pool.

61940.q: During an inversion, −3 °C is measured at 400 m and +5 °C at 1000 m. On average, by how much does the temperature rise per 100 m?
61940.e: The temperature rises by 5 − (−3) = 8 °C over 600 m. 8 ÷ 6 gives about 1.33 °C per 100 m.
61940.m: In an inversion the temperature rises with height.

61941.q: What happens when air is pushed up against a mountain range?
a: Air is lifted, cools down and rains out
Air sinks and all clouds disappear
Air stays completely still in the valley
Air is warmed by the mountains and dries out
61941.e: When air flows against mountains, it has to rise. It cools down, water vapour condenses, and a lot of rain or snow falls on the windward side.
61941.m: When air is pushed against mountains, it rains on the side the wind comes from.

61942.q: When air is pushed against the Alps from the south, it rains heavily in Ticino. Which wind often blows at the same time in the northern Alpine valleys?
61942.e: The air rains out on the southern side and sinks on the northern side. As it does so, it warms up and blows as a warm, dry south foehn.
61942.m: Southerly upslope rain in Ticino often means foehn in northern Switzerland.

61943.q: Roughly how much does unsaturated air cool per 100 m as it rises (dry adiabatic)?
61943.e: Unsaturated air expands as it rises and cools by about 1 °C per 100 m. When it sinks, it warms up by the same amount.
61943.m: Dry air cools by about 1 °C per 100 m as it rises.

61944.q: Why does saturated air cool more slowly as it rises than unsaturated air (moist adiabatic, about 0.5 °C per 100 m)?
a: Clouds absorb a lot of sunlight
Moist air is heavier than dry air
Air pressure is higher in clouds
61944.e: When water vapour condenses into droplets, latent heat is released. This slows the cooling of the rising air.
61944.m: Condensation releases heat and slows the cooling.

61945.q: What is the wall of cloud called that you see over the main Alpine ridge from the north during a south foehn?
61945.e: Clouds piled up on the southern side reach over the ridge. On the northern side they break up as the air sinks, creating a sharp wall of cloud.
61945.m: The foehn wall shows air piling up on the other side of the Alps.

61946.q: Air is 20 °C at 200 m. It rises dry to 1200 m, condenses and rises moist (0.5 °C per 100 m) to 3000 m. Then it sinks dry to 500 m. What temperature does it have there?
61946.m: Foehn air arrives in the valley warmer than it started on the windward side.

61947.q: Air is 18 °C and its dew point is 10 °C. Roughly at what height above the ground do the first clouds form (rule of thumb: 125 m per degree of difference)?
61947.e: The difference is 18 − 10 = 8 °C. 8 times 125 m gives a condensation height of 1000 m.
61947.m: The bigger the dew point difference, the higher the cloud base.

61948.q: Which place in the canton of Uri is known for particularly frequent south foehn?
61948.e: Altdorf lies in the Reuss Valley, which runs north to south. The foehn blows straight through the valley there.
61948.m: Altdorf in the Reuss Valley is a classic foehn town.

61949.q: Which region gets a particularly large amount of rain when air is pushed against the Alps from the north-west?
a: The northern side of the Alps
61949.e: In this situation, moist Atlantic air meets the northern edge of the Alps. There it rises and rains out, while it stays drier further south.
61949.m: When air comes from the north-west, it rains most on the northern side of the Alps.

61950.q: Where is the headquarters of MeteoSwiss?
61950.e: The headquarters is at Zurich Airport. Other sites are Geneva, Payerne and Locarno-Monti.
61950.m: MeteoSwiss has its headquarters at Zurich Airport.

61951.q: How many weather radar stations does MeteoSwiss operate (as of 2024)?
61951.e: The radars stand on exposed peaks in different parts of the country. Together they cover the whole of Switzerland.
61951.m: Five weather radars monitor rain and snow in Switzerland.

61952.q: Since which year has Switzerland had complete measurements from a nationwide network?
61952.e: On 1 December 1863, 88 weather stations started operating. 1864 is the first fully measured year.
61952.m: Swiss measurement series go back to 1864.

61953.q: What was the institution called that preceded MeteoSwiss, founded in 1881?
61953.e: The Federal Council founded the Swiss Meteorological Central Institute (MZA) in 1881. Since 2006 the official name has been the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology MeteoSwiss.
61953.m: The Meteorological Central Institute was the forerunner of MeteoSwiss.

61954.q: Roughly how high does a MeteoSwiss weather balloon rise?
61954.e: The balloon expands as air pressure falls and only bursts at a height of about 35 km. It passes through the whole troposphere and part of the stratosphere.
61954.m: Weather balloons rise into the stratosphere.

61955.q: What does MeteoSwiss observe as part of phenology?
a: When plants come into leaf and flower
The shape and size of hailstones
The movement of the Earth’s crust
The thickness of the ozone layer over Antarctica
61955.e: Phenology records, for example, when trees come into leaf or flower. This shows the effects of climate change.
61955.m: Phenology shows how plants react to the climate.

61956.q: Which federal centre published the CH2018 climate scenarios?
a: The National Centre for Climate Services (NCCS)
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)
61956.e: The scenarios were published under the umbrella of the NCCS. They were developed by MeteoSwiss, ETH Zurich and the University of Bern.
61956.m: The CH2018 climate scenarios come from the NCCS.

61957.q: Which statement is NOT one of the four key messages of the CH2018 climate scenarios?
a: More snow on the Swiss Plateau
61957.e: The four key messages are: drier summers, heavier rainfall, more hot days and winters with little snow. More snow on the Swiss Plateau is not expected.
61957.m: CH2018 expects winters with little snow, not more snow.

61958.q: According to CH2018, to what height could the average freezing level in winter rise from today’s roughly 850 m without climate protection?
61958.e: Without climate protection, the freezing level in winter rises a lot. More precipitation then falls as rain instead of snow.
61958.m: A higher freezing level means less snow at low altitudes.

61959.q: According to CH2018, how will average summer rainfall in Switzerland change in the long term?
a: It will stay exactly the same
61959.e: There will be more days without rain and less summer rain, especially in the west and south. Together with higher temperatures, the soils will dry out more.
61959.m: Summers in Switzerland are getting drier.

61960.q: According to CH2018, how much hotter could the hottest summer days become by the middle of the century without climate protection?
61960.e: Maximum temperatures are rising faster than average values. Summers like 2003 or 2018 could become normal in future.
61960.m: Hot days in Switzerland are getting much hotter.

61961.q: Which emissions scenario in CH2018 stands for a future without climate protection measures?
61961.e: RCP8.5 describes greenhouse gas emissions that keep rising strongly. RCP2.6, on the other hand, corresponds to consistent climate protection.
61961.m: RCP8.5 is the scenario without climate protection.

61962.q: According to CH2018, roughly how much more rain will the wettest day of the year bring by the middle of the century?
61962.e: Warmer air can hold more water vapour. That is why heavy rainfall is becoming more frequent and more intense.
61962.m: Heavy rainfall in Switzerland is getting more intense.

61963.q: What are the climate scenarios called that replaced the CH2018 scenarios in November 2025?
61963.e: The new scenarios were presented on 4 November 2025. They build on CH2018 and on new models.
61963.m: CH2018 was followed by the CH2025 climate scenarios.

61964.q: According to the 2025 climate scenarios, how much has Switzerland already warmed since pre-industrial times (as of 2024)?
61964.e: Switzerland is warming about twice as fast as the global average. One reason is that land warms faster than the oceans.
61964.m: Switzerland is warming faster than the global average.

61965.q: What maximum temperature was measured in Grono on 11 August 2003?
61965.e: At 41.5 °C, more than 40 °C was measured in Switzerland for the first time. This value is still the official national record.

61966.q: In which valley is Grono, where the Swiss heat record was measured in 2003?
61966.e: Grono lies in the Misox in the canton of the Grisons, on the southern side of the Alps. Its low position facing south encourages great heat.
61966.m: Grono in the Misox holds the Swiss heat record.

61967.q: Which place held the Swiss heat record of 39 °C (1952) before 2003?
61967.e: On 2 July 1952, 39 °C was measured in Basel. This record stood for over 50 years.
61967.m: Before 2003 Basel held the Swiss heat record.

61968.q: By how much was June 2003 in Switzerland above the average of the standard period 1991 to 2020?
61968.e: June 2003 had the largest positive monthly deviation since measurements began in 1864. August was also extremely hot.
61968.m: June 2003 was an extraordinarily hot month.

61969.q: According to a study, roughly how many extra deaths in Switzerland were linked to the hot summer of 2003?
61969.e: A study estimated about 975 extra deaths. Older people were particularly affected.
61969.m: Heatwaves are especially dangerous for older people.

61970.q: Which weather pattern caused the long-lasting heat in summer 2003?
a: An omega block with a blocking high
A bise situation with a low in the south
Rain against the Alps from the south for days
61970.e: A stable high blocked the westerly winds for weeks. Under the high, the air could keep heating up.
61970.m: A blocking high can bring weeks of heat.

61971.q: Which kind of fish died in tens of thousands in the High Rhine in summer 2003 because of the warm water?
61971.e: About 52,000 grayling died between the Untersee and Eglisau. Grayling need cool water rich in oxygen.
61971.m: Grayling are very sensitive to warm water.

61972.q: In which year was the Aare water temperature record set in 2003 broken?
61972.e: In the hot, dry summer of 2018 the Aare became even warmer than in 2003. This again put fish under heavy pressure.
61972.m: The summer of 2018 brought new records for water temperatures.

61973.q: According to common estimates, how many people died from the heat across Europe in summer 2003?
61973.e: Estimates range from about 35,000 to 70,000 deaths. This made the heatwave one of the deadliest natural disasters in Europe.
61973.m: The 2003 heatwave killed tens of thousands of people in Europe.

61974.q: In which region is the driest measuring site in Switzerland?
a: In the Visp Valley in Valais
61974.e: The Ackersand measuring site in the Visp Valley is considered the driest place in Switzerland. Valais is surrounded by high mountains.
61974.m: Inner Valais is the driest region in Switzerland.

61975.q: Why does inner Valais get so little rain?
a: It lies in the rain shadow of high mountain ranges
It lies very close to the Mediterranean
The bise blows constantly over Valais
61975.e: Moist air rains out on the Bernese and Valais Alps before it reaches the valley. In the valley the air sinks and dries out.
61975.m: Mountains keep rain away from inner Valais.

61976.q: Roughly how much precipitation falls at Switzerland’s driest measuring site each year?
61976.e: At Ackersand only about 543 mm falls per year on average (standard period 1991 to 2020). That is only a fraction of the amounts on the northern side of the Alps.
61976.m: Even the driest place in Switzerland gets over 500 mm of precipitation.

61977.q: Roughly how much precipitation falls on the Swiss Plateau each year?
61977.e: The Swiss Plateau gets medium amounts of precipitation. They increase towards the Prealps.
61977.m: The Swiss Plateau gets about one to one and a half metres of precipitation a year.

61978.q: Which regions of Switzerland get a particularly large amount of precipitation, about 2000 mm a year?
a: The Alps, Central Switzerland and Ticino
61978.e: These regions lie by mountains where moist air piles up. That is why much more precipitation falls there than in the lowlands.
61978.m: Regions close to mountains get especially high precipitation in Switzerland.

61979.q: In general, how do precipitation amounts in summer and winter differ in Switzerland?
a: About twice as much falls in summer
About twice as much falls in winter
Both seasons are exactly the same
61979.e: In summer thunderstorms and showers bring a lot of rain. The warm air can also hold more water vapour.
61979.m: In Switzerland summer is the season with the most precipitation.

61980.q: How does the amount of precipitation in Switzerland generally change with height above sea level?
61980.e: Air is lifted by mountains and cools down, so water vapour condenses. That is why higher areas usually get more precipitation.
61980.m: It rains and snows more in the mountains than in the lowlands.

61981.q: What amount does 1 mm of precipitation equal?
61981.e: One millimetre of water on one square metre gives 0.001 m × 1 m² = 0.001 m³. That is 1 litre.
61981.m: One millimetre of precipitation is one litre per square metre.

61982.q: With 1200 mm of annual precipitation, how much water falls on a roof with a floor area of 150 m²?
61982.e: 1200 mm is 1200 litres per m². 1200 times 150 gives 180,000 litres.
61982.m: Precipitation in mm times area in m² gives litres.

61983.q: How has precipitation on the Swiss Plateau changed since measurements began in 1864?
a: It has increased, especially in winter
It has decreased, especially in winter
It has stayed the same in all seasons
It has only increased strongly in summer
61983.e: The measurement series show a significant increase in precipitation. It mainly affects winter.
61983.m: On the Swiss Plateau more precipitation falls in winter today than in the past.

61984.q: What does the freezing level tell you?
a: The height above which the air temperature is below 0 °C
The height above which snow stays on the ground
The height of the lowest glacier tongue
61984.e: The freezing level is the height in the free atmosphere at which the air is 0 °C. Above it, it is colder.
61984.m: Above the freezing level temperatures are below zero.

61985.q: How is the freezing level in the free atmosphere measured?
a: With ground stations on the Swiss Plateau
61985.e: As it rises, the radiosonde constantly measures temperature, humidity and pressure. This makes it possible to find the height of 0 °C.
61985.m: Weather balloons provide the measurements for the freezing level.

61986.q: What record value did the freezing level over Switzerland reach in August 2023?
61986.e: In the night of 20 to 21 August 2023, a freezing level of 5298 m was measured. This beat the record from 2022.
61986.m: In summer the freezing level can rise above 5000 m.

61987.q: How has the freezing level over Switzerland developed since about 1970?
a: It goes up and down with no clear trend
61987.e: Because of global warming, the freezing level today is considerably higher on average. The measurement series go back to 1954.
61987.m: As the climate warms, the freezing level rises.

61988.q: A station at 500 m measures 13 °C. Roughly where is the freezing level if the temperature falls by 0.65 °C per 100 m?
61988.e: 13 ÷ 0.65 gives 20, so 20 times 100 m equals 2000 m above the station. 500 m + 2000 m gives 2500 m.
61988.m: The freezing level can be estimated from the ground temperature and the temperature gradient.

61989.q: Roughly how much does the freezing level rise if the air everywhere gets 1 °C warmer (gradient 0.65 °C per 100 m)?
61989.e: 1 ÷ 0.65 gives about 1.54. Times 100 m, that is about 150 m.
61989.m: Even a little warming moves the freezing level up a lot.

61990.q: Where does the snow line usually lie compared with the freezing level?
a: Always at exactly the same height
61990.e: Snowflakes need a certain distance before they have melted in the warm air. That is why it still snows below the freezing level.
61990.m: Snow often falls a few hundred metres below the freezing level.

61991.q: Why does a very high freezing level in summer particularly harm glaciers?
a: Even at great heights, ice and snow then melt
A lot of fresh snow then falls on the glaciers
61991.e: If the freezing level is above the peaks, melting happens across the whole glacier. Precipitation then also falls as rain.
61991.m: A high freezing level makes glaciers melt up to the highest areas.

61992.q: In which weather situation does the freezing level rise especially high in summer?
a: A stable high with very warm air
61992.e: Under a stable high-pressure area, the whole column of air is very warm. Then the freezing level can rise above 5000 m, as in August 2023.
61992.m: Heatwaves push the freezing level far above the peaks.

61993.q: Roughly how much precipitation falls on the Säntis on average each year?
61993.e: At about 2840 mm, the Säntis is the wettest measuring site in Switzerland. Part of it falls as snow.
61993.m: The Säntis is the wettest measuring site in Switzerland.

61994.q: What snow depth was measured on the Säntis in April 1999, the highest ever recorded in Switzerland?
61994.e: In the northern snowfield below the summit there were 816 cm of snow. The winter of 1998/99 was extremely snowy in the Alps.
61994.m: In 1999 there was over eight metres of snow on the Säntis.

61995.q: Which hurricane-force storm brought gusts of 230 km/h to the Säntis on 26 December 1999?
61995.e: The storm Lothar swept across Switzerland on St Stephen’s Day 1999. It caused great damage to forests.
61995.m: The storm Lothar raged at Christmas 1999.

61996.q: Which crime took place on the Säntis in February 1922?
a: The weather observer and his wife were murdered
The weather station was set on fire
A cable car cabin was blown up
61996.e: On 21 February 1922, the weather observer Heinrich Haas and his wife Maria Magdalena were shot dead. The case is known as the Säntis murder.
61996.m: The Säntis murder of 1922 shocked eastern Switzerland.

61997.q: Which three cantons meet on the Säntis?
a: Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden and St Gallen
61997.e: On the Säntis the two Appenzells and St Gallen border each other. The mountain is a landmark of eastern Switzerland.
61997.m: Three eastern Swiss cantons meet on the Säntis.

61998.q: Roughly what is the annual average temperature on the Säntis in the standard period 1991 to 2020?
61998.e: At this summit location, the annual average temperature is just below zero. Even in the warmest month it stays cool there.
61998.m: On the Säntis the annual average is just below zero degrees.

61999.q: Why does so much precipitation fall on the Säntis?
a: It is the first high peak on the northern edge of the Alps to face the westerly winds
It lies right above Lake Constance in the fog
It is the highest mountain in Switzerland
Foehn blows constantly over the Säntis
61999.e: Moist air from the west and north-west hits the free-standing Alpstein without anything in the way. It is lifted and rains out.
61999.m: The free-standing Säntis catches a lot of precipitation from the west.

62000.q: How strong is the bise on Lake Constance usually compared with the Lake Geneva region?
a: About twice as strong as in Geneva
Just as strong as on Lake Geneva
There is never any bise on Lake Constance
62000.e: At Lake Constance there is no narrowing between the Jura and the Alps. The bise there usually only reaches 40 to 50 km/h, while on Lake Geneva it is often much stronger.
62000.m: The further west on the Swiss Plateau, the stronger the bise.

62001.q: What is the temperature called at which air is saturated with water vapour and fog can form?
62001.e: If moist air cools to the dew point, the water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. This is how fog forms.
62001.m: Fog forms when air cools to the dew point.

62002.q: What determines the upper limit of a sea of fog?
a: The height of the inversion layer
The height of the tree line
The height of the highest lake
62002.e: The fog reaches up to the inversion layer, above which warmer, drier air lies. If the inversion is higher, the sea of fog is higher too.
62002.m: The inversion forms the lid of the sea of fog.

62003.q: How does smoke from a chimney behave when it rises up to an inversion layer?
a: It spreads out sideways under the layer
It rises freely into the stratosphere
It sinks straight to the ground at once
It disappears at once in warmer air
62003.e: The smoke is cooler than the warm air above the inversion and cannot rise any further. It therefore spreads out horizontally under the layer.
62003.m: Under an inversion smoke spreads out flat.

62004.q: What does a MeteoSwiss weather radar mainly detect?
a: Precipitation such as rain, snow and hail
62004.e: The radar sends out microwaves that are scattered back by raindrops, snowflakes and hailstones. This shows where precipitation is falling and how heavily.
62004.m: Weather radars show where it is raining, snowing or hailing.

62005.q: How many times a day does MeteoSwiss launch a weather balloon with a radiosonde in Payerne?
62005.e: The balloons go up at 00:00 and 12:00 Universal Time (UTC). This creates regular profiles of the atmosphere over Switzerland.
62005.m: A weather balloon goes up in Payerne twice a day.

62006.q: On which peak in Ticino does one of the MeteoSwiss weather radar stations stand?
62006.e: The radar on Monte Lema monitors precipitation on the southern side of the Alps. Other radars stand on the Albis and the Weissfluh, for example.
62006.m: The weather radar on Monte Lema watches the southern side of the Alps.

62007.q: Which month is on average the coldest on the Säntis?
62007.e: On the Säntis, February is the coldest month at about −7.5 °C. In mountain areas the coldest time often shifts a little later.
62007.m: On the Säntis February is the coldest month.

62008.q: How many litres of water per square metre does 1 mm of precipitation equal?
62008.e: 1 mm of precipitation means the water would be 1 mm deep on a flat surface. On one square metre that is exactly 1 litre.
62008.m: 1 mm of precipitation equals 1 litre per square metre.

62009.q: Why is the weather station on the Säntis especially valuable for climate research?
a: It has measured without a break since the 19th century
It stands on the highest mountain in Switzerland
It lies right on Lake Constance
62009.e: Regular measurements have been taken on the Säntis since 1882. Such long series from the mountains are rare and show clearly how the climate is changing.
62009.m: Long measurement series like those on the Säntis show climate change.

62010.q: Which palm from Asia is spreading more and more in the forests of Ticino thanks to the mild climate?
62010.e: The Chinese windmill palm (Trachycarpus fortunei) was brought in as an ornamental plant. Mild winters help it spread in the forests of Ticino.
62010.m: The windmill palm is growing wild in Ticino thanks to mild winters.

62011.q: What share of Switzerland’s area drains via the Inn to the Danube and so into the Black Sea?
62011.e: Water from about 4.4 per cent of the country, mainly from the Engadine, flows via the Inn and the Danube into the Black Sea. That is the smallest of the four large drainage shares.
62011.m: Only a small part of Switzerland drains into the Black Sea.

62012.q: Through which river system does about 18 per cent of Switzerland’s area drain into the western Mediterranean?
62012.e: The Rhône drains Valais and the Lake Geneva area and flows into the Mediterranean in southern France. Its catchment covers about 18 per cent of Switzerland.
62012.m: The Rhône carries Swiss water to the western Mediterranean.

62013.q: What share of Switzerland’s area drains via the Po into the Adriatic?
62013.e: About 9 per cent of the country, mainly Ticino and the southern valleys of the Grisons, drains via the Po into the Adriatic. That is about half the Rhône’s share.
62013.m: About a tenth of Switzerland drains via the Po into the Adriatic.

62014.q: Roughly how much precipitation falls in Switzerland each year on the national average?
62014.e: On the national average about 1450 mm falls each year. On the Swiss Plateau it is about 1000 mm, in the central High Alps and Ticino almost 2000 mm, because the mountains force moist air to rise and rain out.
62014.m: The Alps make Switzerland a country with a lot of precipitation.

62015.q: Via which river does the Val Müstair drain to the Adriatic?
62015.e: The Rombach flows from the Val Müstair into South Tyrol and joins the Adige there. The Adige reaches the Adriatic as a river of its own, not via the Po.
62015.m: The Val Müstair drains via the Adige to the Adriatic.

62016.q: According to Eawag, roughly how many turbines does Rhine water flow through before it leaves Switzerland?
62016.e: Many river power stations line the Aare, Reuss, Limmat and High Rhine. A drop of water from the Alps therefore drives about 12 to 14 turbines on its way.
62016.m: On its way through Switzerland, Rhine water drives many turbines.

62017.q: According to Eawag, in what form is most of Switzerland’s water supply stored?
62017.e: According to Eawag, about 45 per cent of the water supply is groundwater, about 39 per cent is in lakes and rivers and about 16 per cent is in glaciers. Groundwater is therefore also the most important source of drinking water.
62017.m: Switzerland’s largest water supply lies hidden as groundwater.

62018.q: Which river drains the Valposchiavo via the Adda to the Po?
62018.e: The Poschiavino flows south through the Valposchiavo and Lago di Poschiavo and joins the Adda at Tirano. The Adda reaches the Po via Lake Como.
62018.m: The Valposchiavo drains via the Poschiavino and the Adda to the Po.

62019.q: Which sea areas does the European main watershed separate?
