a: The Atlantic with the North Sea and Baltic from the Mediterranean and Black Sea
The North Sea from the Baltic
The Mediterranean from the Black Sea
The Atlantic from the Arctic Ocean
62019.e: The main watershed separates the catchments that flow to the open Atlantic, the North Sea and the Baltic from those flowing to the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. It runs right across the Swiss Alps.
62019.m: The main watershed separates the Atlantic from the Mediterranean and Black Sea.

62020.q: Which of these passes does NOT lie on the European main watershed?
62020.e: At the Oberalp Pass, water flows into the Vorderrhein on one side and the Reuss on the other. Both belong to the Rhine basin, so the watershed does not separate any seas.
62020.m: The Oberalp Pass only separates two tributaries of the Rhine.

62021.q: Why does the Maloja Pass NOT lie on the European main watershed, even though it is a watershed?
a: Both sides drain into the Mediterranean or the Black Sea
Both sides drain into the Rhine
Water on both sides flows into the same lake
62021.e: From the Maloja Pass, water flows on one side via the Inn and the Danube into the Black Sea, and on the other via the Mera to the Po and the Adriatic. Both areas lie on the same side of the main watershed, which only cuts off the Atlantic area.
62021.m: A watershed between the Danube and the Po is not a main watershed.

62022.q: Which catchments does the Lukmanier Pass separate?
62022.e: To the north the Medelser Rhein flows to the Vorderrhein, to the south the Brenno flows through the Blenio Valley to the Ticino and the Po. The pass therefore lies on the main watershed.
62022.m: The Lukmanier Pass separates the Rhine basin from the Po basin.

62023.q: Which catchments does the Albula Pass separate?
62023.e: On the north-west side the Albula flows via the Hinterrhein to the Rhine. On the Engadine side, water flows into the Inn and on to the Danube.
62023.m: The Albula Pass separates the Rhine basin from the Danube basin.

62024.q: The European main watershed runs close to Lake Geneva. Into which sea does the water of Lake Geneva flow?
62024.e: The Rhône flows through Lake Geneva and then through France into the Mediterranean. North of the main watershed, for example from Mont Pèlerin above Vevey, the water flows instead to the Rhine and the North Sea.
62024.m: Via the Rhône, the water of Lake Geneva flows into the Mediterranean.

62025.q: Which canal was meant to cross the main watershed at the Mormont in the 17th century and link Lake Neuchâtel with Lake Geneva?
62025.e: The Canal d’Entreroches, built from 1638, ran from Yverdon through a cutting in the Mormont to the Venoge near Cossonay. The section to Lake Geneva was never built, because it would have needed about 40 more locks and there was no money.
62025.m: The Canal d’Entreroches crossed the watershed at the Mormont.

62026.q: Which three cantons meet at the point where the Rhine, Rhône and Po catchments divide, near the Witenwasserenstock?
62026.e: The point lies about 224 m east-south-east of the summit of the Witenwasserenstock at 3025 m above sea level. Uri, Valais and Ticino border each other there.
62026.m: Uri, Valais and Ticino meet at the Witenwasserenstock.

62027.q: Roughly how large is the whole catchment of the Inn?
62027.e: The catchment of the Inn covers about 26,100 km² in Switzerland, Italy, Austria and Germany. Only about 1700 km² of it lies in the Grisons.
62027.m: The catchment of the Inn is about 26,000 square kilometres.

62028.q: Which tributary carries more water than the Inn itself at Samedan?
62028.e: At Samedan the Flaz carries on average about 7.9 m³/s, the Inn only about 6.8 m³/s. In terms of hydrology, the Flaz is therefore the main river of the Upper Engadine.
62028.m: At Samedan the Flaz carries more water than the Inn.

62029.q: Why was the Flaz moved into a new bed near Samedan in 2004?
62029.e: The Flaz was moved out of the village into a new channel east of Samedan airfield. This protected the village better from floods, and the river is now about 2 km longer.
62029.m: Moving the Flaz protects Samedan from floods.

62030.q: Which dam on the border with Italy holds back the Spöl to form the Lago di Livigno?
62030.e: The Punt dal Gall dam lies exactly on the national border and holds back the Spöl to form the Lago di Livigno, which is mostly in Italy. The water is used by the Engadine power stations.
62030.m: The Punt dal Gall dam holds back the Spöl on the border with Italy.

62031.q: In which direction does the Inn flow through the Engadine?
62031.e: The Inn flows north-east from Maloja through the Upper and Lower Engadine to the border at Martina. The whole valley runs parallel to the main Alpine ridge.
62031.m: The Inn flows north-east through the Engadine.

62032.q: Near which pass in the Upper Engadine does the Inn rise?
62032.e: The Inn rises in Lake Lunghin above the Maloja Pass. From there it flows through the Engadine into Austria and joins the Danube at Passau.
62032.m: The Inn rises near the Maloja Pass.

62033.q: Which Tyrolean border town next to Bavaria lies on the Inn?
62033.e: Kufstein lies on the Inn on the border between Tyrol and Bavaria and is known for its fortress. Lienz lies on the Drava, Salzburg on the Salzach.
62033.m: Kufstein is the Tyrolean border town on the Inn.

62034.q: What is special about Passau, where the Inn flows into the Danube?
a: The Inn often carries more water there than the Danube
The Inn flows underneath the Danube there
The Danube flows back into the Inn there
The Inn is only a small stream there
62034.e: At the confluence, the Inn on average brings slightly more water than the Danube. Even so, the river keeps the name Danube afterwards.
62034.m: At Passau the Inn often brings more water than the Danube.

62035.q: Near which city does the Ticino flow into the Po?
62035.e: The Ticino joins the Po south-east of Pavia. It is one of the largest left-bank tributaries of the Po.
62035.m: The Ticino joins the Po near Pavia.

62036.q: Which large lake does the Ticino flow through on its way to the Po?
62036.e: The Ticino enters Lake Maggiore at Magadino and leaves it again at Sesto Calende. After that it flows across the Po Valley to the Po.
62036.m: The Ticino flows through Lake Maggiore.

62037.q: Which river from the Italian Ossola Valley also flows into Lake Maggiore?
62037.e: The Toce comes from the Ossola Valley in Piedmont and flows into Lake Maggiore at Fondotoce. Its water leaves the lake with the Ticino.
62037.m: The Toce belongs to the catchment area of the Ticino.

62038.q: Through which gorge does the Ticino flow in the Leventina between Rodi-Fiesso and Faido?
62038.e: At Dazio Grande the Ticino squeezes through the Piottino Gorge and drops down a step in the valley. Further down, near Giornico, comes the Biaschina.
62038.m: The Piottino Gorge is a valley step in the Leventina.

62039.q: What is the electricity from the Ritom power station near Piotta in the upper Ticino valley mainly used for?
62039.e: The Ritom power station uses the water of Lake Ritom and supplies railway electricity for the SBB. It was built in connection with the electrification of the Gotthard railway.
62039.m: The Ritom power station supplies electricity for the railway.

62040.q: Which general defeated a Roman army on the Ticino in 218 BC?
62040.e: In the Battle of the Ticinus, Hannibal defeated the Romans under Publius Cornelius Scipio after crossing the Alps. The battle probably took place near Pavia.
62040.m: Hannibal defeated the Romans on the Ticino in 218 BC.

62041.q: In which area does the Ticino rise?
62041.e: The Ticino rises at the Nufenen Pass and flows through the Bedretto Valley. At Airolo it is joined by water from the Gotthard. Then it flows south through the Leventina.
62041.m: The Ticino rises in the Nufenen and Gotthard area.

62042.q: What is the name of the famous covered bridge over the Ticino in Pavia?
62042.e: The Ponte Coperto originally dates from the 14th century. Until the 19th century it was the only stone bridge over the Ticino between Lake Maggiore and the Po.
62042.m: The Ponte Coperto crosses the Ticino in Pavia.

62043.q: How much water flows over the Rhine Falls at average flow?
62043.e: At the Rhine's average flow, about 373 m³ of water plunge over the falls every second. In winter it is less, in summer more.
62043.m: On average about 373 cubic metres per second flow over the Rhine Falls.

62044.q: How much water flows over the Rhine Falls on average in winter?
62044.e: In winter much of the precipitation in the catchment area falls as snow and stays on the ground. That is why the flow at the Rhine Falls drops to about 250 m³/s on average.
62044.m: In winter the Rhine Falls carry less water than in summer.

62045.q: Why do the Rhine Falls carry more water in summer than in winter?
a: Snow and glacier ice melt in the Alps
Lake Constance is drained artificially in summer
In winter water is diverted to power stations
62045.e: In winter much precipitation stays on the ground as snow. In spring and summer the snow and ice in the Rhine's catchment area melt and the flow rises.
62045.m: Snowmelt makes the Rhine Falls swell in summer.

62046.q: Why has the large rock in the middle of the Rhine Falls hardly been worn away?
a: The Rhine brings little gravel from Lake Constance
It is reinforced with concrete every year
The water flows around it to the side
62046.e: Lake Constance acts as a settling basin where gravel and sand are left behind. Without grinding sediment, the water erodes the limestone rock only very slowly.
62046.m: Lake Constance holds back gravel and so protects the Rhine Falls rock.

62047.q: Roughly how high is the drop of the Rhine Falls?
62047.e: The Rhine Falls are about 23 m high and about 150 m wide. They are impressive mainly because of the huge amount of water, not their height.
62047.m: The Rhine Falls are about 23 metres high.

62048.q: Which English painter captured the Rhine Falls in several studies and paintings in the 19th century?
62048.e: Joseph Mallord William Turner travelled through Switzerland several times and painted the Rhine Falls in several versions. He was famous for his depictions of light, water and the forces of nature.
62048.m: William Turner painted the Rhine Falls several times.

62049.q: Which municipality lies on the right, northern bank of the Rhine Falls?
62049.e: Neuhausen am Rheinfall in the canton of Schaffhausen lies directly on the north bank. Opposite stands Laufen Castle on Zurich territory.
62049.m: Neuhausen am Rheinfall lies on the north bank of the Rhine Falls.

62050.q: Which Zurich municipality does the left bank of the Rhine Falls with Laufen Castle belong to?
62050.e: The left bank with Laufen Castle belongs to the municipality of Laufen-Uhwiesen in the Zurich Weinland. Flurlingen and Feuerthalen lie opposite the town of Schaffhausen.
62050.m: Laufen Castle belongs to the municipality of Laufen-Uhwiesen.

62051.q: What problem arose after the Grosses Moos was drained?
a: The ground froze all year round
62051.e: Drained peat breaks down in the air and becomes compacted. Since the first Jura water correction, the ground in the Seeland has sunk by about 2 m in places.
62051.m: In the Grosses Moos the drained peat soil keeps sinking.

62052.q: Which structure has regulated the water levels of the three Jura lakes since 1939?
62052.e: The Port regulating weir near Nidau controls the outflow from Lake Biel into the Nidau-Büren Canal. This regulates the levels of Lakes Biel, Neuchâtel and Murten.
62052.m: The Port regulating weir controls the water levels of the Jura lakes.

62053.q: The first Jura water correction began in 1868 with the building of which canal?
62053.e: First the outflow from Lake Biel was improved so the lakes could release more water. For this the Nidau-Büren Canal was built from 1868.
62053.m: The first Jura water correction began with the Nidau-Büren Canal.

62054.q: Where was the Aare diverted during the first Jura water correction?
62054.e: Through the new Hagneck Canal the Aare was led into Lake Biel. Before that it flowed past the lake at Aarberg and often flooded the Seeland.
62054.m: Since the first Jura water correction the Aare flows through Lake Biel.

62055.q: Why was the Aare led into Lake Biel during the Jura water correction?
a: The lake was meant to catch floods and sediment
The lake was meant to get more salt
The Aare was meant to flow faster to Bern
The lake was meant to be drained
62055.e: Since then Lake Biel has served as a balancing basin: it absorbs flood peaks and holds back gravel. As a result, the Aare flows more evenly downstream.
62055.m: Lake Biel dampens floods of the Aare.

62056.q: Which natural obstacle in the Aare was removed during the second Jura water correction?
a: The debris cone of the Emme
62056.e: At its mouth the Emme piled up a debris cone in the Aare, the so-called Emme barrier, which dammed the water. It was removed during the second correction.
62056.m: During the second Jura water correction the Emme debris cone was removed.

62057.q: Which three lakes have been regulated together since the Jura water correction?
62057.e: The three Jura lakes are linked by canals. Their water levels are controlled together through the outflow from Lake Biel.
62057.m: Lakes Biel, Neuchâtel and Murten form the system of the Jura lakes.

62058.q: What is the name of the former marshy plain in the Seeland that is now one of Switzerland's most important vegetable-growing areas?
62058.e: The Grosses Moos between Lakes Biel, Neuchâtel and Murten used to be flooded often. After it was drained it became the “vegetable garden of Switzerland”.
62058.m: The Grosses Moos is now a vegetable garden of Switzerland.

62059.q: What was the main aim of the Jura water corrections?
a: Building a shipping route to the Mediterranean
More water for power stations in the Jura
Drinking water for the city of Bern
62059.e: The Seeland used to flood again and again and was marshy. The corrections lowered the lake levels, protected against floods and turned marsh into fertile farmland.
62059.m: The Jura water corrections brought flood protection and new farmland.

62060.q: Which addition to their name did Hans Conrad Escher's family receive in thanks for the Linth project?
62060.e: After Escher's death in 1823 his descendants received the right to add “von der Linth” to their name. In this way his achievement was honoured for good.
62060.m: Hans Conrad Escher was honoured as “Escher von der Linth”.

62061.q: Which human cause contributed greatly to the Linth Plain filling up with gravel?
62061.e: In the 18th century the Glarus slopes were heavily deforested. After that a lot of debris slid into the Linth, settled on the plain and dammed up the river.
62061.m: Deforestation in Glarus led to debris and floods on the Linth.

62062.q: Which mosquito-borne disease was common in the marshy Linth Plain before the correction?
62062.e: Mosquitoes bred in the marshes and transmitted malaria (then called “intermittent fever”). The correction drained the marshes.
62062.m: Malaria was widespread in the marshy Linth Plain.

62063.q: By how much was the level of Lake Walen lowered by the Linth correction?
62063.e: Because the Linth used to drop its debris at Ziegelbrücke, Lake Walen was dammed up. After the correction its level fell by about 5.5 m.
62063.m: The Linth correction lowered Lake Walen by about five and a half metres.

62064.q: Which authority commissioned the Linth project?
62064.e: The Tagsatzung, the assembly of the members of the Old Swiss Confederacy, dealt with the project from 1783. The Federal Council has only existed since 1848.
62064.m: The Linth project was a work of the Tagsatzung.

62065.q: Which canal has led the Linth into Lake Walen since the correction?
62065.e: The Escher Canal leads the Linth into Lake Walen near Mollis, where it drops its debris. The Linth Canal then carries the water on into Lake Zurich.
62065.m: The Escher Canal leads the Linth into Lake Walen.

62066.q: Which two lakes does the Linth Canal connect?
62066.e: The Linth Canal runs from Lake Walen at Weesen across the Linth Plain into Lake Zurich. It is part of the Linth project.
62066.m: The Linth Canal connects Lake Walen and Lake Zurich.

62067.q: Besides safe embankments, what did the project “Linth 2000 flood protection” aim to achieve?
a: An ecological upgrade of the river landscape
The building of a large reservoir
62067.e: The Escher Canal and Linth Canal were renovated and the embankments strengthened. At the same time, the river was given more space in places so that animals and plants could find new habitats.
62067.m: The renewed Linth project combines flood protection and nature.

62068.q: Roughly how much water does Lake Constance contain?
62068.e: Lake Constance contains about 48.5 km³ of water, that is about 48 billion cubic metres. Most of it lies in the deep Upper Lake.
62068.m: Lake Constance contains about 48 cubic kilometres of water.

62069.q: Roughly how long is Lake Constance from Bregenz to Stein am Rhein?
62069.e: From Bregenz at the eastern end to Stein am Rhein at the western end, Lake Constance measures about 69 km. The Upper Lake alone is about 63 km long from Bregenz to Bodman-Ludwigshafen.
62069.m: Lake Constance is about 69 kilometres long.

62070.q: Roughly how long is the Swiss shore of Lake Constance?
62070.e: Of the roughly 273 km of shoreline, about 72 km belong to Switzerland. The canton of Thurgau has most of it.
62070.m: Switzerland has about 72 kilometres of Lake Constance shoreline.

62071.q: Which stretch of water connects the Upper Lake with the Lower Lake at Konstanz?
62071.e: The Seerhein is a stretch of river about 4 km long between Konstanz and Gottlieben. It connects the two main parts of Lake Constance.
62071.m: The Seerhein connects the Upper Lake and the Lower Lake.

62072.q: What is the name of the north-western arm of the Upper Lake?
62072.e: Lake Überlingen is the long, narrow north-western arm of the Upper Lake. The Gnadensee, Zeller See and Rheinsee are parts of the Lower Lake.
62072.m: Lake Überlingen is the north-western arm of the Upper Lake.

62073.q: Which is the largest island in Lake Constance?
62073.e: Reichenau, at about 430 ha, is the largest island, and with its monastery it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Lindau and Mainau follow with much smaller areas.
62073.m: Reichenau is the largest island in Lake Constance.

62074.q: Which country has the longest share of the Lake Constance shoreline?
62074.e: At about 173 km, well over half of the shoreline is in Germany, namely in Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria. Liechtenstein does not border the lake.
62074.m: Germany has the largest share of the Lake Constance shoreline.

62075.q: How many people does the Lake Constance water supply provide with drinking water (as of 2015)?
62075.e: The Lake Constance water supply takes lake water at a depth of about 60 m near Sipplingen. It supplies about 4 million people in Baden-Württemberg.
62075.m: Lake Constance provides drinking water for about 4 million people.

62077.q: Which four cantons have a share of Lake Neuchâtel?
62077.e: Most of the lake belongs to Neuchâtel, Vaud and Fribourg. At the north-eastern end, the canton of Bern also has a small share.

62078.q: Which two lakes, together with Lake Neuchâtel, form the Three Lakes Region?
a: Lake Geneva and Lac de Joux
62078.e: The three Jura lakes are linked by canals. Their water level has been regulated together since the Jura water correction.
62078.m: Lakes Neuchâtel, Biel and Murten form the Three Lakes Region.

62079.q: Which group of fish does the bondelle belong to, which is found only in Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Biel?
62079.e: The bondelle is a species of whitefish known only from Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Biel. In many Swiss lakes, their own whitefish species have developed.
62079.m: The bondelle is a whitefish species of the Jura lakes.

62080.q: At which national exhibition did an artificial cloud of mist float over Lake Neuchâtel near Yverdon-les-Bains?
62080.e: At Expo.02 the “Blur Building” stood near Yverdon-les-Bains, a structure wrapped in water mist. Expo.02 had its arteplages (exhibition sites) on the Jura lakes.
62080.m: Expo.02 took place on the Jura lakes.

62081.q: Which Swiss Army facility lies on the southern shore of Lake Neuchâtel?
a: A tank training ground in the lake
62081.e: At the Forel air firing range in the canton of Fribourg, fighter jets practise shooting at targets over the lake. During exercises, an area of the lake is closed.
62081.m: The Forel air firing range lies on Lake Neuchâtel.

62082.q: Roughly how wide is Lake Neuchâtel at its widest point?
62082.e: The lake is about 8.2 km wide at its widest point. It is long and narrow because it lies parallel to the Jura.
62082.m: Lake Neuchâtel is at most about 8 kilometres wide.

62083.q: How did the marshland of the Grande Cariçaie on the southern shore of Lake Neuchâtel come about?
a: Through the lowering of the lake in the Jura water correction
62083.e: When the lake level sank by about 2.5 m in the 19th century, shallow shore zones dried out. Reeds and fen meadows grew on them, today's nature reserve.
62083.m: The Grande Cariçaie came about through the lowering of Lake Neuchâtel.

62084.q: What rank does Lake Neuchâtel hold by area among all lakes with a Swiss share?
62084.e: Only Lake Geneva, at about 580 km², and Lake Constance, at about 536 km², are larger. Lake Maggiore, at about 212 km², is just smaller than Lake Neuchâtel.
62084.m: Only Lake Geneva and Lake Constance are larger than Lake Neuchâtel.

62085.q: Which arm of the lake is separated from the rest of the lake at Stansstad by a narrows with a bridge?
62085.e: Lake Alpnach is connected to the main lake only by a narrows about 100 m wide between Acheregg and Stansstad, which is crossed by a bridge. The Sarner Aa flows into it.
62085.m: Lake Alpnach is separated from the main lake by a narrow strait.

62086.q: How many paddle steamers does the Lake Lucerne Navigation Company (SGV) operate (as of 2025)?
62086.e: The SGV operates the five paddle steamers Stadt Luzern, Uri, Unterwalden, Gallia and Schiller. The oldest is the Uri from 1901.
62086.m: Five paddle steamers sail on Lake Lucerne.

62087.q: Which road was built along the eastern shore of Lake Uri from 1863 to 1865?
62087.e: The Axenstrasse runs from Brunnen via Sisikon to Flüelen, with many tunnels and galleries in the steep rock face. Today it is part of the A4.
62087.m: The Axenstrasse runs along the eastern shore of Lake Uri.

62088.q: Who is honoured by the 1859 inscription on the Schillerstein, a rock in Lake Uri?
a: The first President of the Confederation
The builder of the Gotthard railway
The founder of the Red Cross
62088.e: In 1859 the original cantons dedicated the rock “to the singer of Tell”, Friedrich Schiller. His play “William Tell” is set on the shores of the lake.
62088.m: The Schillerstein honours Friedrich Schiller as the author of “William Tell”.

62089.q: Between which places does the Engelberger Aa flow into Lake Lucerne?
62089.e: The Engelberger Aa drains the Engelberg valley in Nidwalden. It flows into the lake between Buochs and Ennetbürgen.
62089.m: The Engelberger Aa flows into Lake Lucerne near Buochs.

62090.q: Roughly how long is the shoreline of the very branched Lake Lucerne?
62090.e: Because of its many arms and bays, the lake has a shoreline of about 150 km. That is a lot for its area.
62090.m: Lake Lucerne has about 150 kilometres of shoreline.

62091.q: Roughly at what altitude is the surface of Lake Lucerne?
62091.e: The lake surface lies at about 433 m above sea level. Since 1861 a weir at the Reuss outflow in Lucerne has kept the level slightly above the natural average.
62091.m: Lake Lucerne lies at about 433 metres above sea level.

62092.q: Why is the deep water in Lake Uri warmer than in the Gersau basin?
a: Because of the föhn wind and the warm Reuss water
Because of warm thermal springs on the lake bed
Because Lake Uri is much deeper
Because Lake Uri freezes over in winter
62092.e: The Reuss brings comparatively warm water into Lake Uri, and the föhn often blows through the Reuss valley and churns the water. As a result, the deep water there is warmer than in the Gersau basin.
62092.m: The föhn and the Reuss warm the deep water of Lake Uri.

62093.q: Roughly how much water does the Grande Dixence reservoir hold?
62093.e: The reservoir holds about 400 million m³ of water. It is filled mainly in summer by glacier meltwater and used in winter to produce electricity.
62093.m: Lac des Dix holds about 400 million cubic metres of water.

62094.q: What is the output of the underground Bieudron power station of the Cleuson-Dixence scheme?
62094.e: The Bieudron power station in the Rhône valley has an output of 1,269 MW. That is roughly the output of a large nuclear power station.
62094.m: The Bieudron power station produces about 1,270 megawatts.

62095.q: Roughly what share of the electrical energy that can be stored in Switzerland does Lac des Dix hold?
62095.e: Because of the great head of water and large volume, the lake stores about a fifth of Switzerland's storable energy. This makes it important for the winter electricity supply.
62095.m: Lac des Dix stores about a fifth of Switzerland's storable energy.

62096.q: Roughly how thick is the Grande Dixence dam at its base?
62096.e: As a gravity dam, the Grande Dixence has to withstand the water pressure through its mass. That is why it is about 200 m thick at the base but only a few metres at the top.
62096.m: The Grande Dixence is about 200 metres thick at its base.

62097.q: How many glaciers feed the catchment area of the Grande Dixence via water intakes?
62097.e: The catchment area covers about 375 km² with 35 glaciers and 75 water intakes. Much of the water is brought in through tunnels and pumping stations.
62097.m: The Grande Dixence is fed by 35 glaciers.

62098.q: How long is the main tunnel that carries water from the side valleys to the Grande Dixence?
62098.e: The main tunnel is about 24 km long and runs at about 2,400 m above sea level. It collects water from several Valais valleys.
62098.m: A tunnel about 24 kilometres long collects water for the Grande Dixence.

62099.q: What happened to the first, smaller dam in the Val des Dix when the Grande Dixence was built?
a: It disappeared into the new, larger reservoir
It was converted into a bridge
It was raised to become the world's highest dam
62099.e: The first Dixence dam, built from 1926 to 1934, was about 85 m high. The much larger new reservoir flooded it.
62099.m: The old Dixence dam now lies in the Grande Dixence reservoir.

62100.q: In which Valais valley is the Fionnay power station, part of the Grande Dixence scheme?
62100.e: The water from Lac des Dix is used in stages, including in the Fionnay power station in the Val de Bagnes and the Nendaz station in the Rhône valley. Fionnay produces about 370 GWh a year.
62100.m: The Fionnay power station is in the Val de Bagnes.

62101.q: What does the flow rate Q347 mean in the Swiss Water Protection Act?
a: The flow reached or exceeded on 347 days a year
The flow fallen short of on 347 days a year
The flow 347 m below an intake
62101.e: Q347 is the flow, averaged over ten years, that is reached or exceeded on average on 347 days a year. So it describes a typical low-water flow.
62101.m: Q347 is a low-water value reached on 347 days a year.

62102.q: A stream has Q347 = 100 l/s. What is the minimum residual flow under Art. 31 of the Water Protection Act (up to 60 l/s it is 50 l/s, for each further 10 l/s add 8 l/s)?
62102.e: Above 60 l/s there are 40 l/s more, that is 4 steps of 10 l/s. Calculation: 50 + 4 · 8 = 82 l/s.
62102.m: The minimum residual flow increases step by step with Q347.

62103.q: A river has Q347 = 1,000 l/s. What is the minimum residual flow (at 500 l/s it is 280 l/s, for each further 100 l/s add 31 l/s)?
62103.e: Above 500 l/s there are 500 l/s more, that is 5 steps of 100 l/s. Calculation: 280 + 5 · 31 = 435 l/s.
62103.m: For larger rivers the residual flow share falls in relation to Q347.

62104.q: Why does the Water Protection Act require a minimum residual flow below water intakes?
a: So that streams do not dry up and living things survive
So that power stations produce more electricity
So that ships can navigate the river
So that reservoirs fill up faster
62104.e: Without residual water, stretches of stream below power stations would almost dry out. Fish, small creatures and riverbank plants would lose their habitat.
62104.m: Residual water protects life in the stream below an intake.

62105.q: In which federal act are Switzerland's minimum residual flows regulated?
62105.e: The Federal Act on the Protection of Waters (WPA) of 24 January 1991 regulates residual flows in Articles 29 to 36. It protects rivers and streams from excessive water withdrawal.
62105.m: The Water Protection Act regulates residual flows.

62106.q: When water is taken for electricity, who must make sure that enough residual water stays in the stream?
a: The operator of the power station
The people living by the stream
62106.e: The residual flow is a condition of the licence. The power station operator must comply with it, and the canton checks this.
62106.m: Power stations must release the required residual flow.

62107.q: What is the water called that is deliberately released at an intake so that the residual flow is maintained?
62107.e: If the water flowing over a weir is not enough, extra water is released, the so-called compensation water. It can even generate electricity in small compensation turbines.
62107.m: Compensation water secures the residual flow below an intake.

62108.q: Under Art. 31 of the Water Protection Act, which condition can require the minimum residual flow to be increased?
a: The water depth needed for free fish migration is lacking
The power station is not profitable
The price of electricity has risen
62108.e: The law requires more residual water if, for example, water quality, groundwater recharge, rare habitats or fish migration would otherwise not be secured. The operator's economic reasons do not count.
62108.m: Residual water must, among other things, allow free fish migration.

62109.q: What is the rapid change between high and low flow below storage power stations called?
62109.e: Storage power stations produce mainly when demand for electricity is high, so the flow rises quickly (surge) and then falls again. Fish and small creatures can become stranded.
62109.m: Hydropeaking harms living things below storage power stations.

62110.q: A stream has Q347 = 300 l/s. What is the minimum residual flow (at 160 l/s it is 130 l/s, for each further 10 l/s add 4.4 l/s)?
62110.e: Above 160 l/s there are 140 l/s more, that is 14 steps of 10 l/s. Calculation: 130 + 14 · 4.4 = 191.6 l/s.
62110.m: The minimum residual flow is calculated in stages from Q347.

62111.q: What was the share of foreign nationals in Switzerland's permanent resident population at the end of 2024?
62111.e: According to the FSO, about 2.48 million people without a Swiss passport lived in Switzerland at the end of 2024. That is 27.4 per cent of the permanent resident population.
62111.m: Just over a quarter of Switzerland's residents do not have a Swiss passport.

62112.q: Which country does the largest group of Switzerland's foreign resident population come from (as of 2023)?
62112.e: Since the labour migration of the post-war years, Italians have formed the largest foreign group, just ahead of Germans. Portugal and France follow.
62112.m: Switzerland's largest foreign community is the Italian one.

62113.q: Which canton has the highest share of foreign nationals in Switzerland?
62113.e: In the canton of Geneva, about 40 per cent of the population have no Swiss passport. Reasons include international organisations, multinational companies and its location on the border.
62113.m: Geneva is the canton with the largest share of foreign nationals.

62114.q: In which year did the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons between Switzerland and the EU come into force?
62114.e: The agreement was signed in 1999 as part of the Bilateral Agreements I and came into force on 1 June 2002. Since then, EU citizens with an employment contract can move to Switzerland more easily.
62114.m: Free movement of persons with the EU has applied since 2002.

62115.q: What was the name of the 1970 popular initiative that wanted to limit the share of foreigners in most cantons to 10 per cent?
62115.e: James Schwarzenbach's initiative against “over-foreignisation” was rejected in 1970 with about 54 per cent voting no. Had it been accepted, hundreds of thousands of foreigners would have had to leave the country.
62115.m: The Schwarzenbach Initiative of 1970 was narrowly rejected.

62116.q: With what share of yes votes was the Mass Immigration Initiative accepted on 9 February 2014?
62116.e: The initiative was accepted very narrowly with 50.3 per cent yes votes. It called for Switzerland to control immigration itself with quotas.
62116.m: The Mass Immigration Initiative was accepted extremely narrowly in 2014.

62117.q: Which residence status for foreign workers, which allowed at most nine months' stay a year without family reunification, was abolished in 2002?
62117.e: Seasonal workers were only allowed to work in Switzerland for a season and could not bring their families. With free movement of persons, the status was abolished in 2002.
62117.m: The seasonal worker status banned family reunification and ended in 2002.

62118.q: Since 2018, how many years of residence in Switzerland does federal law require for ordinary naturalisation?
62118.e: With the revised Swiss Citizenship Act of 2018, the minimum period of residence fell from 12 to 10 years. A C permanent residence permit is also required.
62118.m: For ordinary naturalisation you now need ten years' residence in Switzerland.

62119.q: Roughly what was the share of foreigners in Switzerland in the 1910 census?
62119.e: In 1910 the share of foreigners was about 14.7 per cent, mainly because of workers from Germany and Italy in railway building and industry. After the world wars it fell sharply.
62119.m: Even before the First World War many foreigners lived in Switzerland.

62120.q: Which principle of citizenship means that many people born in Switzerland count as foreigners in the statistics?
62120.e: In Switzerland you basically get citizenship through descent, not by being born in the country. That is why even children of the second generation often have no Swiss passport.
62120.m: Swiss citizenship is passed on mainly through the parents.

62121.q: By how many people did Switzerland's permanent resident population grow in 2024?
62121.e: According to the FSO, the population grew by about 86,600 people from the end of 2023 to the end of 2024, that is by about 1 per cent. This took it past the 9 million mark.
62121.m: Switzerland's population grew by about one per cent in 2024.

62122.q: What was the most important cause of Switzerland's population growth in 2024?
a: the excess of births over deaths
62122.e: Immigration clearly exceeded emigration, while births and deaths almost balanced out. So the growth comes mostly from immigration.

62123.q: In 2024 Switzerland's excess of births over deaths, at about 6,200 people, was the lowest since which year?
62123.e: In 2024 there were about 78,000 births and 71,800 deaths. Such a small excess was last recorded in 1918, the year of the Spanish flu.
62123.m: Births and deaths in Switzerland almost balance out.

62124.q: Roughly how large was the net migration of Switzerland's permanent resident population in 2024?
62124.e: About 212,700 immigrations compared with about 125,600 emigrations. 212,700 minus 125,600 gives a balance of about 87,100 people.
62124.m: Net migration is the difference between immigration and emigration.

62125.q: Roughly what was Switzerland's total fertility rate in 2024?
62125.e: According to the FSO, the fertility rate fell to about 1.3 children per woman in 2024, the lowest value ever measured in Switzerland. To keep the population stable without immigration, about 2.1 would be needed.
62125.m: In Switzerland women have on average clearly fewer than two children.

62126.q: With about 9 million inhabitants and an area of 41,285 km², roughly what is Switzerland's population density?
62126.e: 9,050,000 divided by 41,285 km² gives about 219 inhabitants per km². In the Central Plateau the density is much higher, in the Alps much lower.
62126.m: Population density is the number of inhabitants divided by the area.

62127.q: In which year did Switzerland's permanent resident population pass the 8 million mark?
62127.e: At the end of 2012 Switzerland had over 8 million inhabitants for the first time. By the end of 2024 about another million had been added.
62127.m: Switzerland grew from eight to nine million people in just twelve years.

62128.q: Which canton had the strongest relative population growth in 2024?
62128.e: According to the FSO, Schaffhausen grew by 1.8 per cent in 2024, followed by Fribourg and Valais with 1.5 per cent each. Ticino and Appenzell Outer Rhodes grew the least.
62128.m: In 2024 the population grew in all cantons, most strongly in Schaffhausen.

62129.q: From what length of stay do foreign nationals with a permit count as part of the permanent resident population?
62129.e: The permanent resident population includes Swiss citizens and foreigners with a residence permit for at least 12 months. Short-stay residents of under a year count as the non-permanent resident population.
62129.m: Anyone allowed to stay in Switzerland for at least a year counts as a permanent resident.

62130.q: What was the life expectancy at birth for women in Switzerland in 2024?
62130.e: According to the FSO, life expectancy in 2024 was about 86 years for women and 82.5 years for men. This puts Switzerland among the world leaders.
62130.m: Women in Switzerland live on average about 86 years.

62131.q: Which birth years are called baby boomers, whose retirement is currently speeding up population ageing?
62131.e: After the Second World War the number of births rose sharply. These large age groups are now gradually reaching retirement age.
62131.m: The baby boomers are now retiring and making the number of pensioners rise sharply.

62132.q: What does the old-age dependency ratio measure?
a: the number of people over 64 per 100 people of working age
the share of people over 80 in the population
the average age of the population
the number of children per 100 pensioners
62132.e: The old-age dependency ratio compares people aged 65 and over with those aged 20 to 64. It shows how many pensioners there are for every 100 people of working age.
62132.m: A rising old-age dependency ratio puts pressure on pension provision.

62133.q: What shape does the population pyramid of an ageing society like Switzerland's have, with a narrow base and a wide middle?
62133.e: Because of low birth rates, the young age groups are smaller than the middle ones. The pyramid therefore narrows towards the bottom and looks like an urn.
62133.m: An urn shape shows a shrinking and ageing population.

62134.q: Roughly what share of the Swiss population is 65 or older (as of 2023)?
62134.e: About 19 to 20 per cent of the permanent resident population are 65 or older. This share keeps rising because of the baby boomers and high life expectancy.
62134.m: About one in five people in Switzerland is of retirement age.

62135.q: In which year did the Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AHV) come into force?
62135.e: The people accepted the AHV law in 1947, and the first pensions were paid on 1 January 1948. The AHV forms the first pillar of old-age provision.

62136.q: In which year was the three-pillar principle of old-age provision written into the Federal Constitution?
62136.e: On 3 December 1972 the people and the cantons accepted the constitutional article on the three-pillar principle. It covers state, occupational and private provision.
62136.m: The three-pillar principle has been in the Constitution since 1972.

62137.q: Since which year has occupational pension provision (pension fund, BVG) been compulsory for employees?
62137.e: The Federal Act on Occupational Pensions (BVG) came into force on 1 January 1985. The second pillar works on the funded principle.
62137.m: Pension funds have been compulsory since 1985.

62138.q: To what reference age is the retirement age for women gradually being raised by the AHV 21 reform?
62138.e: The AHV 21 reform was narrowly accepted in 2022. From 2025 the reference age for women rises from 64 to 65 in steps of three months.
62138.m: With AHV 21, women and men have the same reference age of 65.

62139.q: In which year did voters accept the initiative for a 13th monthly AHV pension?
62139.e: On 3 March 2024 the people and the cantons said yes to the initiative for a 13th AHV pension. The extra pension is paid once a year from 2026.
62139.m: Since the 2024 vote there has been a thirteenth AHV pension.

62140.q: What is pillar 3a in Swiss old-age provision?
a: tied private pension saving with a tax deduction
free saving with no tax advantage
62140.e: Payments into pillar 3a up to a yearly maximum can be deducted from taxable income. In return the money is tied up until shortly before retirement.
62140.m: Pillar 3a is tax-advantaged saving for old age.

62141.q: Which region of the canton of Bern is French-speaking?
62141.e: The Bernese Jura, with places such as Moutier (until 2025), Saint-Imier and Tavannes, belongs to the French-speaking part of Switzerland. That is why the canton of Bern is officially bilingual.
62141.m: The Bernese Jura makes the canton of Bern bilingual.

62142.q: What share of the population names French as their main language?
62142.e: About 23 per cent of the population give French as their main language. French-speaking Switzerland includes the cantons of Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura and parts of Bern, Fribourg and Valais.
62142.m: Almost a quarter of the population mainly speaks French.

62143.q: Which fundamental right in the Federal Constitution protects the use of your own language?
62143.e: Article 18 of the Federal Constitution guarantees freedom of language. In dealings with the authorities it is limited by the principle of territoriality.
62143.m: Freedom of language is a fundamental right in Switzerland.

62144.q: What is the name for the coexistence of dialect in everyday life and standard German in writing in German-speaking Switzerland?
62144.e: In German-speaking Switzerland people speak Swiss German in everyday life but mostly write standard German. This division of roles between two varieties is called diglossia.
62144.m: In German-speaking Switzerland people speak dialect and write standard German.

62145.q: According to which principle do the cantons decide the official language in their area?
62145.e: Under the principle of territoriality, the language traditionally spoken in an area is the official and school language there. Newcomers have to adapt to it.
62145.m: The principle of territoriality protects the traditional language areas.

62146.q: Apart from the Grisons, Bern, Fribourg and Valais, which canton has more than one official language?
62146.e: Only four cantons are multilingual. Bern, Fribourg and Valais are bilingual, the Grisons is trilingual, and all the others have a single official language.
62146.m: Switzerland has only four multilingual cantons.

62147.q: Why do the shares of main languages in the FSO structural survey add up to more than 100 per cent?
a: People can give more than one main language
62147.e: Since 2010, people surveyed can name several languages as their main language. Bilingual people therefore appear in two language groups.
62147.m: Many people in Switzerland have more than one main language.

62148.q: Since which year has the federal Languages Act, which promotes the national languages and understanding between them, been in force?
62148.e: The Languages Act was passed by parliament in 2007 and came into force in 2010. Among other things, it regulates the official languages of the Confederation and the promotion of multilingualism.
62148.m: Since 2010 the Languages Act has promoted Switzerland's multilingualism.

62149.q: What does the Federal Constitution require regarding the regions of the country when the Federal Council is elected?
a: that the regions and language areas are fairly represented
that at least two members come from the Grisons
that every canton is represented in turn
62149.e: Article 175 of the Federal Constitution requires that the various regions and language areas are fairly represented. However, there is no fixed quota for Latin Switzerland.
62149.m: The language regions should be fairly represented in the Federal Council.

62150.q: Which business unit of the SRG produces radio and television for French-speaking Switzerland?
62150.e: RTS stands for Radio Télévision Suisse, based in Geneva and Lausanne. SRF broadcasts for German-speaking Switzerland, RSI for Italian-speaking and RTR for Romansh-speaking Switzerland.
62150.m: Each language region has its own SRG business unit.

62151.q: How did French-speaking Switzerland vote in the EEA referendum of 6 December 1992?
a: Clearly yes, while German-speaking Switzerland said no
Clearly no, while German-speaking Switzerland said yes
Exactly the same as German-speaking Switzerland
It was not allowed to vote
62151.e: All French-speaking cantons said yes to the EEA, most German-speaking cantons said no. The vote is seen as a classic example of the Röstigraben, the cultural divide between the two regions.
62151.m: The 1992 EEA vote showed the Röstigraben especially clearly.

62152.q: Based on the term Röstigraben, what is the divide between German-speaking and Italian-speaking Switzerland called?
62152.e: Just as rösti is a symbol of German-speaking Switzerland, polenta stands for Ticino. The term (literally “polenta ditch”) describes different voting behaviour on either side of the Alps.
62152.m: The Polentagraben separates German-speaking and Italian-speaking Switzerland.

62153.q: In which policy areas does French-speaking Switzerland especially often vote differently from German-speaking Switzerland?
62153.e: Analyses of votes show that French-speaking Switzerland is often more open towards the EU and a strong welfare state. In such votes the Röstigraben shows most clearly.
62153.m: The Röstigraben shows mainly on European and social questions.

62154.q: Which language problem often makes communication in German-speaking Switzerland difficult for French speakers, even though they learn German at school?
a: Swiss German is spoken in everyday life
Romansh is spoken in German-speaking Switzerland
62154.e: At school French speakers learn standard German, but in German-speaking Switzerland people mostly speak dialect. This makes conversations harder and increases the distance.
62154.m: Dialect is a hurdle for many French speakers.

62155.q: Which proposal was rejected in 1999 although western Switzerland mostly voted for it, a well-known example of the Röstigraben?
62155.e: In June 1999 German-speaking Switzerland clearly rejected maternity insurance, while French-speaking Switzerland voted for it. Maternity pay was only accepted in 2004.
62155.m: Social policy proposals often show the Röstigraben.

62156.q: In most German-speaking cantons far from the language border, which foreign language do children learn first at primary school?
62156.e: In cantons such as Zurich or St Gallen, foreign language teaching starts with English. Only the cantons along the language border start with French, which is often criticised in French-speaking Switzerland.
62156.m: Many German-speaking Swiss children learn English before French.

62157.q: With what share of yes votes was Romansh recognised as the fourth national language in 1938?
62157.e: On 20 February 1938, 91.6 per cent of voters said yes. The clear result was also seen as a statement against Italian claims on Romansh.
62157.m: The recognition of Romansh in 1938 won overwhelming support.

a: A common written language for all the idioms
The oldest Romansh idiom in the Engadine
A dialect from the Val Müstair
A mixed language of German and Italian
62158.e: Rumantsch Grischun was created in 1982 on behalf of the Lia Rumantscha. It uses the form found in most of the idioms and serves, for example, as an official language.
62158.m: Rumantsch Grischun is the common written language of Romansh.

62159.q: After which event in 1464 did the town of Chur become increasingly German-speaking?
62159.e: After the town fire of 1464, many German-speaking craftsmen moved to Chur to help rebuild it. As a result, the town switched from Romansh to German.
62159.m: Chur became German-speaking after the town fire of 1464.

62160.q: With which languages is the Romansh of the Grisons often grouped as the Rhaeto-Romance languages?
62160.e: According to a common classification, the Romansh of the Grisons, Ladin in the Dolomites and Friulian in north-eastern Italy form the Rhaeto-Romance group. Whether they form a unit of their own is disputed among researchers.
62160.m: The Romansh of the Grisons is related to Ladin and Friulian.

62161.q: How many regional written idioms does the Romansh of the Grisons have?
62161.e: The five idioms are Sursilvan, Sutsilvan, Surmiran, Puter and Vallader. In addition there is the common written language Rumantsch Grischun.
62161.m: The Romansh of the Grisons has five written idioms.

62162.q: Which Romansh idiom has the most speakers?
62162.e: Sursilvan is spoken in the Surselva along the Vorderrhein and is the largest idiom. Sutsilvan is the smallest.
62162.m: Sursilvan is the most widely spoken Romansh idiom.

62163.q: What are the three official languages of the canton of the Grisons?
62163.e: The Grisons is the only trilingual canton in Switzerland. The cantonal Languages Act gives special protection to Romansh.
62163.m: The Grisons is the only trilingual canton.

62164.q: From about 2011, what did many Grisons municipalities return to in school teaching after introducing Rumantsch Grischun as the language for learning to read and write?
62164.e: There was resistance in many municipalities to teaching in Rumantsch Grischun. Many schools therefore went back to reading and writing in their own idiom.
62164.m: Many Romansh schools teach in their own idiom again.

62165.q: What is seen as an important reason for the decline of Romansh in the 19th and 20th centuries?
a: German speakers moving in because of tourism and transport
a ban by the Federal Council
62165.e: Railways, tourism and economic links brought many German speakers to the Grisons. As a result, German became the everyday language in many municipalities.
62165.m: Tourism and mobility have pushed back Romansh.

62166.q: What is meant by internal migration?
62166.e: Internal migration covers moves between municipalities, regions or cantons within a country. The national border is not crossed.
62166.m: In internal migration people move within their own country.

62167.q: What is the growth of rural municipalities far outside the urban areas through commuters moving in called?
62167.e: In periurbanisation, people move to rural municipalities beyond the suburban belts and commute to the centres. This increases traffic and urban sprawl.
62167.m: Periurbanisation brings city commuters to the countryside.

62168.q: What is the development called in which core cities such as Zurich have been gaining residents again since the late 1990s?
62168.e: After decades of people moving away, cities became attractive again, for example through the conversion of industrial sites. The city of Zurich has been growing again since the late 1990s.
62168.m: Reurbanisation means the population returning to the cities.

62169.q: Which of the following is a push factor for internal migration?
a: Lack of jobs where you live
A wide range of culture at the destination
62169.e: Push factors drive people away from where they have been living. Pull factors, on the other hand, attract them to a new place.
62169.m: Push factors push people away and pull factors draw them in.

62170.q: What is the upgrading of a neighbourhood called, in which wealthier residents move in and existing ones are pushed out?
62170.e: In gentrification, rents rise after renovations, so that residents on low incomes have to move away. Examples include districts such as Zurich West.
62170.m: Gentrification changes the social mix of a neighbourhood.

62171.q: Which migration movement shaped Switzerland during industrialisation in the 19th century?
a: Rural exodus to the industrial towns
Flight from the cities to the Alps
62171.e: With the factories, many jobs were created in cities and industrial towns. Large numbers of people therefore left rural areas.
62171.m: Industrialisation drew the rural population into the cities.

62172.q: Which federalist factor particularly influences where people choose to live within Switzerland?
a: different tax burdens in the municipalities
62172.e: Cantons and municipalities set their own tax rates. Especially high-earning households therefore often move to municipalities with low taxes.
62172.m: Tax competition influences where people live in Switzerland.

62173.q: What are working people called who regularly travel back and forth between the municipality where they live and where they work, without moving?
62173.e: Commuters change place every day but not their place of residence. So in many cases commuting replaces moving house, which is why it is not internal migration.
62173.m: Commuters work somewhere other than where they live.

62174.q: How many foreign cross-border commuters worked in Switzerland in the 2nd quarter of 2026?
62174.e: According to the FSO, there were exactly 414,262 people in the second quarter of 2026. Their number has more than doubled since the mid-1990s.
62174.m: Over 400,000 cross-border commuters work in Switzerland every day.

62175.q: Which country do most cross-border commuters in Switzerland come from?
62175.e: More than half of cross-border commuters live in France, especially around Geneva and Basel. Italy and Germany follow.
62175.m: Most cross-border commuters come from France.

62176.q: Which canton employs the most cross-border commuters in absolute numbers?
62176.e: Geneva is almost completely surrounded by France and draws very many workers every day from Haute-Savoie and the Pays de Gex. According to the FSO, Geneva has the highest absolute number.
62176.m: Geneva employs the most cross-border commuters.

62177.q: In which canton do cross-border commuters make up the largest share of total employment?
62177.e: Very many commuters from Lombardy and Piedmont work in Ticino. Measured against all employees, their share there is the highest according to the FSO.
62177.m: In Ticino the share of cross-border commuters among employees is the largest.

62178.q: Which permit do cross-border commuters from abroad receive in Switzerland?
62178.e: The G permit is the cross-border commuter permit. B stands for residence, C for permanent residence and L for short stay.
62178.m: Cross-border commuters work in Switzerland with a G permit.

62179.q: How often, at least, must cross-border commuters from EU and EFTA states return to where they live abroad?
62179.e: For EU and EFTA nationals, returning to their main residence abroad once a week is enough. In the past, a daily return was required.
62179.m: Cross-border commuters from the EU go home at least once a week.

62180.q: Since which year has the new cross-border commuter agreement between Switzerland and Italy, which changes how they are taxed, been in force?
62180.e: The agreement came into force in July 2023. Since then, new cross-border commuters are also taxed more heavily in Italy, which changes how attractive a job in Ticino is.
62180.m: Since 2023 a new tax agreement has applied to Italian cross-border commuters.

62181.q: Since which year has the cross-border S-Bahn Léman Express connected Geneva with the surrounding French area?
62181.e: The Léman Express began operating in December 2019. It is meant to shift commuter traffic from France from cars to the railway.
62181.m: The Léman Express has run across the border to Geneva since 2019.

62182.q: What are cross-border commuters in Ticino called in Italian?
62182.e: The word “frontalieri” comes from “frontiera”, the border. They commute to Ticino mainly from the provinces of Como, Varese and Verbano-Cusio-Ossola.
62182.m: In Ticino cross-border commuters are called “frontalieri”.

62183.q: In 2022, which was the largest group by religious affiliation in the Swiss population aged 15 and over?
62183.e: In 2022, according to the FSO, people with no religious affiliation, at about 34 per cent, were ahead of Roman Catholics and Reformed Protestants for the first time. As late as 1970 both large churches were far bigger.
62183.m: In Switzerland people with no religious affiliation are now the largest group.

62184.q: What was the share of Roman Catholics in Switzerland in 2022?
62184.e: According to the FSO, about 32 per cent belonged to the Roman Catholic Church in 2022. The share has been falling for decades.
62184.m: About a third of the population is Roman Catholic.

62185.q: What was the share of people with no religious affiliation in Switzerland in 1970?
62185.e: In 1970 hardly anyone had no religious affiliation; around 2000 it was about 11 per cent. By 2022 the share had risen to about 34 per cent.
62185.m: The number of people with no religious affiliation has risen enormously since 1970.

62186.q: Which canton had the lowest share of people with no religious affiliation in 2022?
62186.e: In Appenzell Inner Rhodes only about 15 per cent had no religious affiliation in 2022. In Basel-Stadt and Neuchâtel, by contrast, more than half have none.
62186.m: Catholic Appenzell Inner Rhodes has the fewest people with no religious affiliation.

62187.q: What was the share of people belonging to an Islamic religious community in Switzerland in 2022?
62187.e: About 6 per cent belong to an Islamic community, many with roots in the Western Balkans or Turkey. The share of other Christian communities is the same size.
62187.m: About one in seventeen people in Switzerland is Muslim.

62188.q: In the 20th century, what contributed greatly to Catholics overtaking Protestants in number?
a: the founding of the federal state
62188.e: Many workers from Italy, Spain and Portugal were Catholic. This shifted the religious balance, which had long been dominated by the Reformed Church.
62188.m: Immigration from southern Europe strengthened the Catholic Church in Switzerland.

62189.q: Which two cantons have an extensive separation of church and state?
62189.e: Geneva separated church and state in 1907, Neuchâtel in 1941. There the cantons do not levy a church tax in the usual sense.
62189.m: In Geneva and Neuchâtel church and state are largely separate.

62190.q: In which year did voters accept the popular initiative against building minarets?
62190.e: On 29 November 2009 the initiative was accepted with about 57.5 per cent yes. Since then the Federal Constitution has banned the building of new minarets.
62190.m: The minaret ban has been in the Federal Constitution since 2009.

62191.q: Which exceptional article from the time of the Kulturkampf banned a Catholic order from any activity in Switzerland until 1973?
62191.e: The Jesuit article came from the Federal Constitution of 1848. The people and the cantons abolished it in 1973; the diocese article was only dropped in 2001.
62191.m: The ban on the Jesuits was removed from the Federal Constitution in 1973.

62192.q: Which federal act of 1974 was meant to slow down people leaving mountain areas by providing low-interest loans for infrastructure?
62192.e: The Investment Aid Act (IHG) financed roads, schools and water supplies in mountain municipalities. It was an important tool of early regional policy.
62192.m: With the Investment Aid Act, the Confederation supported mountain areas from 1974.

62193.q: What is an “albergo diffuso”, as set up in depopulated mountain villages in Ticino?
a: a hotel with rooms in scattered empty houses
a youth hostel in old barracks
a hotel on a mountain farm
62193.e: In an albergo diffuso, empty houses are renovated and used as hotel rooms, with a shared reception. This keeps villages alive and gives them income from tourism.
62193.m: An albergo diffuso spreads a hotel across a whole village.

62194.q: Which foundation has supported people in Swiss mountain areas since 1943 to secure their livelihoods and slow down people moving away?
62194.e: Swiss Mountain Aid funds projects of mountain farmers, businesses and municipalities. The aim is to keep jobs and quality of life in the mountain areas.
62194.m: Swiss Mountain Aid helps the people in mountain areas.

62195.q: What demographic consequence does young people leaving mountain villages have?
a: a rise in the number of births
62195.e: When mainly young people move away, older people stay behind and fewer children are born. This makes the shrinking even worse.
62195.m: Young people moving away makes mountain villages age.

62196.q: What does the Confederation want to achieve with the New Regional Policy (NRP)?
a: Strengthen innovation and value creation in mountain areas
Resettle mountain people in the cities
62196.e: The New Regional Policy came into force in 2008 and replaced older support tools. It supports innovation and value creation in mountain areas and economically weak rural regions.
62196.m: Since 2008 the New Regional Policy has strengthened mountain areas.

62197.q: What is the departure of well-educated young people from a region called?
62197.e: Young people from mountain valleys often study in cities and find suitable jobs there. The region thus loses skilled workers and innovative strength.
62197.m: Brain drain means losing well-educated people.

62198.q: Which branch of the economy has stopped people leaving mountain resorts such as Zermatt or Davos and has even brought people in?
62198.e: Tourist resorts offer many jobs in hotels, mountain railways and businesses. There the population grows, while remote valleys without tourism shrink.
62198.m: Tourism can keep mountain regions alive economically.

62199.q: What are holiday flats in mountain resorts called that stand empty for most of the year?
62199.e: Cold beds bring mountain villages hardly any life and little value outside the season. Warm beds, by contrast, are accommodation that is regularly rented out, such as hotels.
62199.m: Empty holiday flats are called cold beds.

62200.q: Which closure in the village often particularly increases the departure of young families from mountain municipalities?
a: the closure of the village school
the closure of the ski lift
62200.e: Without a village school, children have to travel a long way to school. This makes the place unattractive for young families, which speeds up the departure.
62200.m: Without a school, mountain villages lose their young families.

62201.q: On average, how many people lived in a private household in Switzerland at the end of 2022?
62201.e: According to the FSO, the average household size in 2022 was about 2.18 people. Households have become smaller and smaller over the last few decades.
62201.m: A Swiss household has on average just over two people.

62202.q: Which type of household is the most common in Switzerland?
a: the household with four or more people
62202.e: In 2022 about 37 per cent of households were one-person households and 33 per cent two-person households. Larger households are much rarer.
62202.m: Most often, only one person lives in a Swiss household.

62203.q: Which form of living do statistics count not as a private household but as a collective household?
62203.e: Collective households include retirement and care homes, boarding schools, hospitals or prisons. Shared flats, on the other hand, count as private households without a family core.
62203.m: People in homes live in collective households in the statistics.

62204.q: Where in Switzerland is the share of one-person households highest?
62204.e: In large cities such as Zurich, Basel or Geneva, especially many young adults and older people live alone. There the share of one-person households is much higher than in rural municipalities.
62204.m: In the cities especially many people live alone.

62205.q: How has the number of one-person households in Switzerland changed since 1970?
a: It has stayed about the same
It has risen by 10 per cent
62205.e: In 1970 there were still well under half a million one-person households; today there are about 1.5 million. Their number has therefore more than tripled.
62205.m: Living alone has increased greatly in Switzerland.

62206.q: Which development contributes especially to the falling average household size?
62206.e: Because of higher life expectancy, many older people live alone after their partner dies. Added to this are low birth rates and individualisation.
62206.m: Ageing leads to more small households.

62207.q: About 37 per cent of the roughly 4 million private households are one-person households. So what share of the roughly 8.8 million people in private households lives alone?
62207.e: 0.37 times 4 million gives about 1.48 million people living alone. 1.48 divided by 8.8 million gives about 17 per cent of the population.
62207.m: A high share of one-person households does not mean that just as many people live alone.

62208.q: How has the average household size in Switzerland changed since 1960?
a: It fell from over 3 to about 2.2 people
It rose from 2.2 to over 3 people
62208.e: In 1960 more than three people on average still lived in a household. Smaller families and more people living alone made the figure fall to about 2.2.
62208.m: Households in Switzerland have become much smaller since 1960.

62209.q: What share of private households in Switzerland in 2022 consisted of couples with at least one child under 25?
62209.e: According to the FSO, just under 30 per cent of households were couples with children, and about the same number were couples without children. The classic family has long ceased to be the majority of households.
62209.m: Fewer than a third of households are families with children.

62210.q: Which city forms its own urban area within the Zurich metropolitan area?
62210.e: Besides Zurich, the Zurich metropolitan area includes other urban areas such as Winterthur, Zug or Baden. Basel, Bern and Lausanne lie in other large regions.
62210.m: Winterthur is part of the Zurich metropolitan area.

62211.q: Roughly how many inhabitants did the Zurich metropolitan area have when the association was founded?
62211.e: When it was founded in 2009, about 1.9 million people lived in the Zurich metropolitan area in 238 municipalities. There were also about 900,000 jobs.
62211.m: About two million people live in the Zurich metropolitan area.

62212.q: How is the Zurich Metropolitan Conference organised?
a: With one chamber for the cantons and one for the municipalities
With a single council of cities
With representatives of the Federal Council
With an assembly of business associations
62212.e: The Metropolitan Conference has two chambers with equal rights: one for the cantons and one for the cities and municipalities. In this way both levels of government are represented.
62212.m: The Metropolitan Conference has a cantonal chamber and a municipal chamber.

62213.q: Which criterion mainly decides whether a municipality belongs to the Zurich metropolitan area?
a: Belonging to the canton of Zurich
The official language of the municipality
62213.e: What counts most is how closely a municipality is linked to Zurich by commuter flows. That is why municipalities from neighbouring cantons belong to it too.
62213.m: Commuter flows link the metropolitan area across cantonal borders.

62214.q: Apart from the capital region, how many metropolitan areas does the Swiss Spatial Strategy distinguish?
62214.e: The Swiss Spatial Strategy names the metropolitan areas of Zurich, Basel and the Lake Geneva region. The Capital Region Switzerland is listed separately.
62214.m: Zurich, Basel and the Lake Geneva region are Switzerland's three metropolitan areas.

62215.q: Which transport project has connected Zurich-Altstetten with Killwangen-Spreitenbach all the way since 2022?
62215.e: The Limmattalbahn is a light railway through the fast-growing Limmat Valley. It is meant to steer and concentrate building development along the line.
62215.m: The Limmattalbahn serves the Limmat Valley west of Zurich.

62216.q: What is the difference between the Zurich urban area and the Zurich metropolitan area?
a: The metropolitan area is larger and includes several urban areas
Both terms mean exactly the same area
The urban area is larger than the metropolitan area
The metropolitan area only includes the city of Zurich
62216.e: An urban area (agglomeration) is a continuous built-up area around a core. The metropolitan area includes several urban areas such as Zurich, Winterthur or Zug.
62216.m: A metropolitan area brings together several urban areas.

62217.q: Which facility in the Zurich metropolitan area is Switzerland's largest national airport?
62217.e: Zurich Airport lies mostly on the territory of Kloten. It is the largest airport in Switzerland and an important location factor for the region.

62218.q: Why did the area of urban areas grow much more than their population share with the new FSO definition of 2012?
a: Mainly thinly populated municipalities were added
Many people moved back into the core cities
62218.e: The area of urban areas rose by about a third, from 8,601 km² to 11,356 km². Because mainly thinly populated municipalities were added, the population share rose only slightly.
62218.m: The new definition greatly enlarged the area of urban areas.

62219.q: Since 2012, what does the FSO count besides inhabitants to determine the size of an urban area?
62219.e: The definition counts inhabitants, employees and converted overnight stays together. An urban area needs at least 20,000 of these units. This way places of work and tourism are also captured correctly.
62219.m: Urban areas are measured by inhabitants, employees and overnight stays.

62220.q: According to the 2012 definition, what share of the Swiss population lived in urban areas?
62220.e: About 73 per cent of the population lived in urban areas. The area of the urban areas grew much more than their population share.
62220.m: Almost three quarters of the population live in urban areas.

62221.q: Which feature does the FSO use to assign municipalities to the belt of an urban area?
62221.e: Belt municipalities are closely linked to the core of the urban area by commuter flows. The core itself is determined by density.
62221.m: Commuters tie the belt municipalities to the core of the urban area.

62222.q: Roughly how many municipalities belong to the Zurich urban area, the largest in Switzerland?
62222.e: According to the 2012 definition, the Zurich urban area included 151 municipalities, 21 more than under the 2000 definition. It extends far beyond the canton of Zurich.
62222.m: The Zurich urban area includes about 150 municipalities.

62223.q: Which tool does the Confederation use to plan and help fund transport and settlement in urban areas together?
62223.e: Urban areas submit agglomeration programmes that coordinate transport and settlement. Good programmes receive federal contributions to transport projects.
62223.m: Agglomeration programmes coordinate transport and settlement.

62224.q: Since 2018, from which fund has the Confederation paid contributions to transport in urban areas?
a: From the railway infrastructure fund alone
62224.e: The National Roads and Agglomeration Transport Fund (NAF) was accepted by the people in 2017. It finances national roads and urban transport projects.
62224.m: The NAF finances national roads and urban transport.

62225.q: What is it called when people move out of the core city into the surrounding municipalities?
62225.e: In suburbanisation, people and businesses move from the core city to the surrounding area. As a result, the suburban belts grow.
62225.m: Suburbanisation makes the areas around cities grow.

62226.q: According to Zurich city statistics, what share of the population of the Zurich urban area lived in the core city itself?
62226.e: Of just under 1.3 million people in the urban area, about 30 per cent lived in the city of Zurich. The majority lived in the other core and belt municipalities.
62226.m: Most people in the Zurich urban area live outside the core city.

62227.q: What does the measure “weighted urban sprawl”, which researchers use to record sprawl in Switzerland, take into account?
a: Built-up area, how scattered it is and how densely it is used
Only the number of inhabitants of a municipality
Only the length of the road network
Only the height of the buildings
62227.e: Weighted urban sprawl takes into account how much land is built on, how scattered the settlements are and how densely they are used. It was developed among others at the WSL.
62227.m: Weighted urban sprawl measures how much settlements spread into the landscape.

62228.q: When did Switzerland vote on the Young Greens' urban sprawl initiative?
62228.e: The vote took place on 10 February 2019. The initiative wanted to freeze the total area of building zones.
62228.m: The urban sprawl initiative was voted on in 2019.

62229.q: With what result was the urban sprawl initiative rejected in 2019?
a: With almost two thirds voting no
With just under 51 per cent voting no
With over 90 per cent voting no
62229.e: The people and the cantons clearly rejected the initiative; about 64 per cent voted no. Turnout was about 37 per cent.
62229.m: The urban sprawl initiative failed clearly.

62230.q: What would the urban sprawl initiative have required for every new building zone?
a: An equally large area to be taken out of the building zone elsewhere
62230.e: New building zones could only have been created if an equally large area of similar agricultural value had been taken out of the building zone elsewhere. The building zone area would thus have been frozen.
62230.m: The urban sprawl initiative wanted to freeze the building zone area.

62231.q: Which popular initiative was withdrawn because parliament revised the Spatial Planning Act as a counter-proposal?
62231.e: The Landscape Initiative called for a 20-year halt to enlarging building zones. After the revision of the Spatial Planning Act was accepted in 2013, it was finally withdrawn.
62231.m: The revision of the Spatial Planning Act was the counter-proposal to the Landscape Initiative.

62232.q: Which form of housing is often named as an important driver of urban sprawl?
a: The block of flats in the city centre
The tower block by the station
The housing co-operative in the centre
62232.e: Single-family houses need a lot of land per person and are often built on the edge of settlements. Also, their residents often depend on the car.
62232.m: Detached single-family houses use a lot of land.

62233.q: What are crop rotation areas in Swiss spatial planning?
a: Fallow land to let the soil recover
62233.e: Crop rotation areas are the best arable soils in the country. With the sectoral plan for crop rotation areas, the Confederation secures a minimum area of them, and the cantons have fixed quotas for this.
62233.m: The Confederation protects the best farmland with the sectoral plan for crop rotation areas.

62234.q: Which consequence of urban sprawl puts a particular strain on municipal finances?
a: Expensive servicing with long roads and pipes
Higher contributions to the canton for hospitals
Rising costs for protecting historic monuments
62234.e: Scattered buildings need more roads, water pipes and sewers per inhabitant. Building and maintaining this infrastructure is expensive.
62234.m: Urban sprawl makes infrastructure more expensive per person.

62235.q: When did the Federal Spatial Planning Act (RPG) come into force?
62235.e: The RPG was passed on 22 June 1979 and came into force on 1 January 1980. A first draft had failed in a referendum in 1976.
62235.m: The Spatial Planning Act has applied since 1980.

62236.q: Which basic principle is stated in the first article of the Spatial Planning Act?
62236.e: The Confederation, cantons and municipalities are to make sure that land is used economically. In addition, building areas are to be kept separate from non-building areas.

62237.q: How is responsibility for spatial planning divided according to the Federal Constitution?
a: The Confederation sets principles, the cantons are responsible
The Confederation plans every municipality itself
The municipalities alone decide without rules
Spatial planning is a matter for the army
62237.e: According to Article 75 of the Federal Constitution, the Confederation sets the principles of spatial planning. The actual planning is the task of the cantons and their municipalities.
62237.m: Spatial planning is mainly a matter for the cantons.

62238.q: Who is bound by the cantonal structure plan?
62238.e: The structure plan is binding on the authorities and must be approved by the Federal Council. Only the land use plan is binding on landowners.
62238.m: The structure plan binds the authorities, the land use plan binds landowners.

62239.q: What was the main aim of the revision of the Spatial Planning Act accepted by the people in 2013?
a: To reduce building zones that are too large
To create more building land in the Alps
To promote the building of second homes
62239.e: The revision was clearly accepted on 3 March 2013. It is meant to slow down urban sprawl by reducing oversized building zones.
62239.m: The 2013 revision of the Spatial Planning Act slows down urban sprawl.

62240.q: Which was the only canton to reject the 2013 revision of the Spatial Planning Act?
62240.e: Valais voted against it by a large majority. The canton had especially large reserves of building zones and feared they would be rezoned.
62240.m: Only Valais said no to the revision of the Spatial Planning Act in 2013.

62241.q: Which federal authority is responsible for spatial planning?
a: The Federal Office for Spatial Development (ARE)
The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)
62241.e: The ARE is the federal specialist authority for spatial development and transport planning. Among other things, it examines the cantonal structure plans.
62241.m: The ARE is the federal spatial planning office.

62242.q: What does a canton face if it does not implement the requirements of the revised Spatial Planning Act on time?
a: A ban on new building zones
Loss of its Council of States seat
62242.e: Cantons that did not adapt their structure plan or their levy on increased land value in time were no longer allowed to create new building zones. This sanction was meant to ensure implementation.
62242.m: Cantons that are late may not create new building zones.

62243.q: Which municipal plans decide for each plot of land whether and how it may be built on?
62243.e: Land use plans such as the zoning plan divide the municipality into building, agricultural and protected zones. They are binding on landowners, the structure plan only on authorities.
62243.m: The land use plan decides where building is allowed.

a: Growth within existing building zones instead of on open fields
Moving the population into mountain valleys
