62467.e: A large share of gravel and excavated material transport runs between the city and the Zurich Unterland. The railway relieves roads and villages of heavy lorry journeys.
62467.m: Gravel on rails takes pressure off the roads.

62468.q: Who owns the Swiss Saltworks (Schweizer Salinen)?
a: All the cantons and the Principality of Liechtenstein
62468.e: Schweizer Salinen AG is owned by all the Swiss cantons and the Principality of Liechtenstein. The company is based in Pratteln.
62468.m: The Swiss Saltworks belong to the cantons and Liechtenstein.

62469.q: Which three sites do the Swiss Saltworks operate today?
62469.e: Schweizerhalle is near Pratteln, Riburg near Möhlin and Bex in the canton of Vaud. Bex has been part of the company since 2021.
62469.m: Salt is produced at Schweizerhalle, Riburg and Bex.

62470.q: Why was the discovery of salt near Muttenz in 1836 so important for Switzerland?
a: Switzerland hardly had to import salt any more
It was the first gold find in the country
It led to the building of the Gotthard railway
62470.e: Before that, Switzerland had to import almost all its salt from abroad. With the Schweizerhalle saltworks from 1837, it could largely supply itself.
62470.m: Since 1836 Switzerland has largely been able to supply itself with salt.

62471.q: Which method is used to obtain salt at Schweizerhalle and Riburg?
a: Solution mining with fresh water pumped down boreholes
Digging salt crusts on the surface
62471.e: Fresh water is pumped into the salt layer, dissolves the salt and is brought back up as saturated brine. The brine is then purified and evaporated.
62471.m: In solution mining, salt is dissolved underground with water.

62472.q: What is the cantonal monopoly on the salt trade in Switzerland called?
62472.e: Each canton has the sole right to trade salt on its territory. The cantons have transferred this right to the Swiss Saltworks.
62472.m: The salt regale gives the cantons the salt monopoly.

62473.q: Where can you visit a salt mine with about 50 kilometres of tunnels?
62473.e: Salt has been produced in Bex in Vaud since the 17th century. Part of the extensive tunnel system is open to visitors as a show mine.
62473.m: In Bex you can visit a real salt mine.

62474.q: What is the Saldome 2 of the Swiss Saltworks, opened in 2012, used for?
a: As a store for over 100,000 tonnes of de-icing salt
As a museum of salt history
As a brine bath for guests
62474.e: After shortages of road salt in harsh winters, large salt stores were built. The Saldome 2, with a span of 120 metres, is regarded as the largest wooden dome in Europe.
62474.m: Road salt for the winter is stored in the Saldome.

62475.q: Why has iodine been added to table salt in Switzerland since 1922?
a: To prevent goitre and iodine deficiency
To make it melt ice faster
62475.e: Swiss soils are low in iodine, so in the past many people suffered from goitre. Iodised table salt has largely eliminated iodine deficiency.
62475.m: Iodised salt protects against iodine deficiency.

62476.q: At most, how much salt can the Swiss Saltworks produce per year?
62476.e: Capacity is up to about 600,000 tonnes a year. How much is actually produced depends greatly on the need for road salt in winter.
62476.m: The saltworks can make over half a million tonnes of salt a year.

62477.q: In which geological period did the salt deposits on the High Rhine, from which the saltworks obtain brine, form?
62477.e: The salt layers formed in the Triassic, when a shallow sea evaporated in a hot climate. Today they lie about 100 to 400 metres deep.
62477.m: Swiss salt comes from a Triassic sea.

62478.q: Which bark beetle causes the greatest damage to weakened conifers in Swiss forests?
62478.e: The European spruce bark beetle multiplies massively after storms and in hot, dry summers. Its larvae feed under the bark and cut off the flow of sap, so that whole stands of trees can die.
62478.m: The European spruce bark beetle is the most dangerous bark beetle in Swiss forests.

62479.q: Roughly how much wood is harvested in Swiss forests every year?
62479.e: Forest owners harvest about 5 million cubic metres of wood a year. That is less than grows back, which is why the stock of wood is high in many places.
62479.m: Switzerland harvests about five million cubic metres of wood a year.

62480.q: What rank does wood energy hold among Switzerland's renewable energies?
62480.e: Wood is used mainly for heating in wood chip, pellet and log heating systems. According to the FOEN, wood is the second most important renewable energy source after hydropower.
62480.m: After water, wood is Switzerland's second most important renewable energy.

62481.q: Which principle has applied in Swiss forest law since the Forest Police Act of 1876?
a: The forest area may in principle not be reduced
Any tree may be felled without permission
Forest may only belong to the Confederation
62481.e: After severe floods caused by overuse, the Confederation introduced a ban on clearing forest, first for the mountains in 1876, and extended it to the whole of Switzerland in 1902. If forest is exceptionally cleared, equivalent replacement must be created.
62481.m: Since 1876 the area of Swiss forest has been protected.

62482.q: Which hurricane-force storm caused huge damage in Swiss forests on 26 December 1999?
62482.e: In a single day, Lothar blew down about three times a normal year's harvest of wood. Vivian had already hit Switzerland in 1990, Burglind in 2018.
62482.m: Lothar was the worst storm in the history of the Swiss forest.

62483.q: What is the principle called of using wood first as material, for example as building timber, and only at the end for energy?
62483.e: With cascading use, the carbon stored in the wood stays locked up for as long as possible. Only when the wood can no longer be used is it burned.
62483.m: Wood should first be used for building and only burned last.

62484.q: What is the main task of protection forest in the Alps?
a: Protection from avalanches, rockfall and landslides
62484.e: About half of the Swiss forest protects people, settlements and transport routes from natural hazards. It must be specially cared for so that it keeps its protective effect.
62484.m: Protection forest keeps villages and roads safe from natural hazards.

62485.q: What main reason did Nagra give in 2022 for choosing Nördlich Lägern as the site?
62485.e: Nagra stressed that the geology had been decisive. At Nördlich Lägern, keeping the waste enclosed over a long period is best guaranteed.
62485.m: Geology decided the choice of site for the deep geological repository.

62486.q: Roughly how old is the Opalinus Clay in which the deep repository is to be built?
62486.e: The Opalinus Clay formed in the Jurassic period as fine mud on the bottom of a sea. It is named after the ammonite Leioceras opalinum.
62486.m: Opalinus Clay is sea mud from the Jurassic period.

62487.q: Which property makes Opalinus Clay especially suitable for a deep geological repository?
a: It is very dense and can seal small cracks itself
It is especially porous and lets water through
It contains a lot of usable oil
62487.e: Clay hardly lets water through and swells when it comes into contact with water, which closes cracks again. In addition, clay minerals bind many radioactive substances.
62487.m: Dense clay holds back radioactive substances.

62488.q: Roughly at what depth is the repository at Nördlich Lägern to be built?
62488.e: According to Nagra, the access routes lead more than 800 metres down. That is where the host rock layer, over 100 metres thick, lies.
62488.m: The deep repository lies about 800 metres underground.

62489.q: In which municipality is the surface facility of the planned deep repository intended to be?
62489.e: The surface facility with the access shafts is planned in the Haberstal area in the municipality of Stadel in the Zurich Unterland.
62489.m: The access to the deep repository is planned in Stadel.

62490.q: Where does Nagra plan the packaging facility for spent fuel elements?
a: At the interim storage facility in Würenlingen
At the Gösgen nuclear power station
62490.e: The fuel element packaging facility is to be built at Zwilag in Würenlingen. There the waste will be packed into disposal containers and then taken to the deep repository.
62490.m: The fuel elements are packed in Würenlingen for the deep repository.

62491.q: Besides Nördlich Lägern, which two other siting regions were still in the process in the last stage of the site search?
62491.e: In the sectoral plan for deep geological repositories, three areas were examined in stage 3. In 2022 Nördlich Lägern was preferred over Jura Ost and Zürich Nordost.
62491.m: In the end three siting regions remained in the running.

62492.q: Which waste is to be stored in the Nördlich Lägern deep repository?
a: High-level as well as low- and intermediate-level waste
Only household rubbish from the region
62492.e: A combined repository is planned with separate areas for high-level waste and for low- and intermediate-level waste from nuclear power stations, medicine, industry and research.
62492.m: The planned deep repository is a combined repository for all radioactive waste.

62493.q: Which democratic option exists after the Federal Council and Parliament have decided on the general licence?
a: An optional referendum with a popular vote
A veto by the host municipality
A decision by the host canton alone
62493.e: The general licence is subject to the optional referendum. Any popular vote is expected around 2031; the cantons have no right of veto.
62493.m: The Swiss people can have the last word on the deep repository.

62494.q: According to Nagra's planning (as of 2024), from when is waste to start being placed in the repository?
62494.e: After the licensing procedures and about ten years of construction, placing waste in the repository is to begin around 2050. Until then the waste stays in interim storage.
62494.m: Placing waste in the deep repository is to start around 2050.

62495.q: How did the voters of the city of St Gallen decide in 2010 on the loan for the geothermal project?
a: They approved it by a large majority
They were not allowed to vote on it
62495.e: On 28 November 2010 about 83 per cent voted yes. The high approval showed great support for a local, renewable heat source.
62495.m: In 2010 St Gallen clearly backed its geothermal project.

62496.q: Why is a deep geothermal project like the one in St Gallen financially risky?
a: Only after expensive drilling do you know whether enough hot water flows
Geothermal heat is not available in winter
The price of electricity from geothermal energy is fixed at zero by law
The drilling rigs have to be rebuilt every year
62496.e: St Gallen approved 159 million francs. The drilling cost a lot of money, but only afterwards did it become clear that there was not enough hot water.
62496.m: With deep geothermal energy, success only shows after expensive drilling.

62497.q: Roughly what magnitude was the strongest earthquake triggered by the drilling in July 2013?
62497.e: The earthquake on 20 July 2013 was clearly felt in the region but caused only slight damage. It occurred at a depth of about 4,000 metres.
62497.m: The St Gallen geothermal earthquake had a magnitude of about 3.5.

62498.q: What unexpectedly entered the borehole at a depth of about 4,450 metres in July 2013?
62498.e: While the borehole was being cleaned with diluted hydrochloric acid, natural gas suddenly flowed in. To stabilise the borehole, heavy drilling mud was pumped in, which is thought to have probably triggered the earthquake.
62498.m: A gas inflow caused problems at the St Gallen borehole.

62499.q: According to which principle was the St Gallen geothermal project meant to obtain heat?
a: Hydrothermally, with hot deep water from an aquifer
Petrothermally, by artificially breaking up granite
62499.e: Hot water was to be pumped up from a water-bearing rock layer at a depth of about 4,000 metres. The cooled water would have been returned through a second borehole.
62499.m: Hydrothermal geothermal energy uses naturally occurring hot deep water.

62500.q: Why could the planned geothermal power station in St Gallen not be built?
a: The amount of hot water pumped up was far too small
62500.e: Only about 6 litres per second were measured instead of the roughly 50 litres needed. That made economic operation impossible.
62500.m: Too little hot water stopped the power station in St Gallen.

62501.q: In which gorge on St Gallen's city territory was the drilling site of the geothermal project?
62501.e: The drilling site was in the Sittertobel in the west of the city. From there, drilling went at an angle under the Abtwil area.
62501.m: The St Gallen geothermal drilling started in the Sittertobel.

62502.q: What water temperature was measured at depth in the St Gallen geothermal project?
62502.e: The temperature matched the expected value of about 140 °C. The problem was not the heat but the amount of water.
62502.m: At a depth of 4,000 metres the water is well over 100 °C.

62503.q: Which earlier Swiss deep geothermal project was stopped in 2006 after earthquakes that could be felt?
62503.e: In Basel, water was pressed into hot rock under high pressure, which triggered earthquakes up to magnitude 3.4. That is why St Gallen chose a hydrothermal method.
62503.m: Basel and St Gallen show the earthquake risks of deep geothermal energy.

62504.q: What was the geothermal heat in St Gallen mainly meant to be used for?
a: For the city's district heating network
For greenhouses in the Rhine Valley
62504.e: The municipal utilities wanted to use geothermal energy to expand the district heating network and replace heating oil and natural gas. Smaller-scale electricity production was also planned.
62504.m: Geothermal energy was meant to supply St Gallen with district heating.

62505.q: What were the names of the tunnel boring machines that drove the Gotthard Base Tunnel from the south?
62505.e: From the south, the machines Heidi and Sissi did the boring; from the north, the machines Gabi I and Gabi II. The machines were over 400 m long.
62505.m: At the Gotthard, Heidi and Sissi bored from the south.

62506.q: Which type of traffic was the first to run regularly through the Gotthard Base Tunnel, from September 2016?
62506.e: Freight traffic started on 5 September 2016. Scheduled passenger traffic only followed with the timetable change in December 2016.
62506.m: Freight trains were the first to run through the Gotthard Base Tunnel.

62507.q: Roughly how high did rock temperatures rise at the hottest points during the building of the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
62507.e: The deeper you go below the surface, the warmer the rock. Under up to 2,450 m of overlying rock, the rock reached over 40 °C, so the construction sites had to be cooled heavily.
62507.m: Deep inside the mountain the rock is very hot.

62508.q: How many workers died during the building of the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
62508.e: Nine workers died while the base tunnel was being built. Despite modern safety rules, work deep inside the mountain remained dangerous.
62508.m: Nine workers lost their lives building the Gotthard Base Tunnel.

62509.q: What happened in the Gotthard Base Tunnel in August 2023?
a: A freight train derailed and damaged the western tube
A fire destroyed the north portal
An earthquake made the eastern tube collapse
A water inrush flooded the whole tunnel
62509.e: On 10 August 2023 a freight train derailed and damaged tracks and a crossover door near Faido. Until it was fully back in operation in September 2024, many passenger trains ran over the mountain route.
62509.m: After the 2023 derailment, the Gotthard Base Tunnel could only be partly used for a year.

62510.q: Roughly at what intervals do cross-passages connect the two tubes of the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
62510.e: The two tubes are connected by 176 cross-passages about 325 m apart. This way passengers can quickly reach the safe other tube in an emergency.
62510.m: Every 325 m or so a cross-passage leads to the other tube.

62511.q: Roughly how long is the whole tunnel system of the Gotthard Base Tunnel, with all tubes, galleries and shafts?
62511.e: Besides the two main tubes there are cross-passages, access tunnels and shafts. Together that makes about 152 km of tunnel.
62511.m: The Gotthard tunnel system measures about 152 km.

62512.q: Under which three cantons does the Gotthard Base Tunnel run?
62512.e: The tunnel starts in Erstfeld (Uri), runs under the Surselva near Sedrun (Grisons) and ends in Bodio (Ticino).
62512.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel lies under Uri, the Grisons and Ticino.

62513.q: For what top speed is the Gotthard Base Tunnel designed?
62513.e: The line is designed for passenger trains up to 250 km/h. Freight trains run much more slowly.
62513.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is built for 250 km/h.

62514.q: What happened to a large part of the excavated rock from the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
a: It was processed and used as aggregate for concrete
It was shipped out to sea
It was put back into the tunnel
62514.e: Part of the rock was processed into gravel and sand for the tunnel concrete. Other material was used, among other things, for fill in Lake Uri.
62514.m: Excavated rock from the Gotthard became concrete for the tunnel.

62515.q: Which record did the Lötschberg Base Tunnel hold when it opened?
a: Longest land tunnel in the world
Highest railway tunnel in the world
62515.e: When it opened in 2007, it was the longest tunnel in the world lying entirely under land. Later it was overtaken by the Gotthard Base Tunnel.
62515.m: In 2007 the Lötschberg Base Tunnel was the longest land tunnel in the world.

62516.q: Which company commissioned and built the Lötschberg Base Tunnel?
62516.e: BLS AlpTransit AG built the tunnel on behalf of the Confederation. AlpTransit Gotthard AG was responsible for the Gotthard and Ceneri.
62516.m: BLS AlpTransit AG built the Lötschberg Base Tunnel.

62517.q: When was the breakthrough achieved in the Lötschberg Base Tunnel?
62517.e: The breakthrough took place in April 2005. After that came the interior fittings and railway technology until the opening.
62517.m: The Lötschberg Base Tunnel broke through in 2005.

62518.q: Near which Valais village is there an emergency stop in the Lötschberg Base Tunnel?
62518.e: The Ferden emergency stop lies deep beneath the Lötschental. In an emergency, trains stop there and passengers reach safe rooms.
62518.m: Ferden is an emergency stop in the Lötschberg Base Tunnel.

62519.q: Roughly how long is the old Lötschberg summit tunnel from 1913?
62519.e: The summit tunnel between Kandersteg and Goppenstein is about 14.6 km long. It lies much higher than the base tunnel.
62519.m: The old Lötschberg tunnel is about 15 km long.

62520.q: What did the abbreviation of the railway company BLS originally stand for?
62520.e: BLS was founded as the Bern-Lötschberg-Simplon railway. Its aim was a north-south link from Bern through the Lötschberg to the Simplon.

62521.q: Which company commissioned and built the Gotthard and Ceneri Base Tunnels?
62521.e: AlpTransit Gotthard AG was a subsidiary of the SBB and built on behalf of the Confederation. After completion, the SBB took over operation.
62521.m: AlpTransit Gotthard AG built the tunnels of the Gotthard axis.

62522.q: Which revenue went into the FinöV fund to finance the NRLA?
a: Part of the heavy vehicle charge (LSVA)
62522.e: The FinöV fund was mainly fed by the LSVA, one per mille of VAT and money from the mineral oil tax. In this way lorries help pay for the railway.
62522.m: The LSVA helped pay for the NRLA.

62523.q: What does the Confederation use the money from the Railway Infrastructure Fund (BIF) for?
a: For operating, maintaining and expanding the rail network
62523.e: The BIF was created with the FABI bill, which the people accepted in 2014. Since 2016 it has financed the operation, maintenance and expansion of the railway infrastructure without a time limit.
62523.m: Since 2016 the BIF has financed railway infrastructure.

62524.q: Which NRLA tunnel, at about 57 km, is the longest railway tunnel in the world?
62524.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel opened in 2016 and is about 57 km long. The Lötschberg Base Tunnel measures about 35 km, the Ceneri Base Tunnel about 15 km.
62524.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

62525.q: Which construction method was mainly used to excavate the Ceneri Base Tunnel?
62525.e: At the Ceneri the rock was mostly blasted. At the Gotthard, by contrast, mainly large tunnel boring machines were used.
62525.m: The Ceneri Base Tunnel was mainly blasted.

62526.q: Which connection in Ticino benefited particularly from the Ceneri Base Tunnel?
62526.e: The journey time between Locarno and Lugano was halved to about 30 minutes. Ticino thus grew together into one connected S-Bahn area.
62526.m: The Ceneri Base Tunnel brings Locarno and Lugano closer together.

62527.q: Near which place is the south portal of the Ceneri Base Tunnel?
62527.e: The south portal is in Vezia near Lugano. The north portal is at Vigana in the municipality of Camorino.
62527.m: The south portal of the Ceneri Base Tunnel is in Vezia.

62528.q: Why was the Ceneri Base Tunnel important for the flat railway of the Gotthard axis?
a: It replaces the last climb before Lugano
It takes the railway directly to Milan
It replaces the Gotthard Base Tunnel
62528.e: Without the Ceneri, heavy freight trains still had to climb over Monte Ceneri. Only with it is the line flat all the way.
62528.m: The Ceneri Base Tunnel makes the Gotthard axis flat all the way.

62529.q: In which year was the main breakthrough achieved in the Ceneri Base Tunnel?
62529.e: The main breakthrough took place in January 2016. After that, railway technology and safety systems were installed.
62529.m: The Ceneri Base Tunnel broke through in 2016.

62530.q: Roughly how high is the Monte Ceneri pass, under which the base tunnel runs?
62530.e: The Monte Ceneri pass is at about 554 m above sea level. It is low, but for heavy freight trains the climb was still an obstacle.
62530.m: Monte Ceneri is a low pass at about 550 m above sea level.

62531.q: How is the Ceneri Base Tunnel built?
62531.e: As at the Gotthard, trains run in two separate single-track tubes. Cross-passages connect them for emergencies.
62531.m: The Ceneri Base Tunnel has two single-track tubes.

62532.q: Which major watershed runs across the top of the Grimsel Pass?
a: Between the Rhine and the Rhône
Between the Rhine and the Danube
Between the Rhône and the Po
Between the Inn and the Adige
62532.e: To the north the water flows via the Aare to the Rhine and into the North Sea, to the south via the Rhône into the Mediterranean.
62532.m: At the Grimsel the catchment areas of the Rhine and the Rhône divide.

62533.q: Which research facility does Nagra operate in the area of the Grimsel Pass?
62533.e: At the Grimsel rock laboratory, Nagra studies the rock for the safe storage of radioactive waste. The experiments take place deep in the granite.
62533.m: At the Grimsel rock laboratory, research is done on storing nuclear waste.

62534.q: Which famous glacier lies on the Valais side directly below the Furka Pass?
62534.e: From the Furka Pass road you can see the Rhône Glacier, where the Rhône rises. Near the Hotel Belvédère you can visit an ice grotto.
62534.m: The Rhône Glacier lies at the Furka Pass.

62535.q: In which year could the railway over the Furka be used all the way as part of the Furka Oberalp Railway?
62535.e: The line from Brig over the Furka to Disentis was in operation all the way from 1926. A few years later the first Glacier Express ran there.
62535.m: The Furka Oberalp Railway ran all the way from 1926.

62536.q: What is meant by unaccompanied combined transport?
a: Only containers or trailers travel by rail
Lorries cross the Alps without a load
Drivers travel along in a sleeping car
62536.e: In unaccompanied combined transport, only loading units such as containers, swap bodies or semi-trailers are loaded onto the train. The tractor unit and driver stay behind.
62536.m: In unaccompanied combined transport only the load travels by rail.

62537.q: Which mode of transport today carries the larger share of goods in Swiss trans-Alpine freight traffic?
62537.e: Rail's share of Swiss trans-Alpine freight traffic has been around 70 per cent or more for years. In neighbouring countries such as Austria, by contrast, road dominates.
62537.m: In Switzerland most Alpine freight travels by rail.

62538.q: According to the Freight Transport Transfer Act, by when should the transfer target for trans-Alpine lorry traffic have been reached?
62538.e: The target was to be reached at the latest two years after the opening of the Gotthard Base Tunnel, that is in 2018. The number of journeys did fall, but stayed above the target.
62538.m: The transfer target was aimed for by 2018 but missed.

62539.q: Which tool with tradable transit rights was discussed for Alpine transit but not introduced?
62539.e: With an Alpine transit exchange, the number of journeys would be limited and the rights auctioned or traded. Because of the Land Transport Agreement with the EU, it was not put into practice.
62539.m: The Alpine transit exchange was discussed but never introduced.

62540.q: How does the Federal Council check whether the transfer of freight traffic to rail is making progress?
a: With a regular transfer report to Parliament
With a survey of lorry drivers
Not at all, that is a matter for the EU
62540.e: In the transfer report, the Federal Council shows every two years how lorry journeys are developing and which measures are working.
62540.m: The transfer report is published every two years.

62541.q: How does the Confederation support combined transport through the Alps financially?
a: With operating subsidies for rail services
62541.e: The Confederation pays subsidies so that combined transport by rail can be offered more cheaply. This makes rail more competitive with road.
62541.m: The Confederation supports combined transport with money.

62542.q: At which four Alpine crossings are trans-Alpine lorry journeys counted in Switzerland?
a: Gotthard, San Bernardino, Simplon, Great St Bernard
62542.e: The statistics record the road crossings at the Gotthard, San Bernardino, Simplon and Great St Bernard. By far the largest share goes over the Gotthard.
62542.m: Lorry journeys are counted at four Alpine crossings.

62543.q: When did the people approve the Rail 2000 concept?
62543.e: On 6 December 1987 the loan for Rail 2000 was accepted with 57 per cent.
62543.m: Rail 2000 was accepted by the people in 1987.

62544.q: Which principle is often used to sum up the idea of Rail 2000?
a: As fast as necessary, not as fast as possible
Every city gets a high-speed train
One train a day in each direction
62544.e: Journey times should be just short enough for connections at the hubs to work. High speed at any price was not the aim.
62544.m: With Rail 2000, what counts is the right speed for good connections.

62545.q: When was the first stage of Rail 2000 put into operation?
62545.e: The first stage went into operation with the timetable change of 12 December 2004. It was one of the biggest timetable changes in SBB history.
62545.m: The first stage of Rail 2000 started in December 2004.

62546.q: Which new line is the centrepiece of the first stage of Rail 2000?
62546.e: The new line between Mattstetten and Rothrist is designed for 200 km/h. It considerably shortened the journey time between Bern and Zurich.
62546.m: The Mattstetten to Rothrist line is the core of Rail 2000.

62547.q: What is different about the ETCS Level 2 train control system on the Mattstetten to Rothrist line compared with before?
a: Movement authority appears in the driver's cab, there are no lineside signals
The trains float on magnetic fields
62547.e: With ETCS Level 2, the driver receives the movement authority directly in the cab, so lineside signals are no longer needed. From December 2007 trains ran there at 200 km/h.
62547.m: ETCS Level 2 shows the signals in the driver's cab.

62548.q: To how many minutes did the journey time from Bern to Zurich fall from the end of 2007 thanks to Rail 2000?
62548.e: Before that, the journey took 69 minutes. At full speed on the new line it fell to 56 minutes, just under an hour.
62548.m: Since Rail 2000, Bern to Zurich takes under an hour.

62549.q: What does the hub principle of Rail 2000 mean?
a: Trains arrive at large stations shortly before the full or half hour
Every train stops at every station on the line
Trains only pass through the hubs at night
Long-distance trains bypass all large stations
62549.e: Trains from all directions arrive almost at the same time and leave again shortly afterwards. This creates short transfer times.
62549.m: With the hub principle, trains meet at the same time so people can change.

62550.q: Why do journey times between two hubs in Rail 2000 have to be just under an hour or half an hour?
a: So that trains arrive in time for connections at the next hub
So that drivers can take a break
So that less electricity is used
62550.e: If the journey time is just under the interval, the train reaches the next hub at connection time. That is why particular lines were speeded up.
62550.m: Journey times between hubs are based on the regular interval.

62551.q: Roughly what were the costs of the first stage of Rail 2000?
62551.e: In 1992 Parliament had limited the first stage to 7.4 billion francs. The final bill was about 5.9 billion francs at 1994 prices.
62551.m: The first stage of Rail 2000 cost about 6 billion francs.

62552.q: How did the expansion of the Swiss rail network continue after Rail 2000?
a: With further expansion programmes such as ZEB and STEP
Only buses were used from then on
62552.e: With ZEB (Future Development of Railway Infrastructure), Parliament decided on further expansions in 2009 to improve the hub principle. Later came the strategic development programmes STEP.
62552.m: After Rail 2000 came further expansion programmes such as ZEB and STEP.

62553.q: In which year did the SBB introduce the nationwide regular-interval timetable?
62553.e: The regular-interval timetable came into force in May 1982. It is regarded as a milestone of Swiss railway transport.
62553.m: Switzerland has had the regular-interval timetable since 1982.

62554.q: What is the feature of a regular-interval timetable?
a: Trains leave at the same minute every hour
Trains only run at rush hour
Every train has a different departure time
Trains run on demand without a plan
62554.e: In a regular-interval timetable the departure times repeat regularly, for example always at xx.02 and xx.32. Passengers can easily remember the times.
62554.m: In a regular-interval timetable the train always leaves at the same minute.

62555.q: Which railway project from the 1990s expanded the regular-interval timetable with faster connections between the hubs?
62555.e: With Rail 2000, lines were upgraded so that trains between large hubs such as Zurich, Bern and Basel take just under an hour. This makes connections work at all hubs. The first stage started in 2004.
62555.m: Rail 2000 made journey times fit the regular-interval timetable.

62556.q: A train on a half-hourly timetable leaves at 7:14. When does the next train on this line leave?
62556.e: Half-hourly means a train leaves every 30 minutes. 7:14 plus 30 minutes is 7:44.
62556.m: On a half-hourly timetable, a train leaves every 30 minutes.

62557.q: What is meant by an integrated regular-interval timetable?
a: A coordinated interval with connections at the hubs
A timetable only for freight trains
A timetable without fixed departure times
An interval only for night trains
62557.e: In an integrated regular-interval timetable, trains, buses and boats are coordinated so that at the hubs there are connections in all directions.
62557.m: An integrated regular-interval timetable links all lines with good connections.

62558.q: Besides trains, which means of transport are included in the Swiss regular-interval timetable?
62558.e: In Switzerland, PostBuses, local buses and many boats are also coordinated with the train timetable. This means you can reach even remote places with a connection.
62558.m: PostBuses and boats also run on the Swiss regular interval.

62559.q: In a regular-interval timetable, what is an interval hub?
a: A station where lines meet at the same time
A station where no long-distance trains stop
A set of points on the open line
62559.e: At an interval hub such as Zurich or Bern, trains from different directions arrive at the same time and leave again shortly afterwards.
62559.m: At an interval hub the trains meet at the same time.

62560.q: A train on an hourly timetable leaves on the hour and takes 47 minutes to reach the next hub. How long do travellers wait there until the next full hour?
62560.e: The train arrives 47 minutes after leaving. Until the next full hour there are 60 minus 47 = 13 minutes left.
62560.m: If the journey time does not fit the timetable rhythm, there are waiting times at the hub.

62561.q: How many departures per hour in each direction does a suburban train line running every quarter of an hour have?
62561.e: An hour has 60 minutes. 60 ÷ 15 = 4, so a train leaves every 15 minutes.
62561.m: With a train every quarter of an hour, four trains run per hour.

62562.q: A bus is to bring passengers to trains that leave on the hour. The bus journey takes 17 minutes and you need 4 minutes to change. When must the bus leave at the latest?
62562.e: The bus must arrive at xx.56 at the latest, because you need 4 minutes to change. 56 minus 17 = 39, so it must leave at xx.39 at the latest.
62562.m: For a connection you count back from the train's departure.

62563.q: When does the big yearly timetable change take place in Switzerland and Europe?
62563.e: The timetable change takes place across Europe on the second weekend in December. That is when new connections and intervals come into force.
62563.m: The timetable changes every year in December.

62564.q: Which runway, at about 3,700 m, is the longest at Zurich Airport?
62564.e: Runway 16/34 measures about 3,700 m, 14/32 about 3,300 m and 10/28 about 2,500 m.
62564.m: Runway 16/34 is the longest in Zurich.

62565.q: Since when has Zurich Airport had its own railway station under the terminal?
62565.e: Zurich Airport station opened in 1980. Since then you can reach the airport directly by long-distance trains and S-Bahn trains.
62565.m: Zurich Airport has had a railway station since 1980.

62566.q: Roughly how large is the canton of Zurich's share in Flughafen Zürich AG?
62566.e: The canton of Zurich holds a third of the shares plus one share. This lets it block important decisions, even though the company is listed on the stock exchange.
62566.m: The canton of Zurich owns about a third of Flughafen Zürich AG.

62567.q: Since when have aircraft landed at Zurich Airport from the south at certain times?
62567.e: Because Germany restricted approaches over its territory at off-peak times from 2003, southern approaches over densely populated areas were introduced. This led to political debates about aircraft noise.
62567.m: Southern approaches to Zurich have existed since 2003.

62568.q: What did the people of the canton of Zurich vote on in March 2024?
62568.e: On 3 March 2024 Zurich voters clearly accepted the extension of runways 28 and 32. This is meant to make operations safer and more punctual.
62568.m: In 2024 Zurich voters approved longer runways.

62569.q: On which runway do aircraft mostly land at Zurich Airport during the day in normal operation?
62569.e: In normal operation during the day, aircraft land on runway 14 and take off mainly on runways 16 and 28. With a west wind or the bise (north-east wind), the directions are changed.
62569.m: During the day most aircraft in Zurich land on runway 14.

62570.q: To which large North Sea port does Rhine shipping lead from Basel?
62570.e: The Rhine flows into the North Sea in the Netherlands. Rotterdam is the most important transhipment point for the ships from Basel.
62570.m: Rhine ships sail from Basel to Rotterdam.

62571.q: Since when has Basel been the official home port of the Swiss ocean-going fleet?
62571.e: On 9 April 1941 Basel became the port of registry for Swiss ocean-going ships. In the Second World War the fleet secured the country's supplies.
62571.m: Basel has been the home port of Swiss ocean-going ships since 1941.

62572.q: Near which notable spot is the port of Basel-Kleinhüningen?
a: At the point where three countries meet
At the source of the Rhine
At the mouth of the Rhine
62572.e: At Kleinhüningen port the borders of Switzerland, Germany and France meet. A well-known monument stands there.
62572.m: Kleinhüningen port is at the point where three countries meet.

62573.q: Which treaty of 1868 guarantees free navigation on the Rhine up to Basel?
a: Final Act of the Congress of Vienna
62573.e: The Mannheim Convention of 1868 secures free navigation on the Rhine. Switzerland, as a landlocked country, still benefits from it today.
62573.m: The Mannheim Convention guarantees free passage on the Rhine.

62574.q: Which structure must ships pass through to get from Basel city to the ports of Birsfelden and Muttenz-Au?
a: The lock at the Birsfelden power station
The lock at the Rhine Falls
62574.e: The Birsfelden power station dams the Rhine. Through its lock, ships reach the port facilities further upstream.
62574.m: Ships going to Birsfelden pass through a lock.

62575.q: Through which country does most of the Rhine route between Basel and Rotterdam run?
62575.e: Below Basel the Rhine first forms the border between Germany and France and then flows through Germany. Only in the last section does it reach the Netherlands and flow into the North Sea near Rotterdam.
62575.m: Rhine ships from Basel travel mostly through Germany.

62576.q: Why is transporting heavy bulk goods by Rhine ship attractive for Switzerland?
a: One ship replaces a great many lorries
Rhine ships go directly to Zurich
62576.e: A large Rhine ship can carry as much as many dozens of lorries. This lowers costs and energy use per tonne.
62576.m: A Rhine ship carries as much as many lorries.

62577.q: Between which places does the Glacier Express run?
62577.e: The Glacier Express connects Zermatt in Valais with St. Moritz in the Engadine. On the way it crosses the cantons of Valais, Uri and the Grisons.
62577.m: The Glacier Express runs from Zermatt to St. Moritz.

62578.q: What gauge is the Glacier Express line?
62578.e: The whole line is metre gauge, that is 1,000 mm wide. This allows tighter curves in the mountains than standard gauge.
62578.m: The Glacier Express runs on metre gauge.

62579.q: Where does the Glacier Express get its name from?
a: From the Rhône Glacier on the former Furka mountain route
From the Aletsch Glacier near Brig
From the Morteratsch Glacier near Pontresina
From the Gorner Glacier in Zermatt
62579.e: In the past, the line at the Furka passed close to the Rhône Glacier. Today the train runs through a base tunnel.
62579.m: The Glacier Express is named after the Rhône Glacier.

62580.q: Which equipment do railways like the Glacier Express need on steep sections at the Oberalp?
62580.e: On very steep sections, a cogwheel on the locomotive grips a toothed rack between the rails. This lets the train climb steep gradients safely.
62580.m: The railway climbs steep sections using a rack rail.

62581.q: Which famous viaduct of the Rhaetian Railway does the Glacier Express cross near Filisur?
62581.e: The Glacier Express runs over the Albula line and crosses the Landwasser Viaduct. The Brusio spiral viaduct, on the other hand, is on the Bernina line.
62581.m: The Glacier Express runs over the Landwasser Viaduct.

62582.q: Through which gorge does the Glacier Express run between Ilanz and Reichenau?
62582.e: The Ruinaulta is the Rhine gorge in the Vorderrhein valley, formed after the Flims rockslide. The railway follows the river there.
62582.m: The Glacier Express runs through the Ruinaulta Rhine gorge.

62583.q: Roughly how many tunnels does the Glacier Express pass through on its route?
62583.e: There are 91 tunnels on the line. Many of them help to overcome differences in height in loops.
62583.m: The Glacier Express passes through about 90 tunnels.

62584.q: From which two railways was the Matterhorn Gotthard Railway formed in 2003?
a: Furka Oberalp Railway and BVZ Zermatt Railway
62584.e: In 2003 the Furka Oberalp Railway and the BVZ Zermatt Railway merged to form the Matterhorn Gotthard Railway. It operates the western part of the Glacier Express route.
62584.m: The Matterhorn Gotthard Railway was formed in 2003 from two railways.

62585.q: Roughly how long is the San Bernardino road tunnel?
62585.e: The tunnel is about 6.6 km long. It lies between Hinterrhein and San Bernardino.
62585.m: The San Bernardino tunnel is about 6.6 km long.

62586.q: When was the San Bernardino road tunnel opened?
62586.e: The tunnel was opened to traffic on 1 December 1967. This made the route usable in winter, unlike the pass road.
62586.m: The San Bernardino tunnel has been open since 1967.

62587.q: Which well-known gorge lies on the San Bernardino route between Thusis and Zillis?
62587.e: The Viamala is a narrow gorge of the Hinterrhein. For a long time it was a dangerous obstacle on the way over the San Bernardino.
62587.m: The Viamala gorge lies on the San Bernardino route.

62588.q: What happened on the San Bernardino route in the Misox in June 2024?
a: A storm destroyed a section of the A13
The tunnel was closed for good
A new railway line was opened
An earthquake destroyed the north portal
62588.e: In a severe storm, the Moesa river swept away a section of the A13 near Lostallo. The route was then closed for some time.
62588.m: In June 2024 a storm destroyed parts of the A13 in the Misox.

62589.q: What role does the San Bernardino route play when there are problems at the Gotthard?
a: It is the most important alternative route for north-south traffic
It is completely closed to lorries
It leads to France instead of Ticino
62589.e: When there are queues or closures at the Gotthard, many vehicles switch to the A13. Both routes lead to Ticino.
62589.m: The San Bernardino route is the most important alternative to the Gotthard.

62590.q: Which watershed runs across the San Bernardino Pass?
a: Between the Rhine and the Po
Between the Rhône and the Po
Between the Rhine and the Danube
Between the Inn and the Rhône
62590.e: To the north, the Hinterrhein flows to the North Sea. To the south, the Moesa flows via the Ticino into the Po and the Adriatic Sea.
62590.m: At the San Bernardino the Rhine and the Po divide.

62591.q: How did people cross the San Bernardino before the carriage road was built in the 19th century?
a: On a mule track with pack animals
By stagecoach on a wide road
Through a tunnel under the pass
62591.e: Before the engineered road was built around 1820, only a mule track led over the pass. Muleteers carried goods with horses and mules.
62591.m: Before the pass road, only a mule track led over the San Bernardino.

62592.q: Which language border runs across the top of the San Bernardino Pass?
62592.e: In the Rheinwald to the north people speak German, in the Misox to the south Italian. Both valleys belong to the Grisons.
62592.m: German and Italian meet at the San Bernardino.

62593.q: Who is the San Bernardino Pass named after?
62593.e: The pass and the village are named after the travelling preacher Bernardino of Siena, to whom a chapel there is dedicated.
62593.m: The San Bernardino bears the name of Bernardino of Siena.

62594.q: On which side of the San Bernardino tunnel is the Hinterrhein portal?
a: On the west side in Valais
In the middle of the tunnel
62594.e: The north portal is near the village of Hinterrhein at just over 1,600 m above sea level, the south portal near the village of San Bernardino.
62594.m: The north portal of the San Bernardino tunnel is at Hinterrhein.

62595.q: What did the National Roads Act of 1960 lay down?
a: A nationwide network of motorways and expressways
The introduction of the motorway vignette
A speed limit of 120 on all motorways
The night-time driving ban for lorries
62595.e: The 1960 act decided which roads are of national importance and are to be built as national roads. The vignette and the 120 limit only came in 1985.
62595.m: The National Roads Act of 1960 created the basis for the motorway network.

62596.q: Since when have the national roads belonged entirely to the Confederation?
62596.e: With the reform of fiscal equalisation (NFA), the Confederation took over ownership, operation and maintenance of the national roads in 2008. Before that, the cantons had more responsibility.
62596.m: Since 2008 the national roads have belonged to the Confederation.

62597.q: Which letter replaced N on road signs for Swiss motorways in 1996?
62597.e: Since 1996 motorways have been marked with A on signs, for example A1 or A2. Internally the name N was still used.
62597.m: Since 1996 Swiss motorways have had an A in their name.

62598.q: Which increase in the price of the vignette did the people reject in 2013?
62598.e: On 24 November 2013 the people rejected the price increase to 100 francs. The money would have been used to add more roads to the national road network.
62598.m: In 2013 the people rejected a 100-franc vignette.

62599.q: What happened to about 400 km of cantonal roads in 2020?
a: They were added to the national road network
They were turned into cycle paths
They were handed over to municipalities
62599.e: With the new network decision, the Confederation took over about 400 km of former cantonal roads in 2020. This made the national road network larger.
62599.m: In 2020 the national road network was extended by about 400 km.

62600.q: Which motorway connects Basel through the Gotthard with Chiasso?
62600.e: The A2 runs from Basel via Lucerne and the Gotthard to Chiasso on the Italian border. It is the most important north-south road axis.
62600.m: The A2 is the north-south motorway from Basel to Chiasso.

62601.q: Since when has the speed limit on Swiss motorways been 120?
62601.e: From 1985 the speed limit on motorways was lowered from 130 to 120 km/h. At the same time, a new limit of 80 applied outside built-up areas.
62601.m: Since 1985 the speed limit on Swiss motorways has been 120.

62602.q: For which vehicles is the vignette compulsory on Swiss national roads?
a: For motor vehicles up to 3.5 tonnes
62602.e: Cars, motorbikes and light vans up to 3.5 tonnes need a vignette. Heavier vehicles pay the LSVA (heavy vehicle charge) instead.
62602.m: The vignette applies to vehicles up to 3.5 tonnes.

62603.q: Which federal office is responsible for building, operating and maintaining the national roads?
a: The Federal Office for Spatial Development (ARE)
The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)
62603.e: Since 2008 the national roads have belonged to the Confederation. FEDRO plans, builds and maintains them and also manages traffic. The FOT is responsible for rail and public transport.
62603.m: FEDRO is responsible for Swiss motorways.

62604.q: When is there generally a driving ban for heavy lorries in Switzerland?
62604.e: For heavy motor vehicles there is a night-time driving ban from 10 pm to 5 am and a Sunday driving ban. There are exceptions, for example for perishable goods.
62604.m: Heavy lorries are generally not allowed to drive at night or on Sundays in Switzerland.

62605.q: How many major regions does the Federal Statistical Office distinguish in Switzerland?
62605.e: The FSO divides Switzerland into seven major regions. They are a statistical level above the cantons.
62605.m: Statistically, Switzerland is divided into seven major regions.

62606.q: Which major region does the canton of the Grisons belong to?
62606.e: Besides the Grisons, Eastern Switzerland includes St Gallen, Thurgau, Schaffhausen, Glarus and the two Appenzells. It is the largest major region by area.
62606.m: Statistically, the Grisons belongs to Eastern Switzerland.

62607.q: What are Switzerland's seven major regions mainly used for?
a: For statistical comparisons, including with EU regions
As constituencies for the National Council
As an administrative level with its own government
As fare zones in public transport
62607.e: The major regions are a statistical division used by the FSO. They correspond to the EU's NUTS 2 level and allow comparisons with regions in Europe.
62607.m: Major regions are a statistical division without their own government.

62608.q: Which two major regions consist of only a single canton?
a: Zurich and the Lake Geneva region
62608.e: The Zurich major region includes only the canton of Zurich, the Ticino major region only the canton of Ticino. All the other major regions combine several cantons.
62608.m: Zurich and Ticino are major regions made up of only one canton.

62609.q: Which major region does the canton of Aargau belong to?
62609.e: Northwestern Switzerland includes the cantons of Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft and Aargau.
62609.m: Statistically, Aargau belongs to Northwestern Switzerland.

62610.q: Which major region does the canton of Valais belong to?
62610.e: The Lake Geneva region consists of the cantons of Vaud, Valais and Geneva.
62610.m: Valais belongs to the Lake Geneva region together with Vaud and Geneva.

62611.q: Which major region has the most inhabitants (as of 2024)?
62611.e: Espace Mittelland, with Bern, Fribourg, Solothurn, Neuchâtel and Jura, has just under two million people (as of 2024), more than the Lake Geneva region or Zurich.
62611.m: Espace Mittelland is the most populous major region.

62612.q: What is true of the borders of the major regions?
62612.e: Each major region always consists of whole cantons. That is why the major regions do not exactly match natural landscape areas.
62612.m: Major regions are always made up of whole cantons.

62613.q: In which year did the Jura districts vote for their own canton in a first plebiscite?
62613.e: On 23 June 1974 a majority in the whole Jura voted to form a canton of its own; the southern districts then decided to stay with Bern.
62613.m: The first Jura plebiscite took place in 1974.

62614.q: How did Switzerland decide in 1978 on founding the canton of Jura?
a: The people and the cantons clearly accepted it
The people accepted it, the cantons rejected it
The Federal Council decided without a vote
62614.e: A new canton requires a change to the Federal Constitution and therefore the approval of the people and the cantons. In 1978 over 80 per cent and all cantons said yes.
62614.m: In 1978 Switzerland clearly voted for the canton of Jura.

62615.q: Which native horse breed is named after a plateau in the canton of Jura?
62615.e: The Freiberger comes from the Franches-Montagnes (Freiberge) and is the only native horse breed still bred in Switzerland today.
62615.m: The Freiberger is the horse from the Jura.

62616.q: Which river forms a large loop near Saint-Ursanne in the canton of Jura?
62616.e: The Doubs flows from France into Switzerland, turns at Saint-Ursanne and returns to France; the area it flows around is called the Clos du Doubs.
62616.m: The Doubs makes a striking loop in the Jura.

62617.q: Which canton did the German-speaking Laufental join in 1994, after deciding against the new canton of Jura?
62617.e: The Laufental at first stayed with Bern in 1975 and moved to the canton of Basel-Landschaft in 1994.
62617.m: The Laufental has belonged to Basel-Landschaft since 1994.

62618.q: Which organisation was the most important separatist movement in the Jura conflict?
62618.e: The Rassemblement jurassien campaigned for the Jura to separate from Bern; the Force démocratique represented the side loyal to Bern.
62618.m: The Rassemblement jurassien fought for a canton of Jura of its own.

62619.q: Which political right has the canton of Jura granted to foreign nationals with a settlement permit since 1979?
a: The right to vote and elect at cantonal level
The right to vote on federal matters
The right to a seat in the cantonal parliament
62619.e: Since the canton was founded in 1979, foreign nationals with a settlement permit have been able to vote and elect in the Jura. However, they cannot be elected to cantonal office.
62619.m: In the Jura, foreign nationals with a settlement permit have been able to vote at cantonal level since 1979.

62620.q: Roughly how large is the area of the canton of the Grisons?
62620.e: The Grisons covers about 7,105 km², making it the largest canton in Switzerland by area.
62620.m: At about 7,100 km², the Grisons is the largest canton.

62621.q: Roughly what share of Switzerland's total area does the canton of the Grisons have?
62621.e: 7,105 km² divided by about 41,285 km² gives about 0.17, so roughly a sixth of the country's area.
62621.m: The Grisons covers about a sixth of Switzerland.

62622.q: What is special about the Grisons when it comes to official languages?
62622.e: In the Grisons, German, Romansh and Italian are official languages. No other canton has three official languages.
62622.m: The Grisons is the only trilingual canton in Switzerland.

62623.q: In which year did the Grisons become a full canton of the Confederation?
62623.e: With Napoleon's Act of Mediation, the Grisons became a canton in 1803; before that, as the Free State of the Three Leagues, it was only an associate.
62623.m: The Grisons has been a canton since the Act of Mediation of 1803.

62624.q: From which of the Three Leagues does the name “Graubünden” (Grisons) come?
62624.e: The Grey League in the Vorderrhein area gave the whole region its name. The other two leagues were the League of God's House and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions.
62624.m: The name Graubünden comes from the Grey League.

62625.q: Which Italian-speaking valley of the Grisons lies south of the Bernina Pass?
62625.e: Val Poschiavo, like the Bregaglia, Misox and Calanca valleys, belongs to the Italian-speaking part of the Grisons. In Val Müstair people speak Romansh.
62625.m: Val Poschiavo is an Italian-speaking valley of the Grisons.

62626.q: Which three countries does the canton of the Grisons border?
62626.e: The Grisons borders Italy to the south, Austria to the east and Liechtenstein to the north.
62626.m: The Grisons has borders with Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.

62627.q: Which geological UNESCO World Heritage Site does the Grisons share with St Gallen and Glarus?
62627.e: In the Swiss Tectonic Arena Sardona, older rocks can be seen lying on top of younger ones along the Glarus thrust; it has been a World Heritage Site since 2008.
62627.m: The Tectonic Arena Sardona shows how mountains form.

62628.q: Roughly how large is the area of the canton of Basel-Stadt?
62628.e: Basel-Stadt covers about 37 km², making it the smallest canton in Switzerland by area.
62628.m: At about 37 km², Basel-Stadt is the smallest canton.

62629.q: Which municipality, together with Basel and Riehen, forms the canton of Basel-Stadt?
62629.e: The canton consists of only three municipalities: the city of Basel and the rural municipalities of Riehen and Bettingen. Allschwil, Binningen and Muttenz belong to Basel-Landschaft.
62629.m: Basel-Stadt consists of Basel, Riehen and Bettingen.

62630.q: Where is the highest point of the canton of Basel-Stadt?
62630.e: The canton's highest point, at about 520 m, is near St. Chrischona, where a television tower can be seen from far away.
62630.m: St. Chrischona is the highest point of Basel-Stadt.

62631.q: How many seats does the canton of Basel-Stadt have in the Council of States?
62631.e: Basel-Stadt is a canton with half a cantonal vote and therefore sends only one person to the Council of States.
62631.m: Basel-Stadt has one seat in the Council of States.

62632.q: What is special about the administration of the city of Basel?
a: The cantonal authorities also run the city.
The city is run by the Confederation.
The city is run from Riehen.
62632.e: The municipality of Basel has no executive of its own; the cantonal government and the cantonal parliament (Grosser Rat) take on its tasks.
62632.m: In Basel the cantonal government also governs the city.

62633.q: Which two neighbouring countries does the canton of Basel-Stadt border?
62633.e: To the north and east the canton borders Baden-Württemberg, to the north-west French Alsace; the three countries meet at the border triangle on the Rhine.
62633.m: Basel-Stadt lies at the border triangle with Germany and France.

62634.q: Where does the name “Engadin” (Engadine) probably come from?
a: from the Romansh name of the Inn
from the Latin word for a narrow pass
from the name of a bishop
from the Celtic word for glacier
62634.e: The Inn is called “En” in Romansh; the name of the valley is usually derived from it.
62634.m: The Engadine is the valley of the Inn, En in Romansh.

62635.q: Where is the border between the Upper and Lower Engadine?
62635.e: The border is formed by the stream Ova da Punt Ota with the bridge of the same name between Cinuos-chel and Brail.
62635.m: The Lower Engadine begins at Punt Ota.

62636.q: In which Lower Engadine village is the picture book story of “Schellen-Ursli” (A Bell for Ursli) set?
62636.e: Selina Chönz and Alois Carigiet set their 1945 story in the village of Guarda with its typical Engadine houses.

62637.q: Which region has the Vereina Tunnel connected with the Lower Engadine since 1999?
62637.e: The Vereina line of the Rhaetian Railway runs from Klosters in the Prättigau to Sagliains in the Lower Engadine.
62637.m: The Vereina Tunnel connects the Prättigau with the Lower Engadine.

62638.q: What is special about Samedan airfield in the Upper Engadine?
62638.e: Samedan airfield lies at around 1,700 m, making it the highest airfield in Europe.
62638.m: Samedan has the highest airfield in Europe.

62639.q: Which is the largest of the Upper Engadine lakes by area?
62639.e: At about 4 km², Lake Sils is larger than Lake Silvaplana, Lake Champfèr and Lake St. Moritz.
62639.m: Lake Sils is the largest lake in the Upper Engadine.

62640.q: Which spring custom is celebrated in the Engadine on 1 March with bells?
62640.e: At Chalandamarz, children walk through the village with cowbells to drive away the winter.
62640.m: At Chalandamarz, Engadine children ring in the spring.

62641.q: Which technique is used to decorate the façades of many Engadine houses?
62641.e: In sgraffito, a light layer of lime is placed over darker plaster and then scratched away to create patterns.
62641.m: Engadine houses often have scratched sgraffito patterns.

62642.q: What causes the holes in Emmental cheese?
a: Carbon dioxide from propionic acid bacteria
62642.e: Propionic acid bacteria break down lactic acid and produce carbon dioxide. The gas collects to form the typical holes.
62642.m: The holes in Emmental cheese come from gas made by bacteria.

62643.q: Which traditional team sport, in which a “Nouss” is struck, is very popular in the Emmental?
62643.e: In Hornussen, a player hits the Nouss with a long flexible stick, and the opponents try to stop it with wooden boards.
62643.m: Hornussen is a typical sport in the Emmental.

62644.q: Which natural event of 1837 did Jeremias Gotthelf describe in a story of its own?
a: a flood of the river Emme
62644.e: In “Die Wassernot im Emmental” (The Flood in the Emmental), Gotthelf describes the devastating storm of August 1837.
62644.m: Gotthelf wrote about the flood in the Emmental.

62645.q: Which mountain rises to around 1,400 m on the border between the Emmental and the Entlebuch?
62645.e: The Napf is 1,408 m high and is the centre of a deeply cut hilly landscape.
62645.m: The Napf is the local mountain of the Emmental.

62646.q: What rock is most of the Napf upland made of?
62646.e: The Napf area is a large debris fan from the Molasse period; the cemented pebbles are called Nagelfluh.
62646.m: The Napf upland is mainly made of Nagelfluh.

62647.q: What are the typical ridges and narrow valleys in the Emmental called?
62647.e: Streams have cut deep into the soft Molasse rock; in between are narrow ridges, the Eggen, and tight valleys, the Gräben.
62647.m: The Emmental is a landscape of Eggen and Gräben.

62648.q: What is typical of the traditional Emmental farmhouse?
a: ground floor built of rubble stone
62648.e: The Emmental farmhouse combines living quarters, cowshed and barn under an enormous hipped or half-hipped roof that reaches far down.
62648.m: Emmental farmhouses have huge roofs that reach far down.

62649.q: Which doctor and politician from Nidau is considered the initiator of the Jura Water Correction?
62649.e: Johann Rudolf Schneider campaigned for decades to drain the Seeland, which suffered from floods.
62649.m: Johann Rudolf Schneider started the Jura Water Correction.

62650.q: Why has St Peter's Island no longer been a real island since the first Jura Water Correction?
a: It was filled up with earth.
62650.e: When Lake Biel was lowered by about two metres, a strip of land to Erlach appeared, the Heidenweg.
62650.m: The Heidenweg connects St Peter's Island with Erlach.

62651.q: Which town is the main town of the Seeland administrative district?
62651.e: The Seeland administrative district covers the rural part of the region; its seat is the small town of Aarberg.
62651.m: Aarberg is the main town of the Seeland administrative district.

62652.q: Which nickname is used for the Seeland with the Grosses Moos?
62652.e: A great many vegetables are grown on the drained marsh soils of the Grosses Moos.
62652.m: The Seeland is known as the vegetable garden of Switzerland.

62653.q: Why was a second Jura Water Correction needed between 1962 and 1973?
62653.e: After drainage, the peat soils of the Grosses Moos sank considerably, and floods happened again.
62653.m: The sinking of the peat soils made a second correction necessary.

62654.q: Which town is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland?
62654.e: In Biel/Bienne, German and French are used equally in everyday life and in the administration.
62654.m: Biel/Bienne is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

62655.q: Which philosopher lived on St Peter's Island in Lake Biel in 1765?
62655.e: Rousseau spent a few weeks on the island in 1765 and later described it as the happiest time of his life.
62655.m: Rousseau found refuge on St Peter's Island.

62656.q: Since which year have the prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, including in the Seeland, been a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
62656.e: The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps became World Heritage in 2011; several sites lie on the lakes of the Seeland.
62656.m: The pile dwellings have been UNESCO World Heritage since 2011.

62657.q: In which district of Upper Valais is Zermatt?
62657.e: Zermatt lies at the far end of the Matter Valley, a side valley of the Visp Valley, and belongs to the district of Visp.
62657.m: Zermatt belongs to the district of Visp.

62658.q: In which district of Upper Valais does the Rhône rise?
62658.e: The Rhône rises from the Rhône Glacier near Gletsch in the uppermost part of Goms.
62658.m: The Rhône begins in Goms at the Rhône Glacier.

62659.q: Which pass connects Brig with Domodossola in Italy?
62659.e: The Simplon road was built under Napoleon; the pass leads at 2,005 m from Upper Valais to Italy.
62659.m: The Simplon takes you from Brig to Domodossola.

62660.q: Which forest near the language border is considered one of the largest pine forests in the Alps?
62660.e: The Pfyn Forest between Leuk and Sierre lies in the border area between Upper and Lower Valais.
62660.m: The Pfyn Forest is a large pine forest in Valais.

62661.q: What status did Lower Valais have until 1798?
a: Subject territory of the Upper Valais Zenden
Part of the Duchy of Milan
Bailiwick of the canton of Bern
62661.e: After fighting with Savoy, the Zenden of upper Valais ruled Lower Valais from the late 15th century until the French invasion of 1798.
62661.m: Lower Valais was a subject territory until 1798.

62662.q: What were the seven territorial units of upper Valais called in the early modern period?
62662.e: The Republic of the Seven Zenden (Goms, Brig, Visp, Raron, Leuk, Sierre, Sion) was the centre of power of old Valais.
62662.m: Old Valais was divided into seven Zenden.

62663.q: Which pass connects Lower Valais with the Aosta Valley?
62663.e: The Great St Bernard leads from Martigny through the Val d'Entremont to Aosta; the famous hospice stands at the top of the pass.
62663.m: The Great St Bernard takes you from Lower Valais to Aosta.

62664.q: Near which town does the Rhône turn north in a striking bend?
62664.e: At Martigny, the Rhône turns from its westward course towards the north, heading for Lake Geneva.
62664.m: The Rhône makes its bend at Martigny.

62665.e: The Toggenburg is formed mainly by the valley of the Thur and the Neckertal.
62665.m: The Thur flows through the Toggenburg.

62666.q: Which place is considered the main town of the Toggenburg?
62666.e: Wattwil is the largest place and the centre of the valley. Wil already lies outside, in the Fürstenland.
62666.m: Wattwil is the main town of the Toggenburg.

62667.q: Which work did Ulrich Bräker from Wattwil write in the 18th century?
62667.e: Bräker (1735 to 1798) described his life as a small farmer and yarn trader; the book is an important autobiography from the lower classes.
62667.m: Ulrich Bräker told the story of the poor man of Toggenburg.

62668.q: Which mountain range forms the southern border of the Toggenburg and drops steeply to Lake Walen?
62668.e: The Churfirsten are the landmark of the Toggenburg; their south side plunges in steep cliffs to Lake Walen.
62668.m: The Churfirsten border the Toggenburg to the south.

62669.q: Which war broke out after the death of the last Count of Toggenburg in 1436?
62669.e: Count Frederick VII died in 1436 without a will; the dispute over his inheritance between Zurich and Schwyz led to the Old Zurich War.
62669.m: The death of the last Toggenburg count started the Old Zurich War.

62670.q: To whom was the Toggenburg sold in 1468?
62670.e: Petermann von Raron sold the Toggenburg to the Prince-Abbey of St Gallen for 14,500 guilders.
62670.m: From 1468 the Abbot of St Gallen ruled the Toggenburg.

62671.q: Which war of 1712 arose from a conflict over the Toggenburg?
62671.e: The dispute between the people of Toggenburg and the Abbot of St Gallen grew in 1712 into the Second War of Villmergen (Toggenburg War).
62671.m: The Toggenburg War of 1712 is also called the Second War of Villmergen.

62672.q: At 2,502 m, which mountain is the highest peak in the Toggenburg area?
62672.e: The Säntis in the Alpstein massif is 2,502 m high and clearly towers above the Churfirsten.
62672.m: The Säntis is the highest mountain by the Toggenburg.

62673.q: Which river flows through the Leventina?
62673.e: The Ticino rises in the Gotthard area and flows through the Leventina as far as Biasca.
62673.m: The Leventina is the valley of the Ticino.

62674.q: Between which places does the Leventina stretch?
62674.e: The valley reaches from the foot of the Gotthard Pass at Airolo to Biasca, where the Brenno flows in.
62674.m: The Leventina reaches from Airolo to Biasca.

62675.q: Which place is the main town of the Leventina?
62675.e: Faido is the main town of the Leventina district and was already the centre of the valley under the rule of Uri.
62675.m: Faido is the main town of the Leventina.

62676.q: Which canton ruled the Leventina as a subject territory until 1798?
62676.e: With its victory at the Battle of Giornico in 1478, Uri secured rule over the valley; it lasted until the end of the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1798.
62676.m: The Leventina was a subject territory of Uri until 1798.

62677.q: What happened in the Leventina in 1755?
a: the building of the Gotthard road
the founding of the canton of Ticino
62677.e: The Leventina uprising was directed against the rule of the bailiffs; it was bloodily put down, and three leaders were executed in Faido.
62677.m: In 1755 the Leventina uprising was bloodily put down.

62678.q: How does the old Gotthard railway overcome the steep steps in the Leventina?
62678.e: In the Piottino and Biaschina gorges, the railway gains height in circular spiral tunnels without the gradient becoming too steep.
62678.m: The Gotthard railway climbs through spiral tunnels in the Leventina.

62679.q: Near which place in the Leventina is the southern portal of the Gotthard Base Tunnel?
62679.e: The 57 km long Gotthard Base Tunnel runs from Erstfeld to Bodio.
62679.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel ends in the south at Bodio.

62680.q: What is special about the Trümmelbach Falls in the Lauterbrunnen Valley?
62680.e: The Trümmelbach Falls are glacier waterfalls that have cut into the rock and can be visited inside the mountain; they drain the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.
62680.m: The Trümmelbach Falls thunder inside the mountain.

62681.q: On which peak is the revolving restaurant “Piz Gloria”, known from a James Bond film?
62681.e: “On Her Majesty's Secret Service” was filmed on the 2,970 m high Schilthorn in 1969.
62681.m: The Piz Gloria restaurant is on the Schilthorn.

62682.q: Roughly how high are the Staubbach Falls near Lauterbrunnen?
62682.e: The Staubbach Falls drop around 297 m freely over a rock face into the Lauterbrunnen Valley.
62682.m: The Staubbach Falls are almost 300 m high.

62683.q: Which pyramid-shaped mountain on Lake Thun has a staircase with over 11,000 steps?
62683.e: The Niesen stairway beside the funicular has 11,674 steps and is considered the longest staircase in the world.
62683.m: The longest staircase in the world leads up the Niesen.

62684.q: Since when has the Jungfrau-Aletsch region been a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
62684.e: The Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch were added to the World Heritage List in 2001 as the first natural heritage site in the Alps.
62684.m: Jungfrau-Aletsch has been World Heritage since 2001.

62685.q: Where is the Ballenberg Open-Air Museum?
62685.e: The museum is in Hofstetten near Brienz and shows over 100 historic buildings from all over Switzerland.
62685.m: The Ballenberg Open-Air Museum is near Brienz.

62686.q: At which waterfall near Meiringen does Arthur Conan Doyle let Sherlock Holmes seemingly die?
62686.e: In the story “The Final Problem”, Holmes and Moriarty plunge into the depths at the Reichenbach Falls.
62686.m: Sherlock Holmes fought at the Reichenbach Falls near Meiringen.

62687.q: Which cattle breed is named worldwide after a valley in the Bernese Oberland?
62687.e: Simmental cattle come from the Simmental and are now bred all over the world.
62687.m: Simmental cattle come from the Bernese Oberland.

62688.q: On which lake is the Italian exclave of Campione d'Italia?
62688.e: Campione lies on the eastern shore of Lake Lugano and is completely surrounded by Swiss territory and the lake.
62688.m: Campione d'Italia is on Lake Lugano.

62689.q: Why did Campione not belong to the territory of what later became Switzerland in the Middle Ages?
a: It was owned by a Milanese monastery.
It belonged to the Diocese of Chur.
It was part of the Duchy of Savoy.
It was a free imperial city.
62689.e: Toto of Campione left the village in 777 to the monastery of Sant'Ambrogio in Milan, which owned it until 1797.
62689.m: Campione belonged to the Milanese monastery of Sant'Ambrogio for a long time.

62690.q: What changed for Campione d'Italia on 1 January 2020?
a: It joined the EU customs territory.
It became a province of its own.
62690.e: Until the end of 2019, Campione was in the Swiss economic area; since 2020 it has belonged to the EU customs territory.
62690.m: Since 2020 Campione has been in the EU customs territory.

62691.q: How large is the municipal area of Campione d'Italia including the lake surface?
62691.e: Campione covers about 2.6 km², of which only just under 1 km² is land and the rest is lake.
62691.m: At around 2.6 km², Campione is very small.

62692.q: What were the “Maestri campionesi” known for?
62692.e: From the 12th to the 14th century, stonemasons, sculptors and architects from Campione worked on churches all over northern Italy.
62692.m: The Maestri campionesi were famous master builders.

62693.q: Which Ticino municipality did Switzerland once offer, unsuccessfully, in exchange for Campione?
62693.e: Ticino tried to acquire Campione in 1800 and in 1814/15 and offered Indemini in return, which however stayed with Ticino.
62693.m: An exchange of Campione for Indemini never happened.

62694.q: Which Italian region does Campione d'Italia belong to?
62694.e: Campione belongs to the province of Como in Lombardy.
62694.m: Politically, Campione d'Italia is in Lombardy.

62695.q: Why do many tourists go shopping in Samnaun?
a: Many goods there are duty-free and cheaper
There is no VAT on rents there
People pay in euros instead of francs there
All shops there are also open at night
62695.e: Samnaun has been a customs-free zone since 1892. Goods such as perfume, alcohol, tobacco or fuel are therefore often cheaper than in the rest of the country.
62695.m: In Samnaun you can shop duty-free.

62696.q: For what reason was Samnaun originally excluded from the Swiss customs territory?
a: There was no road over Swiss territory.
Until then the valley belonged to Austria.
The municipality was too small for a customs office.
A treaty with Italy required it.
62696.e: Samnaun could only be reached via Tyrol, so goods arrived in the valley with duty paid and were expensive. The duty-free status first applied until a road was built and was later extended.
62696.m: Samnaun became duty-free because it could only be reached via Austria.

62697.q: From which valley in the Grisons can you reach Samnaun on Swiss roads?
62697.e: The Samnaun road branches off at Vinadi in the Lower Engadine. It is narrow, so many people drive via the Austrian side.
62697.m: From Switzerland you reach Samnaun via the Lower Engadine.

62698.q: Which dialect is spoken in Samnaun today?
62698.e: Samnaun is the only Swiss municipality in the Bavarian dialect area; people speak a southern Bavarian Tyrolean.

62699.q: Which language was spoken in Samnaun until the 19th century?
62699.e: In the 19th century, the population gradually switched from the Romansh idiom Vallader to German.
62699.m: Samnaun was once a Romansh village.

62700.q: With which Austrian resort does Samnaun form the Silvretta Arena ski area?
62700.e: The Silvretta Arena connects Samnaun across the national border with Ischgl in the Paznaun valley.
62700.m: Samnaun and Ischgl share a ski area.

62701.q: Which technical innovation was used for the first time in Samnaun?
62701.e: Samnaun ran the world's first aerial cable car with two floors in each cabin.
62701.m: The first double-decker cable car ran in Samnaun.

62702.q: What is forbidden in the Swiss National Park?
a: Staying overnight at the Hotel Il Fuorn
62702.e: The National Park is a strict nature reserve. Nature should develop without human interference, so hunting, logging and mowing are forbidden. Visitors may, however, hike on the paths.
62702.m: In the National Park, nature can develop without human interference.

62703.q: Which tree species dominates the forest in the Swiss National Park?
62703.e: Mountain pines and dwarf mountain pines make up around 90 per cent of the trees. About a third of the park is forested.
62703.m: Mountain pines are the main trees in the National Park.

62704.q: Roughly how old are the fossils of Monte San Giorgio?
62704.e: The layers are about 245 to 230 million years old. That makes them older than most dinosaur finds.
62704.m: The fossils of Monte San Giorgio are around 240 million years old.

62705.q: Between the arms of which lake is Monte San Giorgio?
62705.e: The mountain lies in southern Ticino between the two southern arms of Lake Lugano. The area is close to the border with Italy.
62705.m: Monte San Giorgio is on Lake Lugano.

62706.q: Which reptile from Monte San Giorgio is named after the canton of Ticino?
62706.e: Ticinosuchus was a land-living reptile related to crocodiles. The name contains the Latin Ticinum for Ticino.
62706.m: Ticinosuchus has the canton of Ticino in its name.

62707.q: Where does the name of the marine reptile Ceresiosaurus come from?
62707.e: In Italian, Lake Lugano is called Lago Ceresio. So Ceresiosaurus is named after the lake where it was found.
62707.m: Ceresiosaurus is named after Lago Ceresio.

62708.q: Which Ticino architect designed the fossil museum in Meride that opened in 2012?
62708.e: Mario Botta rebuilt and extended the museum. It shows originals and replicas of the finds.
62708.m: Mario Botta designed the fossil museum in Meride.

62709.q: Why are the fossils of Monte San Giorgio so exceptionally well preserved?
62709.e: At the bottom of the basin the water had little oxygen, so hardly any scavengers or bacteria broke down the bodies. That is why complete skeletons were often preserved.
62709.m: Low-oxygen water protected the animal remains from decay.

62710.q: What is the main aim of a UNESCO biosphere reserve such as the one in Entlebuch?
a: To protect nature and do business sustainably at the same time
To leave nature completely without people
To build as many hotels as possible
62710.e: In a biosphere reserve, people should live and work, for example in farming, forestry or tourism. At the same time, valuable habitats such as moors are protected.
62710.m: A biosphere combines nature protection and sustainable use.

62711.q: Which habitat is especially typical of the UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch?
62711.e: The Entlebuch has some of the largest and most numerous moorland landscapes in Switzerland. They are protected by national moorland protection.
62711.m: The Entlebuch Biosphere is rich in moorland landscapes.

62712.q: Which national label has the UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch also held since 2008?
62712.e: Since 2008, the Entlebuch has also been a regional nature park of national importance. It therefore carries both a national and an international label.
62712.m: Since 2008 the Entlebuch Biosphere has also been a regional nature park.

62713.q: Which mountain with extensive limestone pavements lies in the UNESCO Biosphere Entlebuch?
62713.e: The Schrattenfluh is made of limestone that rainwater has dissolved into karren (grooves). The Napf and the Rigi, by contrast, consist mostly of Nagelfluh.
62713.m: The Schrattenfluh in the Entlebuch is a karst landscape.

62714.q: In which year did Swiss voters accept the Rothenthurm initiative to protect moors?
62714.e: The initiative was accepted on 6 December 1987. Since then, moors of national importance have been protected in the Federal Constitution.
62714.m: The Rothenthurm initiative was accepted in 1987.

62716.q: Which building project in the Rothenthurm moor triggered the moorland protection initiative?
62716.e: The army wanted to build a training ground in the largest raised bog in Switzerland. Those affected then launched the initiative with the support of WWF.
62716.m: A planned army training ground led to the Rothenthurm initiative.

62717.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what is basically forbidden in moors of national importance?
a: New installations and changes to the ground
62717.e: Since the Rothenthurm initiative, no installations may be built and no changes to the ground made in protected moors. Gentle use is still possible.
62717.m: In protected moors, building is basically not allowed.

62718.q: Where does a true raised bog get its water from?
